SPECIMENS OF HENRY CHALK WEBB'S PATENT DIA- CHROMATISED WOOD, have been REMOVED from the Furniture Exhibition, AGRICULTURAL lIALL, to CANON. STREET HOTEL. As no written description can adequately convey to I svEsroßs the value and importance and wide adaptability of this re- markab.e invention, Mr. Webb, of Worcester. has decided, simultaneously with the issue of the Company's prospectus's, to exhibit specimens of the process and work:ng models by which the extraordinary results are produced. See Opinions of the Press. This ExhibiO ion will be open free to the public at the Cannon- street Hotel, from 11 in the morning uutil ti in the evening, from Wednesday, the 17th May, 1832, until further notice. The Share List is now open. Incorporated under the Joint Stock Companies Acts of 1862 to 1880, for the purchase of the English end foreign patents and Improvements of Mr. H. O. Weise. Registered as HENRY CHALK WEBB and COMPANY, Limited, of Worcester (as a going concern). Trade mark " Diak- romos." Capital £lOO,OOO, in 50.000 shares of £2 each. First issue, .C 59,000 in 29,500 shares of £2 each; 4,500 of which are taken by the vendor, in part payment of the purchase-money. The remaining 25,000 shares are offered to the public at par, payable-10s. on application, lOs on allotment, 10s. on the 19th August, 10s. on the 20th November, 1882. (Shareholders can pay up in lull if they desire, but no discount will be allowed). The calling up of the capital is definitely fixed, in order to save the expense of making calls in the future. DIRECTORS. Daniel Rowlinson Ratcliff, Esq., J.P , Managing Director of Milner's Safe Company, Limited, and of Arley Hall, War- wickshire, and 8, Lancaster Terrace, Regent's Park, Lon- don, W. Major-Gensral Henry Y. D. Scott, 0.8., F.R.S., Assoc. Inst. C. F., Silver dale, Sydenham, Kent. Arthur Wellington Peaty, Esq., of Messrs. Esdaile. and Co., City Saw Mills, London, N., and of Fairnihurst, Kingston Hill, Surrey. Joseph Williams Coznyns Carr, Esq. C.E., 85, Gracechurch Street, Lon- don, E. 0., and of Woodside Grange, Finchley, Middlesex. George Moffatt Rhys Layton, Esq., Managing Director Arlesey Brick and Lime Company, Limited, and of Sherwood, Roe- hamptora Vale, Surrey. John Wilesmith, Esq., of Messrs. T. and J. Wilesmith,. Timber Importers and Merchants, Bath Road, Worcester, and of Waverley House, Worcester. *Samuel Roberts, Esq' 49, Finsbury Pavement, London, E 0., and of Algernon Road, Brondesbury. Middlesex. *Henry Chalk Webb, Esq., of the Worcester Tileries Company, and of Shrub Hill House, Worcester (Managing Director); * 'These gentlemea will j. in the Board after allotment. BANKERS The London Joint Stock Bank, Princes-street, London, E.C. Worcester City and County Banking Company, Limited; Worcester, Birmingham, and other Branches. SOLICITOR—Thomas Cave, Esq., 37, Walbrook, London, Et C. BROKER—GePrge Ftederick Davenport, Esq,, 7, Drapers' Gardens, and London Stock Exchange. AUDITORS—Messrs. Tribe, Clarke and Co., •Moorgate-streets Buildings, London, E.C. ; also at Bristol, Cardiff, Swansea, and Newport. SECRETIRY—H. S. Cooke, Esq. REGISTERED OFFICES-49, Finsbury Pavement, London, E.C. ABRIDGED PROSPECTUS. This Company is formed for the purpose of acquiring, by' purchase, the works, stock, plant, and machinery, as a going concern, at Worcester, also the English and Foreign patent rights and improvements in a most valuable and extraordinary Invention, known as Diachromatised Wood. The invention consists of a simple method of producing colour patterns and designs, and decorations, in and upon wood, leather, cardboard. or other materials, and thereby accomplishing or obtaining in- stantaneously and inexpensively Works of Exquisite Art and Beauty, equal to hand painting or inlaying. ADAPTABILITY AND FUTURE PROSPECTS.—The extended ap- plication of this extraordinary invention renders it impossible at this early stage of the business to form any adequate idea as to the different and varied purposes to which it may be applied. It will prove a most beautiful and inexpensive decoration for the interior of cathedrals, churches, chapels. institutions, public halls, libraries, mansions, theatres, concert halls, state and ball rooms, hotels, clubs, cafés, snips' cabins of ocean and river steamers, saloons, Pulrnan ears, and is applicable to every species of decorative household furniture. COST or PRODUCTION.—The cost is one-fourth of the price now paid by the trade for productions in painting or inlaying (leaving a handsome margin of profit for the Company). RESEMI3LANCE.—(to Hand Painting and Inlaid Work).—The clear and artistic manner in which the process is executed "is so perfect," that even an experienced eye would be unable to detect any difference between hand painting or the finest speci- mens of inlaid work. USEFUL AND ARTISTIC.—For dados, and in the place of parquetry and other artistic work, for pianos, organs, harmo- niums, drawing-room cabinets, sideboards, wardrobes, tables, and panels of doors, tte application is unsurpassable. The most delicate lines of any subject are plainly and clearly main- tained. WEAR AND TEAR —Where durability and hard wear are necessary, as, for instance, aisles and entrances to churches and public buildings, and where decorative flooring is used, the design and colour can be substantially traced through the blocks, slabs, or other articles under treatment. The advan- tages claimed for these woods for pavements are as follows:- Ist. They are very beautiful in appearance, are guaranteed durable, and are moderate in price. 2nd. The pattern is indes- tructable. being deep into, or, if required, right through the sections. 3rd. If defaced by rough wear, the pattern can be restored by scraping with a steel scraper. 4th. The wood being used end grain (not plankwise, as under other systems of par- quetry) gives good foothold, with the best wears and is warm and noiseless. sth. For pavements, the sections can be fixed exactly as encaustic tiles are, viz., on concrete or boards—a bituminous compound, quite waterproof, being used for bedding the sections into, instead of Portland Cement. By this means, a perfectly dry floor can be scoured in damp situations. ORDERS AND CONTRACTS.—Contracts have been entered into for flooring two churches, and large and profitable orders are in hand for banks and buildings, and from leading furniture warehouses. MANAGEMENT.—The works at Worcester will be under the management of Mr. Henry Chalk Webb, who for many years has so successfully conducted the business of the Webls's Worcester Tileries Company, Limited. SALE OF FOREIGN PATEIsTS —The Directors will be prepared to negotiate for the sale of the Foreign Patents, those for France. Germany, and Belgium, have already been obtained, and arrangements are being made for America, and also to secure Patent rights for such other countries as ii ay be deemed desirable. Proposals are under consideration for the purchase of the whole of the Foreign Patents, the value of which has been estimated at a price which would leave the Company in possession of the English Patent free of cost. GRANTING LicEissEs.—The Directors believe that the grant- ing of Licenses throughout the kingdom for using the Machines will prove a distinct and important source oh revenue. BONUSES.—From the sale of the Company's Foreign Patent Rights, and the granting of Licenses, the Directors hope to declare Dividends and Bonuses at an early date. PRESENT WORKING.—Six Machines are now at work, capable of producing 200 yards of pavement per week, and the follow- ing is the approximate cost of production and rate of profit; the cost (including every incidental charge for producing 200 yards of the material) is £5O; Whclesale selling price, £9O. Leaving a profit on six machines (every week) of £4O. The directors propose erecting 60additional machines, which, In full operation, would, at the foregoing rate, yield a profit (per week) of £440, or (per annum) £22,880, or at the rate of over 30 per cent per annum on the capital of the company. This is exclusive of general purposes for which the patent and Invention are available, and indicates only a portion of the profit which may be realised. FREEDOM FROM SPECULATION.—This enterprise is compara- tively free from the elements of speculation; calculations of profits have been based on actual results, and the orders in hand far exceed the present powers of production. MEDALS. Special Medal, Sanitary Institute of Great Britain, 1880; Medal, Sanitary Exhibition, Eastbourne, 1881. TERMS OF CONTRACT.—The contracts affecting the company are as follows: One with H. C. Webb anti Co., Limited, and H. C. Webb, dated April 29th, 1882; one with H. C. Webb and EL Roberts, dated May Ist; one with B. Roberts and H. O. Webb and Co., Limited, dated May Ist, 1882, which can be seen at the offices of the solicitor to the company. The English and foreign patent rights and improvements of Mr. H. O. Webb In connection with his patents for diachromatised wood, to- gether-with the stock-in-trade, plant, and machinery at the works, Worcester, are sold to the company for the sum of £31.678 and 50 per cent. on future prices realised for the foreign, colonial, and continental patents, payable as follows: £22,678 in cash and £9,000 in fully paid shares of the company; this includes all charges and expenses for printing, advertising, and preliminary expenses incidental to and up to the date of allots to t, except brokerage, registration, legal and patent office fees; and the services of the patentee have been secured to the company for a period of three five, or eight years. Prospectus and Forms of Application for Shares may be ob- tained from the Bankers, Solicitor Auditors, the Secretary of the Company, or at the Cannon-street Hotel, London, during the Exhibition of Mr. 11. C. Webb's Patent Diachromatised Wood. AGENTS ABS. REQUIRED in every important town in the United Kingdom, to Lease, under Royalty, Webb's Patent (Diachromatised Wood) Machines.

div.p: COWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOLS.

DEAR Sir,—As Mayor, I have received many communica- tions concerniug the present posit ion of th above Schools, and in every instance these communications have been accompanied by expressions of deep and sincere regret, that the town is suffering from the loss of the educational benefits which this valuable Esta lishmen', when in operation, will secure. I most heartily sympathise with the efforts of the gentlemen who have in the past striven to raise the necessary funds to complete the Schools, and to launch them on their course of usefulness; I haue confidence in the liberality of my fellow- townsmen, and of others concerned in the prosperity of St. Helens; and believe that if the necessity for the Schools were fully understood, amall. means would speedily , be forthcoming to secure their -immediate completion. I may here very briefly allude to the scope of the operation of the Schools, to show the valuable work wh'cli would now be its vigorous actien were the buildings completed. They would provide accommodation for /50 boys and 100 girls. The curri- culum wculd embrace the subjects of a good and sound English. education, with Mathematics, Latin, French. and German, and also Chemistry and Natural Selence, thus fitting the scholars' for either Manufacturing, Commereial, or Scientific pursuits, or for entry into the Universities. The scheme also pr,..vides for Exhibition, both at these Schools, and also at Colleges or Uuiversities, to be awarded on the results of Examinations, to pupils in the various Elementary Schools of the town. These Exhibitions offer a reward to promising young persons of tal- ent in the Borough, the payment of whose fees would enable their parents to let them develope their abilities at these higher scholia, and they will also give a most valuable stimulus to the general working of the Elementary Schools. The Fees of the Schools run from a minimum of .24 to a maximum of AlB perannum, with an entrance fee not exceeding £l, and an additional yearly fee not exceeding £3, for special instruction in Chemistry or Natural Science. A perusal of Clauses 31, 32, 40, and 56, which relate to the re- ligious instruction to be given in the Schools, wiil show that such instruc ion is under the control of the Governors, on whose Board every important denomination In the town is represented, and in addition to this, that it is en- tirely optional with parents whether their children receive or do not receive religious teaching in the Schools; and that thus children of every religious belief may attend without fear of interference with their religious training or principles. I have entered thus fully into the scheme of the Schools for the purpose of showing the great work they might be performing in our midst, and the low rate at which this most invaluable service to the community would be secu'ed ; and it may here be remarked, that it is proposed to utilise the ad- vantages of the establishment iu imparting, by means of Night Classes, and the special Laboratory with which the Schools wilt be f urnished, chemical,scientific, and artistic technical knowledge to the artisan classes. The funds needed at the commencement of this month to complete and furnish the establishment were, In round numbers, £1,300. I purpose in the course of a few days' time cal ing a meettng of all persons taking an interest in the welfare and progress of ouri own, with a view to making • a strong and united effort to obtain this money. My object in sending you this letter is to place the claims ()Mills very im- portant edu-ational trust and its wants before you, so that you may give it the kind consideration wiich I feel it deserve,. and with a view to secure your valued aid in finishing this excellent work.—l am, dear sir, your faithful servant, RICHARD PILEINGTCN. Town Hall, St. Helens, 11th May, 1882.

THE POET'S EMPTY CHAIR. Prom the chair the children gave him, where he sat as on a throne, While they clustered round him fondly, claiming hi ni as all their own. He has gone, the poet stately, aurecled with snowy hair; If we looked, we could not find him in this wide world any- where. If we called, he would not answer—he so swift to smile and bless Every little child who sought him, with a gracious tenderness; Though we wept, he would not hear us: he has gone too far away, Ard the children's chair in Cambridge is a vacant throne to- day. Mut we'll hie to fair 3lcunt Auburn, hand in hand with April

days, There to wreath the children's garland, 'mid the green immor- tal bays; ehy arbutu., valley lillies. violets breaking into bloom. likarkling with the children's tear-drops, shall adorn the poet's tomb.

--- There he slumbers, oh, so deeply! all his earthly labours done, Never more a care to vex him, 'neath the ever circling sun; Of all sweet things said about him, this shall farthest fragrance send— That the poet, sage, and scholar was the children's loving friend. Like his Master, he would suffer tiny hands to pluck his gown; Fearlessly the small feet thronged him, unrebuked by word or frown; Surely he was met in heaven by a white robed shining band, Since before Our Father always do the children's angels stand.

A tart temper never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue Is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use. A lady who drew a gentleman's dressing-gown at a recent bazaar now wishes to draw a good-looking young man to pat in it. "Father," said an inquisitive boy, "what is meant by eolo relations ?" "Close relations, my coo," replied the father, "are relations who never give you a cent." Children are sent into the world to teach 113 how lovely . angels are; but when a man finds himself pasted to the seat et a chair by a piece of treacle toffee he never thinks of this. A little girl, when asked by her mother about suspicious bites in the sides of a dczem apples, answered, " Perhaps. mother, they have been frost bitten; it was so cold last Bight. "Is there any opening here for an intellectual writer ?" asked a seedy, red-nosed individusl of an editor. " Yes,my friend," replied the man of quills, "a considerate carpenter, foreseeing your visit, left an opening fur you. Tarn the knob on the right." A phrenologist, strolling through a churchyard, perceived a gravedigger tossing up the earth, among which were two or three skulls. The craniologist took one up, and after t,..coneidering it a little time, said, " Ah, this was the skull of a philosopher." "Very like, sir," said the gravedigger, for I do see it is somewhat cracked." In county Down, a conaryman whose old horse had soddenly died took the skin to a ta an er. The tanner said, In the scotch dialect peculiar to the district, "I canna gie you fall price for this skin; it's ower sale." The reply was," That's quare. The ant' horse wore it twenty years and mair, and niver made oily complent about it being ower

sale." Young George having iniportueed his father for a horse, the indulgent parent presented him with the ancient steed which had for years carried him. A few days afterwards the affectionate son interviewed leis father and renewed the request, saying, "Father, can't you give me a horse a little nearer my own age, that would be more of a companion for me ?"- There was, many years ago, a Lazy Man's Society organ- ised in a rural village. o,e of the articles required that no man belonging to the society should ever be in a hurry. 1. should he violate this article he must stand treat to the other members. Now it happened on a time that the doc- t r was driving post-baste through the street to visit a patient. The members of the society saw him, and chuckled over the idea of a treat; and on his return reminded him of his last driving and violation of the rules. "Not at all," said the doctor. "The truth is, my horse was determined to go, and I felt too lazy to atop him." They did not catch him that time. PROMOTED BY MISTARE.—It is not often, we imagine, that Mr. Pond made a mistake, but accidents will happen in the best regulated establishments. Some time ago, dufing one of his rounds through one of the many palatial hotels conducted by Soiers and Pond, Mr. Pond entered a room suddenly, and discovered a window-cleaner leisurely en- gaged reading a newspaper. Being very active himself, he had no use for a lazy manor a man who slights his work. Be discharged his cleaner on the spot, and told him to go to the office for his pay. The man obeyed, got his money, went to his room on the upper floor, arrayed himself in his Sanday suit, packed up his duds, and descended to the ser- vants' apartment, to take leave of his former associates. About this time Mr. Pond entered, but he did not recognise his quondam employe in his different clothes. "Here, my man, you look as though there was good work in yen; do you want a joa ?" - The ex,cleaner admitted that he stood in nerd of one. "Can you clean windows ?" The man allowed that he could. " Well," said Mr. Pond, "I've just discharged a man who has been doing that sort of work. I paved him a pound a week, but if you take his Place and go straight to werk I will pay you a guinea." The proposi- tion Was quickly accepted, and in half an hour the discharged -employe was cieaning away in the same old room. - EN3LISH PIGHEADEDNESS.—It is a notable 'circumstance, nevertheless, that, small as has been the effect as yet on the ~e totals of English trade, wherever one travels there are signs „X.. of almost frantic endeavours to supplant English manufac- a 'tures in every department, and oue hears constantly of the • success cf these efforta. That English trade is losing its position of undis- puted supremacy in the world is apparentlir true, and it is equally true that English manufacturers are wilfully blind _ to the true causes thereof. THE DAYS BEFORE RAILINTAYS.—It would be an inter- esting subject of etudy, the effects of modes of travelling upon national nainncr3 and habits. In the religious world, in the present day, ministers and others, when announcing a sermon or a lecture, or a public meeting, are careful to lay "God willing," or "DV.," in order to indiCate their cociinvi dependence upa ri ovine Providonta, The. ;anie devout "eeaille'On Wei Used by the oner qt ttilge coaches gn the times of our forefathers, They were advertised to start, "God willing," and as seemed good, or at "about" a certain time. The coach was said to have &rept at certain places night after tight on the way, and towards the end of the journey "the coach was shaved," which operation was sometimes performed by a woman. The want of proper roads, while it made some things, such as farming produce, excessively cheap, made other things excessively dear. Lon. eon was mostly supplied by sea; but the price of goods conveyed inland from London was enormous; the carriage to Birmingham being from £5 to £7 a ton, and from London to Exeter, £l2. It is needless to remark what facilities the state of things afforded for highway robbery, wnich was then rather a flourishing occupation. The state of the popu- lation in winter, so far as their relations with the outer world were concerned, resembled that of a blockaded city, or an American 'village snowed tip. They laid in a stock of pro- visions and goods of all sorts for that dreary season, during which the men, wher• they could not work, pealed the whole of the time in athletic sports, drinking, or gambling, and the women in sitting round the lance blazing fire on the hearth- stone, by the light of which they went on with their spin- ning and sewing, as windows were then a rare luxury, and Candles were neither good nor cheap. When the season opened, the chapmen cauie in gangs, for mutual protection, upon their packhorses, in order to supply the various country towns with goods. No one travelled through the ry except from necessity, and England was an nn- kconuonwtnland to Most of its inhabitants. The news of public events travelled very slowly. The death of Queen Elizabeth was not known in Devon tiil the days of court mourning p were ended. The chief meene of intercomee were in the fairs which were great teetive ccAhioni, on which the - Population turned eut aed enjoyed a holiday. Acts of Parliament, however, Wet,: passed for the construction of geod turnpike roaos around London, which gavean immense advantage to the farmers and market gardeners who sup- plied the metropolis with provieions, and constituted a mo- nopoly which, of course, they were very ansions to retain unimpaired. Accordingly, they vehetnently protested against the extension of the turnpike roads into the country. But at last common sense prevailed, anl in the course of time enginee-s and practical scientific men did not .thinkit beneath their dignity to bestow their attention upon rid- making. One of the most remarkable and interesttng of the memoirs which Mr. bmiies h.is given us in his valuable work, "The Lives of the Engieeere," is that of John Met - cliffs, a blind man, coremenly known as " Biind Jack of Euareshoroagh," tha conerructor of nearly 200 miles of capital roads. It is a eingulae thing that a blind man should have been the pioneer of social progress, ae the first great profssitionel road meter in England.—Gassell's Histo;y of England.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. It is stated that in compiling the forthcoming American census the wheat statistics were collected by the Department of Agriculture, and those of flour by the Department of Manufactures. On comparing results, it was found that there were 55,000,000 lbs. more of flour manufactured than there were of wheat grown. The public is indebted to the Washington correspondent of the Baltimore San for the de- tection of this error in official statieties. A Usernn INTENTION.—A letter from Rome annonncee that a priest of Ravenna, named Ravaglia, has constructed an electrical apparatus, which can be set in operation by simply pressing a button, and by which the doors of a large building can be instantaneously opened. The apparatus was tried during the last week of April at the Alighieri Theatre, in Ravenna, with the most satisfactory result. All the nine doors Opened simultaneously, as if through some spiritual agency. The inventor hopes to improve his ap- paratus, so that should a fire break out on the stage of a theatre the rise in temperature would itself set the machinery in motion. A REMEDY FOR BURNS AND SCALDS.—A writer in the Popular Science Monthly states he has discovered that a saturated solution of bicarbonate of soda in either plain or camphorated water is most effectual in immediately re- lieving the acute burning pain. For this purpose all that is necessary is to cut a piece of lint, or old soft rag, or even thick blotting paper, of a size sufficient to cover the burned or scalded parts, and to keep it constantly well wetted with the sodiac lotion, so as to prevent its drying. By this means it usuallr happens that all pain ceases in from a quarter to half an flour, or even in much less time. When the main part of a limb, such as the hand and fore-arm, or the foot and leg, has been burned, it is best, when practicable, to plunge the part at once into a jug or pail, or other con- venient vessel, filled with the soda lotion, and keep it there until the pain subsides; or the li nb may be swathed or or encircled with a surgeon's cotton bandage previously soaked in the saturated solution, and kept constantly wetted with it, the relief being usually immediate, provided the solution be saturated and cold. A LIFE'S WORE.—A correspondent writes: With the commencement of April last, Mr. George Fawcett, or, as he is popularly termed, George Pest," completed his 47th year of service in the Post-office as a rural messenger. A ' statement of the distance thus travelled by a public servant of so old a standing may not prove uninteresting. For five years, 1835 to 1840, he rode between Sedliergh and Kendal daily with the mails, thus traversing 40,150 miles; for one year, 1840.1, he rode between Sedbergh and Hawes, a total of 146,000 miles • for one year, 1841.2, he rode between Kendal and Dent, 12,410 miles; and from 1842 to 1882 he has walked daily between Sedbergh and Dent, in a 11175,200 miles. The total distance thus amounts to 242,360 miles. To obtain a better conception of these figures, we may call it a distance of about 10 times the circumference of the I world, nearly 80 times the dictates from England to America, and 2,360 miles farther than from the earth to the moon! During his 47 years be will have sorted, carried, and delivered some 7,060,000 or 8,000,000 letters, exclusive of newspapers, Sm.— Westmorland Gir:ette. AN ELECTRICAL CONTROVERSY.—Fr:ction is not abso- lutely essential for the production of the disturbed molecular state recognised as electrical activity. In certain circum- stances the mere contact of bodies, without the slightest rubbing of their surfaces together, is capable of producing the same condition. This is the great discovery which was made by the Italian anatomist, Galvani, in 1791, from the mere accident of having burg some dead frogs on an iron balcony by means of capper hooks. The limbs of the sus- pended frogs were observed to be thrown into convulsive twitchings whenever they came into contact with the iron of the balcony. Galvani at once perceived that these move- ments must be due to electrical instrumentality, but in the , first instance he thought that the electricity was an outflow from the muscles and nerves of the dead animals, and that the iron and copper were in no way conducive to the result. Professor Velte. of Como, who shortly afterwards repeated the experiments of Galvani, was of a different opinion, and in the end proved thilt the muscles and nerves of the frogs i were mere passive elements in the process, and that all the essential effects of the electrical disturbance could be pro- duced by merely laying a! small plate of zinc upon a similar' plate of copper, with a -piece of moistened paper between, and that the electrical action was the consequence of the contact of the surfaces of copper and zinc with the moisture lurking in the pores of the paper. For some time each of these celebrated men energetically advocated the view which he had adopted, and a kind of controversy was in this way established ; but in the end the names of both controversial- ists came to be honourably connected with the new kind of electrical action which had been discovered, so that it is now spoken of indifferently either as galvanic or as voltaic electricity.--Shience for All. PHOTO•CHROMY ON PORCELAIN.—ThiS invention of M. Grermeuil Bonnaud is calculated to effect great changes in an important branch of Industry. It is a process for pro- ducing on porcelain, by means of photography, portraits and pictures in natural tints and colours, and is applicable to vases, plates, tiles, caskets, and indeed everything of the nature of china which has hitherto been found sus- ceptible of artistic decoration. The perfection in which this kind of decoration may bfe obtained by the new process is something to marvel at, the most expert connoisseurs being deceived as to the method of its production. This perfection is due to the fact that in certain particulars it is somewhat similar to hand-painting on china. A number of inventions have during the last few years seen the light, having for their object the mechanical decoration of porce- lain, and some have even made use of the resources of pho- tography. These methods of decoration, have not, how- ever, comprehended any variety of tints and colours in nature, and, besides this, they have not assured any per- manence, as when the decoration was applied, it was simply covered with a glaze, which was easily injured, and which afforded no adequate protection for the decoration itself. M. Bonnand's process, on the other hand, obtains pictures in colours, and in a high degree of artistic beauty, which being burnt in, like in ordinary painted china, are absorbed Into the material itself, and cannot be effaced by any for- tuitous damage. At the late Paris Exhibition. Mesters. ' Brown and Meaethead exhibited sixteen vases, treated in the Limoges style, which were sold for £3OO, and which had been sixteen times in the kiln. At the earns Exhibi- tion it was as nothing to see plates priced at £4O and up- wards. Now, it is no exazgeration to say that effects quite as pleasing can be obtained by M. Germeuil Bonnand's pro- cess at a fraction of the prices we have quotes, and for the reasons that he has substituted s mechanical process for hand-painting, and one 83 nicely suited to the exigencies of the porcelain that it requires, when laid on, but one baking to render it, not merely a surfocc ornamentation, but as much an integral and indelible portion of the porcelain as hand-painting iteelf would be. In some respects the pro- ducts of the new procees are even superior to those turned out by hand, as, photography Meg a prime element in its ,evoritiog, the range of possible eubjecte iS elide more cora- prehensive, and their truthful rcprodacCon more reliable. i Tem FORMATION OF COAL.—AII attempts to explain satisfactorily the formation of coal have thus far proved unsuccessful, though it is generally understool that it is the product of the decomposition of vegetable matter. Just how that decomposition has been brought about chemically is a matter which cherniets have not as yet been elle to solve. The principal difficulty has been that it has been impossible to obtain a clear insight into the chemical con- stitution of coal. It has been thought hitherto, and this is still the popular belief, that coal is in the main pure carbon, mixed with varying quantities of bitaminoue substances. It has been generally believed that, as the product of the diet!llation of coal is principally carben, it woei e sae to conclude that free carbon actually does exist in coal. The fact that sugar, starch, ttc., under similar circumstances - leave a residum consisting of carbon has never been con- sidered a proof that that element existed in these bodies in a free state. It is well-known that coals whit'et may the same percentage of carbon, hedree- " een, d not by any means, in cooking, - an oxygen, do ( distillation and we have • cid the same products of a behavi complete analogy for this in the ont , celltilOie and etarrh when subjected to distilla- tion: Evidence pointa to the conclusion that coal is a mixture of many and complex compounds; and the dif- ficulty, amounting almost to an impossibiity of separating these compounds hiss much to do in rendering a chemical solution of the questions involved in the formation of coal a ' very arduous task. The production of coal by artificial means is twat by great obstacles, among which the absence of all kteawledge concerning tho conditions under which that process actually took place is the principal one. The question whether the vegetable matter to which our coal veins owe their origin was amassed by driftine, or was carbonised in situ, has been much debated, and there has been much discussion on the point whether it was obtained from water or from land plants. Dr. Muck, of Bochum, in a recent work to which we shall refer at greater length in the future, takes up the theory that alghe have mainly con- tributed to the formation of coal. It is urged that the re- mains of marine plants are rarely found in coal veins, and that shells, Sec., are not often met with. Dr. Muck calls attention to the fact that marine plants decompose early and completely, losing their form entirely; and that the disappearance of the calcereons remains of mollusks is readily explained by the formation of large quantities of carbonic acid gas during the process of carbonisation. In accepting the marine origin of coal, it is not necessary to resort to the assumption of immense pressure and high temperature to explain decomposition and the total des- truction of the structure of the original substance. Dr. Muck combats Fremy's bog theory at length. His views are well supported by recent investigations made by Herr P. F. Reinscb, who has examined 1,200 sections of coal, coming to the conclusion that that mineral substance has not been formed by the alteration of accumulated land. plants. Herr ReinEch claims to have discovered that coal consists of microscopical organic forms of a lower order of protoplasm; and though he carefully examined the cells and other remains of plants of a higher order, he computed that they have contributed only a faction of the matter of ttie coal-veins, however numerous they may be in some instances.—Scientific American.

The clergyman seemed struck with a fresh thought, and replied quickly, "We don't read of any." But madam'inade herself even with him when she rejoined with quite as much quickness," Well, we read of only one such man, and from the fuss that's made about him, it's plain they're scarce." •

In a month, then, after the re- jection of this petition, the general committee of the Catho- lics, after passing a vote of thanks to the worthy old John Keogh for "his long and faithful services to the cause of Catholic Emancipation," isseed an address to all the Cetho- lies of Ireland, urging upon them a new and more combined form of political action, and bearing the signature of "Daniel O'Connell, Chairman." We 'nave already seen that the cry for Repeal had been raised in Dublin, and there can be no doubt that the Repeal of the Union was dearer to O'Connell's heart than Emanci- pation. But the latter was more practicable than the former. O'Connell saw that it* was so, and devoted himself to it accordingly. Emancipation once achieved, he might begin to look for Repeal. For the present he contented himself in grappling with what we have no doubt he con- sidered a minor question, and yet most assuredly a grand and noble one—" Catholic Emancipation." The greatest of O'Connell's early triumphs was on the Veto Question. This question was first mooted in 1799, when Mr. Pitt and Lord Castlereagh were intriguing for support to the Union. "During that year ten of the Irish Bishops constituting the Board of Maynooth College hap- I pened to be convened in Dublin on the arrangement of some ecclesiastical business, when Lord Castlereagh, the then Secretary for Ireland, availed himself of their presence, and submitted for their adoption two vitally momentous measures originating from the British Ministry. By the first of these it was proposed that his Majesty should be I invested with the power of a veto in all future ecclesiastical promotions within this kingdom • and agreeably to the second, the Catholic clergy of Ireland were to receive a pen- sion out of the Treasury; at the same time assurances were solemnly pledged by Government that, on the acquiescence of the Irish hierarchy in these State measures, the fate of that great national question, Catholic Emancipation, entirely depended. Thus beset by the proffers of the Minister on the one band, and by the alarming posture of the country on the other, the Bishops already alluded to agreed 'That in the appointment of Roman Catholic prelates to the vacant sees within the kingdom such interference of Government as may enable it to be satisfied of the loyalty of the person appointed, is just, and ought to be agreed to.' This state- ment was accompanied with an admission 'That a provision through Government for the Roman Catholic clergy of this kingdom, competent and secured, ought to be thankfully accepted.'" (Brenan's Ecclesiastical History of Ireland.) This transaction remained a secret for several years. It was not until 1810 that the eesolutions of the clerical trustees of Maynooth College came to light. When the real nature of the proposals was explained and fully known, there was no little stir about it. The controversy both in England and in Ireland was immense and lasted for many years. The advocates of the Veto were many and powerful. Grattan and Ponsonby supported it. The Irish aristocracy gave it their countenance. The English Catholics, in their petitions for relief, offered to accept Emancipation on such terms. Even Rome seemed to be in favour of it. A letter in the name of the Pope written by one Quarantotta whom ono of the papers called "an underetrapper of the Propaganda." was freely circulated, in which the Pope was made to cons,- eel the Irish Catholics to give in their adhesion to the measure. But under the potent influence of O'Connell a resolute spirit of resistance manifested itself in the whole Catholic population against any order or recommendation coming even from Rome itself tending to enchain the
POLITicAL ITEMS.

Mr. John Holms, M.P., will succeed the Hon. Evelyn Ashley as Secretary of the Board of Trade. We (Daily News) understand there is no chance of the Rivers Conservancy Bill being further proceeded with dar- ing the present session.
-Mr. George Otto Trevelyan, the new Chief Secretary for Ireland, was on Wednesday re-elected for the Border without opposition, Mr. Trevelyan was not present at the nomination.

Mr. Labouchere intends on an early day to ballot for another opportunity of moving his resolution, whith declares that the House of Lords is obstructive, dangerous, and ought to be removed. • A Bristol paper publishes a report that the Attorney- General, Sir Henry James will stand in the Liberal interest for Bristol at the next general election, in the place of Mr. Samuel Morley, who, it is understood, will not seek re- election.

It is intended at an early day to hold a meeting of the leaders of the Land League movement in Paris, in order to discuss the existing position of affairs. Mr. Davitt has left for the French capital to consult Mr. Egan, and it is antici- pated that Mr. Dillon and probably some other Irish mem- bers will follow bin% Mr. Bradlaugh attended on Tueseay afternoon in the House of Commons under the Peers' Gallery. It is stated that upon an early day he may again take some decided measure for asserting his rights as a duly elected member, possibly by presenting himself once enore at the.table of the House, even if such action should again void the seat. A meeting of Radicals was held on Sunday on Clerken- •well Green, Mr. Daniel Smith presiding. A resolution was passed declairing that the continued application of coercive measures in Ireland was not calculated to bring peace and happiness to that country, and calling for the cessatien of coercion, and the initiation of a policy of justice. The Daily News says that Sir Wilfrid Lawson intends to call the attention of the House of Commons to the unsatis- factory nature of the Government's proceedings with refer- ence to the proposed visit of Cetywayo to this country, and to move that in the opinion of the House the continued im- prisonment of Cetywayo is not only opposed to international usage, but is also inexpedient and unjust. A meeting of members will shortly be held to consider Sir W. Lawson's motion. It having been stated that the Duke of Argyll was going to join the Conservative party next session, his grace has been communicated with as to the veracity of the statement. The Duke replies :—" I can only say that I adhere to the principles which I consider to be Liberal, and that I desire to be free from all ties which would hamper me in the as- sertion of them, whether by one Minister or another." The National Agricultural Labourers' Union have received the following letters in reference to an intended meeting on the extension of the county franchise :—Mr. Gladstone's secretary says: " The Premier regrets that he is unable to add to his recent speech on Mr. Arnold's resolution." Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan, M.P., writes "that he shall he very glad when the Government is able to bring in the Franchise Bill; it will then become a question of days." Mr. W. H. Smith says: "No one is more anxious to improve the material and social position of the labourer, but I cannot concur in Mr. Arch's line of action.

National Church. Almost every element of power seemed to be against him. But over all O'Connell triumphed. How dare," exclaimed our hero indignantly, at one of the meetings, " How dare Qaarantotti dictate to the people of Ireland? We disclaim his authority to interfere in making us accept of an Act of Parliament. He desires us to be grateful for it. How dare he talk of gratitude to US? By his orders we are to accept it as beggars—like aliens with our hats in our hands and a submissive bend of the body! Never will we obey such orders; we will as much allow his right to interfere with the Act of Parliament as we will allow the King or the King's Ministers to interfere with the appointment of the prelates of the Catholic religion in Ire- land." At the same meeting he also made this bold and enaphatie declaration ;—" I would as soon receive my politics from Conetantinople as from Home. For the head of my Church I have the highest respect, but in the present case I put theology—of which I know nothing and desire to know nothing—out of my consideration wholly. It is on the ground of its danger to civil liberty that I objected to the late Bill. It would have the effect, if passed into law, of placing in the hands of the Minister a new and ex- tensive source of patronage; and for that reason I would rather the Catholics should remain for ever without Emanci- pation than that they should receive it upon such terms." On another occaston O'Connell was opposed by Stephen Woulfe, a man who, after distinguishing himself both at the lay Cellege of Maynooth, and in Trinity Cellege, was now one of the most promising of the Catholic lawyers—indeed, one of the most intellectual men, Catholic or Protestant, to be found at the Irish Bar. At a great public meeting held in Limerick to pronounce against the Veto, Woulfe at- tempted to address the meeting, but as he was known to differ in opinion from O'Connell, Woulfe was unable to ob- tain a hearing. O'Connell came forward and asked as a favour to himself that the learned gentleman might be allowed to speak. This silenced the tumult, and Woulfe delivered a carefully prepared and most powerful speech on the subject in favour of yielding to the Government. When he ceased O'Connell arose to reply. "I am not going to make a speech treday," he said, in his sweet but impres- sive voice, "you have had a fine speech from a gentleman who has just sat down. I will tell you a story: Once upon a time a flock of sheep were living peaceably together under the care of their watchdogs, when an attempt was made to get rid of the dogs. And who made the attempt? It was the wolves. A meeting of the sheep took place. Then the learned wolf came forward, and tried to persuade the inno- cent sheep to give up their dogs. They followed the advice, and mark the consequences. They were quickly devoured, and so would the Catholics of Ireland if they acted in the same manner as the sheep and followed the advice of Woulfe." The meeting at once saw the drift of the story, and cheered O'Connell to the echo. It is needless to say the Vetoists were thoroughly beaten, and Woulfe turning to a friendly Dean, said, "How useless it is to compete with O'Connell. Here have I been elaborating a speech for a month, and O'Connell demolishes me by a flash of humour and a pun on my name." The project of enslaving the Irish Church to the English Protestant State was at last defeated, and this may be re- garded as the greatest of O'Connell's early triamphs. Had the proposed compromise been made, the policy he had laid out for himself would have been completely frustrated. A public spirit would not have been formed among the Catho- lics by a protracted struggle. Emancipation would have been a boon which was conceded, not a triumph which was won, and the Episcopacy in a measure would have depended on the Crown.

A terrible accident happened on Saturday at the Blomfield Ironworks, Fipton, the property of Messrs. Barrow, one of the largest boilers in the yard exploding. Brickmaking by machinery is largely carried on at the works. About 30 men and boys are employed on the establishment, and the majority of these were at work at the time the accident occurred. The portion of the works lying between the engine-houses at the top and the offices at the entrance to the brickyard was reduced to a mass of ruins. The works were established in 1806, and have since grown to immense preportiona. The exploded boiler was comparatively a new one, made of the best Staffordshire plates. The tubular end was blown clean out, and flew to the upper portion of the ' works, while the great bulk of. the boiler was carried in a straight line through theidrying sheds and past the offices. A girl named Perry and her brother and a collier named Clifton were killed. Jibson (the engineer) could give no explanation of the accident, although he was on duty all night, The young man Perry was filling a barrow at the time of the explosion. He was horribly mangled when found among the ruins., John Coleye,was cut badly about the head, and John Randall and John /Varnall were scalded. The injuries inflicted on the girl Perry were so ghastly that the body had to be covered over. The death of Clifton was caused by a brick, which was carried a considerable distance. He has left a wife and six children. Several persons engaged at the works had wonderful escapes. The works were insured against tire, but not against other destructive causes. Thedamage to the buildings is estimated at. £6OO. Mr. Hopper, the South Staffordshire coroner, opened the inquest on Monday. The jury having viewed the (oodles, two of which presented a shocking appearance, the inquiry was adjourned to await the report of the Government inspectors as to the Cause of the explosion. Tiie-yoting woman who was killed was to have been married on Sunday. The injured persons aro recovering satisfac- torily.

div.head: LITERATURE.
div.p: LITERATURE.

• We have to acknowledge the usual parcel of serials from Messrs. Cassell, Petter, Galpin and Co. In Cassell's Magazine for this month the little understood duties and responsibilities of the newspaper sub-editor are explaine4 to the general reader by a gentleman intimately connected with the pro- fession, and a specimen of flimsy "is engraved in fac-simile for the inspection of the uninitiated. This article is well written, and is certainly instructive. A lady correspondent, who has recently been on a tour through the United States for the purpose of inquiring into the subject, records the re- sult of her observations on " The business girls of America." The correspondent arrives at the conclusion that the "condi- tion of the baeiness girls in America is no better than at home, nor are their ultimate prospects brighter," and there are few if any who know anything about the matter who will not be found to endorse the same opinion. The other contributions to the magazine are of the customary attrac- tive class.—ln the Quiver " Whither. Drifting" is the sug- gestive title of a new serial story from the pen of the popular authoress, Mrs. Louisa Crow, the first chapters of which ap- pear in the May part, and awaken a lively interest in what is to follow. ' The story seems to be full of striking incident, and inculcates the blessedness of large-hearted Christian charity. " One of his little ones" is a touching story, it will be continued through several numbers, and will be illus- trated with full page and other engravings.—Little Folks is this month an excellent part, and its contents are admirably adapted for its readers. The puzzle pages are exceptionally good, and so are the jottings and pencillings here, there, and everywhere by the.editor. It is a pleasure to nets the success of the " Little Folks" Humane Society, which promises to grow with such proportions as will before long extend its influence throughout the kingdom. Already, though scarcely three months have elapsed since its formation, nearly 7,000 children have joined the ranks of the society, while the nuns- her of names received daily increases rather than diminishes. The movement has now spread to the schools, from one of which over 100 names arrived in a single day, with promise of more. In connection with this society prizes are offered monthly for essays, poems, dze., on the subject of kindness to animals, and the May part of the periodieal contains several of these prize compositions, which will be of special interest to children—Familiar Garden Flowers has reached its 39th part, in which two faithful illestrations are given of the " cineraria " and " pontic azalia," both of which are des- cribed.—Old and New Edinburgh and The Popular Educator have each reached the 18th part, and their excellence is still maintained.

Messrs. Wand. Lock, ik Co. (Warwick House, Salisbury Square, E.C.,) have forwarded their monthly complement of serial literature. Amateur IP ork seems destined to grow in public favour. With the May part -is presented a supple- ment containing working drawings of a fan in fret work, which would form an ornamental screen for the fire-grate in summer, and a fire-guard in winter, together with eight designs illustrating and suggesting embellishments for the fire place in summer. The contents comprise articles, all of them carefully written, on "French polishing and spirit varnishing," "Violin making," Elects° plating," " Gymnas- tic apparatus, and how to make it," Wood carving," "Bookbinding," and a variety of other subjects of no less importance. Each is profusely illustrated, and the informa- tion given is so complete that the veriest novice may learn. One of the best contributions in the present part is that by Mr. A. W. Roberts, on the utilisation of old tin cans, the uses to which they may be applied being manifold.—The illustrated History of the World has now reached part 7, and brings the reader as far as the third Punic war; while Rollin's-Ancient History, of which seven parts have also been issued, carries the student as far as the history of Alexan- der's successors. In the Epochs and Episodes of History, is given a concise history of the great Reform Bill of 1832, which is of special interest at the present moment in view of another similar measure; and the other contributions are scarcely less important, while they are equally well written. The remaining publications by this firm are too numerous to particularise, suffice it to say that each, in its particular sphere, is of a high-class character, and that collectively they are a powerful aid to education. SACRED SONGS AND SOLOS, Nos 1 and 2 combined, com- piled and sun..' by Ira D. Sankey (London: Morgan and Scott, office of The Christian, 12, Paternoster Buildings, London, EC.).—This volume, a copy of which is before us, comprises 441 sacred pieces with music. The popularity of the hymns and tunes are undisputed, and some of them, such as " Hold the Fort," and " Safe in the Arms of Jesus," seem to be known by everybody. Many of these sacred songs, which are al ways associated with Messrs. Moody and Sankey, had an existence prior to the commencement by these gentle- men of their evangelistic work in the year 1873, though it was Mr. Sankey's remarkably effective rendering of them, and the striking manner in which be succeeded in empha- sizing the Christian truths they embodied that caused the selection to spring into so universal notice and favour. Amongst the recent additions to the "Songs and Solos," the new and old editions of which are now published in this form for the first time, are many which are likely to prove highly acceptable. Of these may be named—" Waiting at the Door," which has an effective chorus; " Must I go— and empty handed? " written in connection with the death of one who was summoned hence very shortly after conver- sion ; "Ye must be Born Again," a good gospel hymn; "Pease! Be Still !" ; and " Will Jesus Find us Watching?" The greater number of the hymns have stirring choruses, in , which congregations can readily join, and which greatly add to the effectiveness of the pieces. We feel confident that Messrs. Morgan and Scott's publication, on whom the work reflects credit, will serve to make the hymns more popular than ever, if that be possible. There has been forwarded to us a copy of ROMEO AND JULIET (London : Bickers and Son, 1, Leicester-square), as arranged for the stage by Mr. Henry Irving, and presented at the Lyceum Theatre. In a preface Mr. Irving states that he has availed himself of every resource at his command to illustrate without intrusion the Ital'ian warmth, life, and romance of this enthralling love story, a task which has beel judiciously performed ; and among the restorations is to be found that of Romeo's unrequited love for Re-saline, . omitted amongst other things in Garrick's Georgian version. This will tend -to make the performance of the , tragedy more acceptable to the public than it has hitherto I been. The fact that it has bad such a long run at -the Lyceum is, we take it, an evidence of Mr. living's success lin his work. To those engaged in the histrionic art this I new arrangement of the play may be studied with profit. The cast of the tragedy is, it may be added, given. I THE RAPID SHORTHAND WRITER (London: William 'Dawson and Sons, 121, Cannon-street).—This is an interest- ', ine little work by Francis John Lock, proprietor of the !Leicester School of Shorthand, in which meny useful hints I are given not only for learners but experleaced writers of shorthand. The chapter devoted to reporting has evidently been written by one who is well acquainted with the duties , of a reporter ; and the "Reminiscences of2a young phono- grapher " is good reading. The A B C Or FREE TRADE (London: Cassell, Potter, Galpia and Co.)—This is an address delivered by E. N. I Buxton to the West Ham Liberal Association on March Orb I last, and published for the Cobden Club. 'rho principles of free, as opposed to fair trade, are clearly placed before the readers, and the illustrations are so conclusive that they roust careSe conviction with them as to the soundness of free I trade principles. We have confidence in commending the little work to all interested in this important Tiestion. A copy of LONGFELLOW'S POEMS (Messrs. Wiird, Lock and Co.) is before us. It is another of the sixpenny editions of popular antlers now becoming so plentiful, and is ' uniform in size and make-up with the other cheap editions -published by the same firm. The illustrations by Major Seacornbe are excellent, and so also is the letterpress. Of the poems themselves it is unnecessary to speak here. They are the productions of the best of American poets, and afford 'unbounded pleasure and delight to all who peruse and study them.

Tun CHAMPION or THE FAITH is the title of a new venture published by Messrs. Wade and udgate Arcade, London, E.C., and edited by the Co.,Rev. James McCann, D.D., F.G.S. The contents of its pages, eight in number, are characterised by much ability, and at a time when there is so much scepticism and infidelity abroad "The Champion of the Faith" will serve a good purpose in counteracting their evil influence. • Sulvia's Home Journal (Messrs. Word, Lock, and

Co.)--With the May part of this journal is presented a large coloured plate of walking dresses, alSo a cut-out paper pattern of a jacket, the latter being very neat. The fashion engrasings are as usual numerous, varied and chaste in design, and described in detail ; and of the literature, we wonld particularly direct attention to the continuation of the article on "Servants in former .days and at the present time" as affording some interesting information. "In quest of a wife " is the title of a tale of the Bavarian Highlands, from the German of Herman-Schmid, and if the future in- stalments be equal to the first readers will have no cause to complain of either the matter or the manner of its treatment. --illyra's Journal of Dress and Fashion, Afyra's Mid- Afonthly Journal and Children's Dress, and Myra's Three- penny Journal (London: Messrs. Goubaud and Son, 39 and 40, Bedford-street, Covent Garden).—These publications are to milliners and dressmakers, and to all interested in dress and fashion almost indispensable. The coloured fashion plates, diagram sheets, the cut-out paper patterns, and the engravings are all of them good, while the various literary contributions are of considerable merit. There are also many novelties about the journals which must commend them to their numerous readers.—Le Alonteur de he 21,10de (Messrs. Gouleaul and S)n) is a comparatively new fashion- able journal, with which is incorporated the " Milliner and Dressmaker." With No. 3, which is before us, is presented four beautifully coloured fashion plates, expressly designed for the journal, and certainly they are very artistically got up. There are also no less. than 103 other illustrations, besides carefully compiled articles on new and coming fashions, society and fashion in Paris, fashionable tine art needlework ; and the "Echoes from everywhere" is a pleasing feature of the journal, the price of which, however, is somewhat higher than the others, being one shilliag. This may be said to be recouped in the excellence of the plates.— Welclon's Ladies' Journal of Dress, Fashion, Needlework, Literature, and Art (London : Weldon and Co., 7, Southampton-street, Strand).—The contents of this periodical for May, with which is presented a coloured plate of spring fashions, may be consulted by the ladies with pleasure, and profit as well, comprising as theyelo informa- tion on a variety of subjects of epnial interest to them The articles are not confined solely to questions affecting dress, but other matters of greater moment arc touched upon.— Mrs. Leach's Practical Family MYSSilialeer (London : Mr. H. S. Cartwright, 8, Johnson's Court, Fleet-street) is again to hand. The puce of it is only twopence, and for this small expenditure it is astonishing the amount of practical knowledge that can be obtained. We have pleasure in again !commending the publication, which is this month fall of +illustrations of summer fashions, to the notice of the ladies.

ROUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY. The Bishops' bill for procuring the release of Mr. Green was read a second time.—The LORD CHANCELLOR pointed out that under the " miscalled" Public Worship Regulation Act Mr. Green would be deprived of the living in St. John's in August next, when three years will have elapsed sinca the inhibition was issued.—The Unreformed Corporation Bill was read a second time, and their Lordships discussed, in an approving spirit, the doings of the Salvation Army.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEspAy.

LOCAL FINANCIL-Mr. DODSON, in reply to Mr. Pell, stated that it would be irregular to make a Ministeral state- ment in reference to local finance on going into committee on the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill.—Mr. Pell gave notice that he would move that the House should not go into committee on the Bill until a Ministerial statement respecting local taxation had been made.
THE GOVERNMENT AND THE EILMAINHAM CORRESPONDENCE:
THE ALLEGED COMPACT.

Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE remarked that the infor- mation conveyed as to the release of the Suspects could ' not remain in its present position, and he there- fore asked for further information. He desiredto know what other Ministers of the Government, besides those mentioned on Monday night, had communications with the hon. member for Cork before his release; whether those communications were made known to the Government as a whole, or the Chief Secretary in particular ; whether any member of the Government had personal interviews with Mr. Parnell before his release; and whether the release of Michael Davitt was stipulated. for or mentioned as a matter that ought to be included in any arrangement. Mr. CiLA.DSTONE replied that the release of the three mem- bers had no connection whatever with the question of arrears or with Michael Davitt ; it was simply a question of duty under the letter and spitit of a law of exceptional powers. He was not prepared to admit that he had communications directly or indirectly with the hon. member for Cork. He had no knowledge ot the matter except the information which was in possession of the Government as a whole; no member of the Government had to his knowledge had per- sonal interviews with Mr. Parnell ; and as to Davitt's re- lease nothing whatever was stipulated for. Mr. Orrstow asked if the right hon. gentleman would read the letter sent to him personally by Mr. O'Shea, the reply to which had already been read. Mr. GLADSTONE said the letter had no connection what- ever with the liberation of Mr. Parnell. It was an interest- ing letter on Tri§h politics generally, and in one part of it Mr. O'Shea stated distinctly that Mr. Parnell had no con- nection with the initiative he was taking. Captain AYLMER asked if when the Cabinet came to the conclusion that the prisoners must be released they had re- ceived information of the conversation with reference to Mr. Sheridan.

Mr. GLADSTONE replied in the affirmative. Sir H. D. WOLF asked if it was decided to release the pri- soners after the statement of Lord Cowper, that the Suspects had been steeped to the lips in treason. Mr. GLADSTONE was unable to say. Mr. LABOUCHERE asked if it was usual for an ex-Cabinet Minister to read the precis of a private conversation without the consent of his colleagues, and if such consent had been obtained. Mr. GLADSTONE said there bad been no communication between Mr. Forster and himself. That right hon. gentle- man acted on his own responsibility, and he (Mr. Gladstone) had no right to pass any judgment upon the course taken by his right hon. friend. Mr. FORSTED said he should never have thought of read- __ _ _ _ . _ .

log the memorandum if it had not been for the account given by Mr. O'Shea, which involved imputations upon his (Mr. Forster's) personal honour. Mr. O'SHEA complained of the gloss which had been put upon his conversation with Mr. Forster. The right hon. gentleman must have known that he (Mr. O'Shea) had taken no part in the organisation of the Land League, and knew nothing of Mr. Sheridan. The SPEAKER ruled that the hon. member was out of order in entering into a question of controversy. Mr. A. BALFOUR moved the adjournment of the House. He contended that, however it might be disguised in words, there had been a compact between Mr. Parnell and the Government, and that it was regarded in that light by the late Chief Secretary. He had no desire to use strong lan- guage, but he believed that the whole transaction stood alone in its infamy. If a darker touch could be added it had been added by the Home Secretary, who before the compact was concluded went down to Derby and brought down the cheer's of his constituents by accusing the Conservative party of having entered into a league with the Irish. He thought the Government was degraded by treating and associating with men "steeped to the lips in treason," and its power would be weakened for years to come. Mr. GLADSTONE congratulated the hon. member on the height to which he had wound up his Parliamentary courage. The hon. gentieman charged the Government with having entered into a compact with the released prisoners, and in doing so gave the lie to members who had grown grey in the service of the country. He retorted that the.charge was wholly groundless, and conjured up simply by the strength of party passion, and without the slightest substratum of fact. There was not a word of truth as to any compact with the member for Cork who never knew that he was to be released until he was released. He urged that the hon. member for Hertford having put forward the charge was bound to go through with it. Personally he (Mr. Gladstone) denied that Mr. Parnell knew either that be was lobe released or what course the Government intended to take upon the question of arrears. What was it that the Government knew? The hon. member said they knew that peace was to be brought about in Ireland through the hon. member for Cork. He wished to God he had known it. He would have gone a loag way to bring it about. But he re- garded the peace of Ireland in a very different light from that in which the hon member regarded it. Mr. Gladstone read a letter written by himself immediately after receiving Mr. Parnell's letter, in which he distinctly stated that the Government had no right to expect the co-operation of Mr. Parnell, and which he rather thought they had no right to accept at present. So much for the accusation that the Government had entered into a corrupt compact. The hon. member for Hertford went further and alleged that the Government were tainted with infamy, that they uttered falsehoods in the House, and had degraded their administra- tion. But the height to which he carried his conclusions was to move the adjournment of the House. Having made the charges the hon. member was bound to carry them further and to substantiate and sustain them. It was in- tolerable that charges of this kind were to be made and not , sustained. Mr. GIBSON asked, if the transaction was a fair and honest transaction, why was it kept back? Sir W. HARCOURT urged that the member for Hertford had no right to charge the Government with infamy unless he was prepared to bring it to a test, and, as that had not been done, be (Sir William) treated the language with the contempt due to men who made insolent charges which they knew they were incapable of sustaining. As to the tran- sactions to which Mr. Gibson had referred, the simple fact was that Mr. Forster parted from his colleagues because of 14 gentlemen one thought the security was not sufficient and the other 13 thought it was. As to the immorality of seek- ing the aid of these suspects to keep the peace all he could say was that in the present state of Ireland he sould seek and desire the assistance of every man who would be on the side of peace and order. With the assurance brought by Captain O'Shea that the members did desire to use such influence as they possessed for the purpose of restoring tranquility in Ireland, no compact of any kind was wanted. Lord J. MANNERS thought there was nothing more calcu- luted to dismay the loyal and dishearten the courageous than this truckling to men of whose antecedents there could be no doubt. Mr. FORSTER explained that in his opinion the promises male by the imprisoned members were conditional through- out, and that was to his mind rather an aggravation of their offence. Sir W. BARTTELOT asked if there was any truth in the rumour that the most important paragraph in Mr. Parnell's letter had been omitted at the suggestion of the President of the Board of Trade. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN informed him that the rumous had not the slightest foundation in fact. Mr. O'Shea withdrew the paragraph of his own accord, as he believed it might give rise to misrepresentation. In regard to the omission of the passage when it was read, it had made so little impression upon him that when the letter was read he bad not the slightest idea that that was the letter from which Mr. O'Shea wished to have a sentence withdrawn. As far as the views of Mr. Parnell were concerned, he understood that when the bon, member passed through London on his way to Paris he had stated to more than one of his friends that every patriotic Irishman should aid in —,p,ceventing out- rages in Ireland ; but it was also Made,knOlll that the hon gentleman ' attributed them 4,itt.,'"tbe ,vlctions which resulted from the attempt to coniet airears. question, the Government decided upon releasing them, be- lieving that their ful ther detention was unnecessary. and wou!d not conduce to the restoration of peace and order. He believed that the future action of Mr. Parnell and his col- leagues would justify the course which the Government had taken. In regard to Mr. Forster's Memorandum, it might convey the words of Mr. O'Shea, but it was absurd to sup- pose that a cool and able man like the member for Cork would ever have admitted that he had been engaged in a conspiracy in favour of the perpetration of outrages. in regard to the position of the Government, he justified the course they had taken in acting upon information calculated to ensure the peace of Ireland, and he thought they would have been justified if in the past they had not only acted on such information, but had even sought it. Sir S. NORTHCOTE remarked that they had arrived at a considerable amount of interesting information. They now knew a great deal which it was very important they should know, but he was not quite sure that they knew all. After what had taken place, the impression would go abroad that submission had been made to the powers of the Land League. Sir H. FLETCHER was speaking at ten minutes to seven, when the debate terminated, and the sitting was suspended. At nine o'clock the House reassembled, but was imme- diately counted out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

Inisn POOR-LAW REMOVAL BILL.—The greater portion of the sitting was occupied in a debate on the Irish Poor- law Removal Bill, the second reading which was moved by Sir H. Bruce. The main object of the bill was to make it unlawful to remove to Ireland any pauper who had resided in England, Wales, or Scotland for three years before be- coming chargeable to the parish. Amongst those who op- posed the second reading was Mr. WHITLEY, who said there was a very strong feeling in Liverpool that this bill, if passed, would cause a great increase in the number of vag- rant paupers. He was of cpinion that they would not be able to deal effectually with the subject raised by this bill till they were prepared to deal with the question of the re- moval of the pecuniary burden from local to imperial taxation. Mr. DODSON, who spoke as the representative of the Government, pointed out that by this bill Irishmen in England would be placed in a better position thin an Englishman, because three years' residence would give the former a settlement in any part of the country, while the Englishman could only acquire the right in the particular locality in which he resided. On this ground, and Lecause if any alteration was to be made in the law of settlement he should prefer to see it dealt with by the Government, he could not assent to the second reading of the bill. On a division, the bill was rejected by 172 to 91 Votes. THE ALLOTMENTS BILL.—A Bill introduced by Mr. JESSE COLLINS, to enable the trusteets of lands held for charitable purposes to let the land in small plots at a fair agricultural rent was, after some discussiou, read a second time.—Mr. HUMERI', in stating, during the debate, that the Government supported the principle of the bill, said that some of its clauses would require ccnsiderable alteration in committee. .
