The SPEAKER said that, if Mr. O'Donnell's amend- ment was negatived, no other could be made. In reply to Mr. Stanley Leighton, Mr. GLADSTONE said a warrant dated the 21st of January, 1882, for' the arrest of Mr. Sheridan had not been executed because the authorities had not been able to execute it. TIIR WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS.—Mr. GLADSTONE ex- plained the course the Government intend to adopt with regard to the Coercion Bill and the Arrears Bill. The former, he hoped, would be read a second time to-day, and in that case the committee stage could be begun on Tues- day, after which the measure would be proceeded with day by day. Monday would thus be opened for the second read- ing of the Arrears Bill, and if the House disposed of thesti two measures and passed a vote of credit for a month before Whitsuntide, then the usual Whitsuntide holiday could be taken; otherwisa that was doubtful. The announcement that the House would sit every day next week, not omitting Derby day, was received with cheers. , SECOND BEADING OF THR PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELAND) BILL.—On the motion for the second reading of the Prevention of Crime in Ireland Bill, Mr. O'Donnell, who had an amendment on the paper de Tlaring that the bill could only act as a provocation to discontent, and as a fatal obstacle to good government, order, and tranquility, attri- buted outrage and disaffection in Ireland to evictions and the action of the magistrates.—Colonel COLTHURST main- tained that the outrages in County Cork at all events were for disobeying the "no-rent" manifesto. —Mr. RATHBONE urged the House to put aside party rancour, and appealed to the noble example of the relatives of the late Lord F. Cavendish in support of the tone which sholud prevail in dealing with Ireland. He rebuked the Tories for saying to the Irish people and their representa- tives," Because you have been accomplices with O'Donovan Hossa, we will throw you back to your evil courses;" and he held that if the Government had refused to accept the assistance of Mr. Parnell and his party they would thereby have proved their unfitness to govern Ireland. What was wanted was to put aside party objects in favour of a patriotic support of the Government, and if that were done Ireland coulA be governed.—Mr. BRYCE argued that as the difficulty in Ireland was that crimes were undiscovered, the bill should aim at making detection easy, not not at multiplying offences. The fault of the bill was that it lumped together political and ordinary offences, and he did not think that its provisions regarding public meetings and newspapers were wisely conceived.—'Fho debate was continued by Mr. Loamy, Mr. Reid, Mr. Labouchere, and others.—Mr. REDMOND said he had always denounced violence, and did so recently at Manchester, after hearing of the death of Lord F. Caven- dish, but before he had learned that Mr. Burke had also been killed. Next day the Times pointed out that he had omitted to refer to Mr. Burke's death, and when he wrote to the editor explaining the circumstances, his letter was refused insertion. This, he said, was an example of how Irish matters were misrepresented in England. He did not object to a bill putting down secret societies, but the present one, by suppressing public agitation, would stimulate them, —Mr. TREVELVAN made his maiden speech in his new capa- city, and with a sort of apology far not being an Irishman, claimed to have studied Irish affairs for the last seventeen years. He reviewed the operation of the Peace Preserva- tion Act, and traced the results of subsequent modifications of that law, taking up a tone of undoubted firmness as to the necessity of dealing strongly with crime in Ireland. He believed that when the new bill was passed and the people of Ireland, the great majority of whom were sick of terrorism, saw the Goverment's intentions, they' would rally to their side. Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN said it was admitted that the measure now before the House was the most severe and drastic enact- ment proclaimed for Ireland since the date of the penal laws.—Mr. SEXTON moved the adjournment of the debate.— Mr. GLADSTONE consented, on the understanding that the debate should be brought to a close at the morning sitting on Friday.

with alkali waste. In conclusion, Mr. Chance remarked that, as it was, the recovery of sulphur from alkali waste seemed at last to be within a measurable distance of accom- plishment, and to Messrs. Schaffner and Helbig belonged the credit of having originated a process which promised a new lease of life to the rranufacture of alkali, as invented by Leblanc. Considerable discussion followed the reading of the paper, amongst the gentlemen taking part being Mr. Mac Tear, Glasgow; Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Liverpool; Col. Gamble, St. Helens; Mr. John Brock, Widnes; Mr. Carey, Widnes; Mr. Dickson, Newcastle; Mr. Glover, Newcastle, &c, Sic. At the close a vote of thanks was awarded Mr. Chance for his valuable contribmtion to this interesting subject.
MISCELLANEOUS.
We (Pall Hall Gazette) understand that Mr. John Morley will retire from the editorship of the Fort eight.y Review in
November next.
_ _ Two conflagrations, involving an aggregate of about £120,000 damage, took place on Saturday, one in a.brewery
at Wandsworth and the other in a tannjy. in Galashiels. It is feared that five fishing smacks sailing out of Lowestoft, and carrying 25 hands, were lost in the gale _ _
of the 29th ult., nothing- having been heard of them since
that time.

On Monday, direct access with Leicester was gained through the Tilton-on-the Hill extension of the Great Nor- thern Rai way. The new line is eleven miles long, opens up a fertile agricultural- district, and will prove a valuable feeder to the trunk line.

George Battams, labourer, was committed for trial at Leighton Buzzard, on Saturday, on a charge of wilfully murdering his wife, whose head he hacked to pieces with a billhook. Medical evidence was called to prove that pri- soner had been suffering from brain softening. A very numerously attended meeting was held in Hyde Park, on Sunday, in support of the claim of Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., to take his seat in the House of Commons. It was estimated that 60,000 persons took part in the proceedings. James Nichol Fleming. formerly a director of the City of Glasgow Bank, was brought before the Sheriff in Glasgow ma Saturday afternoon, charged with the embezzlement of part of the funds of that bank, and was formally committed for trial on that charge. The amount in question is said to be nearly one million sterling. On Monday, Dr. Diplock held an inquest at Hammer- smith on the bodies of Eliza Gardner and her three chil- dren, aged four years, two years, and three months respec- tively, all of whom were found with their throats cut last Friday. The jury fcund that the woman, whilst tempo- rarily insane, had killed her children and committed

suicide. Mr. J. F. May, one of the Macclekield solicitors, sentenced on November 28, 1881, to nine months' imprisonment for bribery, was on Saturday discharged from Knatsford prison by order of Sir William Harcourt, on the ground of ill- health. Mr. Mair, the Liberal agent (Mr. May having acted for the Conservatives), who was sentenced for a similar term, remains in the prison. The Gazette announces the elevation of Mr. H. Hussey Vivian, M.P., Mr. A. Matheson, of Lockalsh (Ross) ; Mr. F. A. Milbank, M.P., Mr. M. A. Bass, M.P., Mr. J. W. Pease, M.P., Mr. C. E. Adams, of Blair Adam (Kinross); Mr. C. J. Freake, of Cromwell House, Kensington • Mr. John Bennet Lawes, of Rothamsted (Hert) ; and Air. Samuel Stephens Marling, of Kingstanley and Ticlenharn, Gloucestershire, to the dignity of the baronetcy. The execution of Osmond Otto Brand, skipper, for the murder of Wm. Pepper, the Hull fisherboy, on the high seas, has been fixed by the High Sheriff of Yorkshire to take place at Armley gaol, Leeds, on Tuesday, the 23rd inst. The culprit was unmoved when the date was communicated to him by Mr. Keene, the governor of the gaol. He has been visited by his wife and her sister. No efforts have yet been made to obtain a reprieve. Brand, it is stated, eats and sleeps well. Mr. Pennington, the legal adviser of the Conservative party at Bolton, said in a speech which he delivered last week that "if Joe Chamberlain had been stabbed in the park on Saturday night he would have met the just deserts of his own policy." Several persons took the trouble to bring these words under the notice of Mr. Chamberlain, who in acknowledging his correspondents' letters speaks of Mr. Pennington as a "peculiarly rabid variety of the genus Tory." -.- BRIDAL DISAPPOINTMENT IT WALES.—On Monday a wedding party arrived at the village church of Wales at the time appointed for the marriage to take place, but there was no clergyman present to perform the nuptials. The party decided to wait till the clergyman came, as they thought he must be detained by some important business. After they had been kept in dreadful suspense for an hour, the minister arrived. But, alas for the hopes of the brideand bridegroom, the time was past twelve, and the minister told them he dare not then tie them together. The pair had to leave the church unmarried.—Sheffield Telegraph. The meetings of the district committees of the Wesleyan Society were commenced on Tuesday. The. Pturns of membership are generally favourable. Manchester district reports an increase of 199, Bolton 447, Liverpool 777, Mac- clesfield 248, Leeds 605, Halifax and Bradford 787, Hull 1,462, York 278. and Nottingham and Derby 915. The increase in the entire Connexion, so far as ascertained, is stated to be about 12,500, the largest gain for several years. The trial of the persons charged with being implicated in long-firm frauds' which has been going on at the Central Criminal Court for several days, was concluded on Monday afternoon. The prisoners were found guilty, and Trevelli, Schneider, and Jacobs were sentenced to five years' penal servitude; Lorenz, Wright, Kendrick, Erne, and Welham were sentenced to 18, Garth to nine, and Hiller and Tatters- field to six months' hard labour.

Mr. Mapleson writes :—"Madame Adelina Patti is en- gaged to me for six months in the United States, com- mencing in October next, to sing at least twice a week, for which she is to receive £917 a night. The sum of £9,170 has been already placed to her credit at her banker's in New York as .a guarantee for the payment of the last ten nights' services. In addition to this, Madame Patti will have her private Pullman travelling car, containing drawing and dining-rooms, and sleeping accommodation for the whole of her servants, as well as two cooks, who will accompany the expedition."

A meeting under the auspices of the National Agricul- tural Labourers' Union, in favour of the extension of house- hold suffrage to counties, was held in London on Wednes- day night, Mr. J. Collings, M.P., presiding. The chairman said the delay in passing the franchise reflected discredit on the Government, but admitted the Irish land question was of She first importance. A resolution was passed urging the introduction of a measure for the assimilation of the county with the borough franchise, and declaring their opinion that it should become law at the end of the present Par- liament.

ANTICIPATED SETTLEMENT OF THE CHORLEY TRADE DISPUTE.—There is some prospect of a settlement of the strike and lock-out in the cotton trade, which has existed for the past twelve weeks at Chorley. The executive of the Spinners' Amalgamated Society have passed the following resolution :—" That with a view to terminate the unfortu- nate dispute in the Chorley cotton trade, we hereby offer to submit the question of calculating wages by indicative length of yarn spun, to arbitration and in the event of our proposal being accepted by the employers, we agree to in- strut the men locked-out to resume work pending such reference."

Mr. Megsou, of Market-street, Manchester, received inti- mation from the Home Secretary on Saturday morning that he had advised Her Majesty to commute the sentence of death passed on Benjamin Bouch at the last Manchester Assizes for the murder of his two sons, to one of penal ser- vitude for life. The prisoner, it may be remembered, was recommended to mercy by the jury, with the full approval of Mr. Justice Mathew, who tried the case. A letter to the same effect as that received by Mr. Megson was sent by the Home Secretary to Mr. Mulligan, of 3, Church-lane, Urmston.

PROFESSOR HUXLEY AND ORPHAN INSTITUTIONS.—A. few rather bitterly satirical remarks were dropped by Professor Huxley at the annual dinner in connection with the Artists' Benevolent Institution, on Saturday. It appears that there is in connection with the institution an orphan fund, and on learning that the bulk of the fund was really devoted to the benefit of the orphans, the professor remarked that it seemed to be an institution "of a wholly unprecedented kind." His experience of orphan institutions, he went on to explain, was that those having the spending of the money first built a large orphanage, then appointed a principal, then a chap- lain, then a master and mistress, servants, cooks, and bottle- washers, and then, if there happened to be any money left, caught a few stray orphans, IMPORTANT DECISION.—Sir Rupert Kettle, county court judge, gave a decision at Dudley, on Tuesday, which will excite a good deal of interest in factories and workshops. The widow of a sinker who had lost his life at the Earl of Dudley's collieries sought compensation. The negligence to which the man's death was attributed was admitted, but it was pleaded for the defence that the deceased, like the other workpeople of his lordship, had contracted himself out of the Employers' Liability Act in return for certain stipulated ' benefits. The report of the judgment is not very full, but ' His Honour seems to have ruled—in addition to his finding that there was an absence of mutuality and a want of suffr- cient consideration on which to found a contract—that the bargains of individuals to prevent the operation of a system of public policy specifically established by an Act of Parlia- ment for the benefit of the whole community were not law- ful; in other words, that it is not competent for workmen ta contract themselves out of the Employers' Liability Act. The widow was awarded £l5O. THE ALLEGED NEXT-OF-KIN FRAUDS.—At the Manches- ter City Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr. C. H. Rickards and Mr. P. B. Ferguson, J. S. Rogers, William Evans, A:. M`Kenzie. J. H. Shakespear, and Albert Edward Beeton were again placed in the dock and charged on remand with con- spiring together to defraud. Mr. W. Cobbett, on behalf of Treasury, prosecuted; Mr. Boote appeared for Shakespear, and Mr. Hockin for M‘Kenzie. Mr. Cobbett said that, in accordance with the understanding entered into when the case was last before the court, he had to apply for a further remand until Tuesday next, when he hoped to be fully pre- pared with the Case for the prosecution. Mr. Hockin and Mr. Boote assented to this course. Rogers said he wished to see the books from the Birmingham office, and Mr. Cobbet promised that, if a list of the required books were made outt he would see that the prisoner had the opportunity of ex, amining them. Rogers said he would at once proceed to make out the list. div.head: RECOVERY OF SULPHUR FROM ALKALI WASTE.
div.p: RECOVERY OF SULPHUR FROM ALKALI WASTE.

Before the Chemical and Physics Section of the London Society of Arts, on Thursday, a most interesting paper was read by Mr. Alexander M.Chance, of Birmingham, on "The recovery of sulphur from alkali waste (Shaffner and Hel- big's process) : a record of recent results." There was a very large attendance, and amongst the gentlemen present we observed several connected with the chemical trade in Lancashire and other parts of the country in which this industry is a main feature. After a few remarks from the chairman (Mr. Walter Weldon), Mr. Chance proceeded with the reading of his paper' which set out by observing that, invented and applied in France, by Leblanc, about the year 1790, and first introduced into England by Mr. Muspratt, in 1823, the manufacture of soda from common salt—gener- ally known as the alkali trade—had gradually extended, until it had become the most important of all the chemical processes in Great Britain, and in this manufacture there were two by-products, one of which was alkali waste. Mr. Chance quoted statistics with regard to the imports of brimstone and pyrites into the United Kingdom, and he showed that, taking 350,000 tons as being the amount of pyrites actually imported for the manufacture of soda, from 80 to 90 per cent, of the sulphur was lost in the alkali waste, representing a money value of £357,000. This had hitherto been regarded by manufacturers as part of the cost of pro- duction, but recently the method known as the ammonia- soda process has been so successfully established on a large scale in England that soda ash was being produced by it more, nay, much more, economically than by Leblanc's process, and thus the recovery of the sulphur ftom alkali waste, as a means of cheapening the cost of production by Leblanc's process, had become of vital importance. Having passed in review various sulphur recovery processes, Mr. Chance referred to that of Messrs. Schaffner and Helbig as seeming to offer a satisfactory solution of the question. Although patented in England in March, 1878, it did not become known to us until its publication in extenso in Pro- fessor Lunge's treatise on the alkali trade, issued in 1880. Mr. Chance then described at length the chemical reactions and combinations constituting the process discovered by Messrs. Schaffner and Helbig, and he illustrated his subject by several diagrams and models of 'the plant used, from which it appeared that dollomite or magnesite, which had been specially supplied by Mr. George G. Blackwell, of Liverpool, played a very important part in the operation. He remarked that the chemical combinations discovered and applied by Messrs. Schaffner and Helbig fully realised the conditions claimed for them—that, from 90 to 95 per cent. of the sulphur in the vat waste might be recovered in a commercial form; that practically the whole of the calcium compounds were also recovered, principally as car- bonate of lime, and that the -re-agent by which these remarkable results were obtained . was itself recovered, with the exception of _ the .unavoidable losses due to the manipulation of the process. div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
It is reported that the Government have ordered a gun- boat to be sent to the scene of hostilities on the West Coast of Africa.

Great damage has been done in Cherokee City, Indian Territory, by a cyclone. Forty houses were destroyed, two persons were kind, and 13 injured. The convention settling the mode of payment of the Russo-Turkish war indemnity was signed on Sunday by the Russian and Turkish plenipotentiaries. The min buildings and annexes of the Hygienic Exhibi- tion at Berlin were destroyed by fire on Friday night. Two lives were lost. The exhibits, a valuable portion of which was destroyed, were insured for 2,300,000 marks. An official decree is published giving effect to the Con- vention between France and Great Britain regulating the commercial and maritime relations between the two countries. Great distress has resulted in Andalusia from the failure of the crops. The Madrid Government are considering the expediency of opening the ports for the free importation of corn, and inquiries have been made as to the available stocks in Russia and other countries.

A Turkish transport, with troops on board, has run aground at a place called Rozban Bogaz, near the entrance of the Bosphorus. Some 200 soldiers were on board at the time of the accident, and of these no less than 50 have been drowned. An apocryphal rumour has been revived in Paris that the late Prince Louis Napoleon was killed in Zululand by a party of Communists, who went to South Africa for the purpose. At the last meeting of the Academie Royal of Belgium, Mr. W. E. Gladstone was elected a foreign associate. It is a curious circumstance that the vacancy thus filled by the election of the English Premier was caused by the death of Lord Beaconsfield.

—.— THE SENTENCE ON GIIITEAII.—A Washington telegram says :—The Supreme Court of the district of Columbia has unanimously overruled the bill of exceptions in the case of the assassin Guiteau, and refused to grant a new trial, at the same time affirming the sentence of death passed upon the prisoner. THE RING THEATRE DISASTEIL—The verdict in the case against the officials of the Ring, Strausse Theatre and others, arising out of the recent disastrous fire, was given on Tuesday. Francis Jaumer, formerly manager of the theatre; Nitsche, the workman; and Gehringer, steward, were found guilty, and sentence was deferred. Breithofer, a workman; Landeseiner, councillor of the Imperial ' police ; Wilhelm, the town engineer; and Herr, an employe of the fire brigade, were acquitted. DEATH , OF A SPANISII NOTABLE.—The death of the Marquis of Santa Cruz de Mudela, at the age of 74, is announced from Madrid. His career was remarkable, and proves that even the proud aristocracy of Spain is not so ex- clusive as to debar a man from gaining admission to its ranks by a constant and assiduous devotion to commercial pursuits. Born at a small village called Biscay, he began business when scarcely 15 years old in a very subordinate position in Granada. In a few years he started on his own account, and after a singularly successful career, was created Marquis in 1867. Besides directing mineral mines and iron works near to Bilbao he applied himself very suc- cessfully to the cultivation of the vine, his " Bodegas de la Mancha" having become famous. It is stated that he never undertook a State contract, his fortune having been amassed entirely by private enterprises, one of his most important contracts being with Krupp for a supply of iron for the manufacture of ordnance. THE :HERZEGOVINA REVOLT.

A considerable renewal of agitation is reported in Eastern Herzegovina. Two well-known patriots who took a con- spicuous part in theevents of 1875( prior to the Russo-Turkish war) nave re-entered the country from Servia, and are organising strong insurgent bands. A telegram from Bel- grade says that the organs of M. Ristics have republished the appeal of the Herzegovinian and Bosnian insurgents of April 18 last to the European Powers praying for a revoca- tion of the Austrian occupation. 78 INDIANS KILLED. - -

According to advices brought to Liverpool, it appears that the Indian troubles in the Arizona territory, United States, are likely to be put an end to shortly,considering the checks which the hostile Indians are receiving. The despatch is dated from Fort Bowie, the 4th inst , and states that during the previous two weeks it was estimated that at least 141 whites had been killed by the Apache Indians, who had also carried off 500 head of stock and destroyed property to the amount of over $70,000. The same despatch reported a Jesperate encounter with some Mexican cavalry and the Indians near Janno. The Indians, ,who were under the leader Loco, were being pursued by the United States troops, commanded by Colonel Forsyth. The Mexican soldiers, under General Garcia, were lying in ambush, near Janno, and as soon as the Indians came near the Mexicans met

-- -- them. The Indians fled precipitately, leaving 28 dead on the field. Four companies of Mexican cavally pursued the Indians into the mountains, killing 50 of them. The total number of killed on the Indian side was 78, whilst 33 others were taken prisoners. The leader of the band, Loco, was reported to be amongt the dead. The Mexicans also captured a large quantity of stock from the enemy. It was thought that this engagement would have a most salutary effect, as. the depredations of the Apaches, under Loco, were causing their very name to be dreaded in and about the Arizona territory. The Indians during the encounter fought with great desperation, and 18 of the Mexican troops were killed.

div.head: EGYPTIAN QUESTION.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

The Egyptian difficulty entered on Sunday upon a new phase. The Prime Minister Mahmoud Pasha, sent in his resignation, and he is succeeded by the former Minister for Foreign Affairs' but Ourabi Pasha retains his place in the Government. The President and other members of Lhe Chamber of Notables" interceded " with the Khedive on be- half of the Ministers, but His Highness refused to hold any terms with "rebels." The Porte subsequently sent a mes- sage to the Egyptian Government in which emphatic asser- tion was made of the sovereign rights of the Sultan, and the " rebels " were informed that any act contrary to orders of the Khedive in conformity with the wishes of the Imperial Sovereign would entail heavy responsibility upon the authors. The Port protested against the declaration of the Egyptian Ministry that they would offer armed resistance if the Ottoman Goverment sent troops or a special mission to the country. In view of the critical state of affairs the English and French Governments decided to send three vessels each to Suda Bay (Crete). The French vessels anchored in Suda Bay on Tuesday, and they have probably been joined by the Alexandra, the Superb, and the Invincible, from Sir Beauchamp Seymour's fleet. On hear- ing that the fleet were ordered to Alexandria the Minister ordered the army reserves to be called out—a step which gave rise to a panic at Cairo, and numbers of women and children were at once sent off to Alexandria. Upon the arrival of the squadron, Sir E. Mallett was to open negotia- tions for the settlement of the Egyptian difficulty, and hopes are entertained that there will be a satisfactory solution without the necessity of employing force, as Ourabi has come to the conclusion that the game has been played out. It appears that the President of the Council of Ministers at Cairo has waited upon the English and French Consuls General, and expressed a hope that in view of the arrange- ment of the difficulties between the Khedive and his Minis- ters the combined squadron would be withdrawn, but the Consuls declined to hold out any hope that such a step would be taken. The British Consul General has issued a circular to the Consuls under his jurisdiction stating that the visit of the fleets is of a friendly character, and that there will be "no danger if all goes well." It is expected at Cairo that the Porte will withdraw its protest after re- ceiving satisfactory ' explanations from the English and French Governments.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY,
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY,

OPENING THE NATIONAL BARRACKS. ! Two meetings were held on Saturday by the Salvation Army—one in the afternoon and another in the evening— to inaugurate the opening of their new National Barracks , and Congress Hall. The buildings are situated in Lower Clapton, and stand on over two acres of ground. The pre- mises were formerly known as the London Orphan Asylum. The property originally cost £60,000, but was purchased by the Salvation Army for £15,000, and fitted up at a further cost of £7,000. The Congress Hall, formed by covering in what was the quadrange of the eld building, seats 4,700 persons. It has ten entrances, and is fitted up in the circus style, with an iron fire-proof corridor round the top. It is lighted by means of 54 panels of stained glass, IGft. by 51t. Gin. In front of the porch and colonnade approached by steps, is an open-air space, 401 t. by 280 f t., and a much larger one, en- closed with high walls behind, FO that drill, reviews, aod open-air demonstrations on a large scale can be conducted on the premises. , The meetings on Saturday were held in the Congress Hall, " General " Booth presided, and was sup- ported by Mrs. Booth, Rev. W. Tyler, Admiral Fishborn, Col. Pepper, and Commissioner Railton. The "General " made a statement setting forth the progress of the Salvation Army movement. Several hymns were sung and prayers recited. The staff band of the Salvation Army accompanied the solos and choruses. Each hymn was repeated three i times, every person in the hall loining. THE present week has been an exciting one in Parliamentary circles. Ever since the Government released from Kilmainham the three Irish Members of the House of Commons, and announced their inten- tion of adopting in part, if not in whole, the pro- gramme of the Irish party, hints have been thrown out by the occupants of the front Opposition bench, and by lesser lights of the Conservative party as well, of a secret compact between the Government and Mr. Parnell. From time to time attempts have been made to get at the bottom of this supposed agreement, but for the very sufficient reason that no such agreement —written or verbal—exists, these have, of course, signally failed. It may be remembet ed that in answer to certain questions put at the time Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and °Melly were liberated, Mr. Gladstone stated that the Cabinet had arrived at their decision on certain documentary and other evidence which had been placed before them, and which led them to believe that if set free the hon. members would be found ranging themselves on the side of law and order. On Monday evening Mr. Puleston, the member for Devonport, tried to extort this docu- mentary evidence from the Prime Minister, who, how- e,ver, would not be drawn; but Mr. Parnell—and on I this occasion he proved himself not quite so skilful a diplomatist as we had given him credit for— immediately the Premier sat down, jumped up and read a letter from himself to Captain O'Shea, the member for Clare, which Mr. Parnell said he under- stood formed the documentary evidence alluded to in Mr. Puleston's question. In this letter Mr. Parnell urges upon the Irish party, through Captain O'Shea, the necessity fora settlement of the arrears question in Ireland, the admission of leaseholders to the fair- rent clauses of the Land Act, and also the further extension of the purchase clauses of that Act, and then he adds,—" The accomplishment of the pro- gramme I have sketched out to you would, in my judgment, be regarded by the country as a practical settlement of the land question, and would, I feel sure, enable us to co-operate cordially in future with the Liberal party in for warding Liberal principles, and the Government at the end of the session would, from the state of the country, feel themselves thoroughly justified in dispensing with further coer- sive measures." The foregoing is the substance of the letter. In order to prevent misapprehension or misunderstanding that portion relating to co-opera- tion with the Liberal party was omitted in the copy read by Mr. Parnell, but it was subsequently supplied by Captain O'Shea. This communication as a whole formed the chief documentary evidence—and in our opinion it was amply sufficient—on which the Govern- ment relied in arriving at their decision that it would be advisable to give the imprisoned members their liberty. Captain O'Shea, who had previously written to Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain on the Irish question, communicated the contents of this letter to one or more members of the Cabinet, Mr. Forster in- eluded, and it is because the Cabinet acted upon it that the attempt has been repeatedly made to charge the Government with having entered into a compact with Mr. Parnell, and has evoked so much indigna- tion from the Opposition. What is there, we ask, to support the charge which has been formulated by the youthful member for Hartford, Mr. Balfour, who says,—" Each party, before the transaction took place, knew perfectly well what they were going to give and what they expected to receive. The Govern- ment, on their behalf, were going to give liberty to hon. gentlemen behind him and a bill with regard to arrears. The hon. gentlemen were going to give to the Government peace in Ireland and parliamentary support." It cannot be disputed that Captain O'Shea had been in communication with ar. Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain, that he had seen the hon. member for Cork in London while on parole and subsequently in Kilmainham, and that he had after- wards had an interview with Mr. Forster ; but there is not a tittle of evidence to show that Captain O'Shea's negotiations with Mr. Parnell were—until after the Prime Minister had declared himself on the necessity for further redressing Irish grievances—known to the Government. The fact remains,therefore,that the letter is the only piece of evidence on which it is possible to found so extraordinary a charge. What is there to show an arrears bill was promised? The arrears question is one which was very pointedly brought under the notice of the Government at an early period of the present session by the hon. and learned member for Dundalk, Mr. C. Russell, who presented to the Prime Minister an influential petition praying that it might be dealt with in a liberal spirit, and Mr. Gladstone then promised on behalf of the Government that it should have careful considera- tion; but still more recently, on the 26th of April last, Mr. Gladstone in his place in the House of Com- mons, when Mr. Redmond introduced the bill framed by Mr. Parnell and his fellow prisoners for the amendment of the Land Act, intimated the intention of the Government to deal with the arrears question immediately, and broadly hinted that it would be done on the lines of the measure then being submitted to the House. This took place as we have said on the 26th of April, whilst Mr. Parnell was in Kilmain- ham, and before he had even thought of his letter probably, hence the Government were pledged to an arrears bill before that now celebrated communication was penned. What evidence is there of a promise by the Government of liberty to the three members? So far as can be gleaned from the debates, there is none what- ever. It is quite true that subsequent to the debate on the 26th Captain O'Shea was able through the courtesy of Mr. Forster to see the member for Cork in Kilmainham, but he does not appear to have been the bearer of any message from the Government, or, indeed, from any quarter, and if he had been, certain it is Mr. Forster would have known of it and would this week have exposed it. Captain O'Shea says he did

not then know anything of the contemplated re- lease of the hon. members, and we are bound to accept his statement. It is evident, however, that the gallant member must have been in one of his most persuasive moods,for he completely overcame the member for Cork,who immediately after he had gone sat down and penned one of the meekest effusions which it was possible for him to compile. In it, to our mind, the hon. member made a complete surrender, and almost prostrated himself at the feet of the Government. But even though Mr. Parnell had thus committed himself to better be- haviour, and it was brought under the notice of the Government, the Prime Minister appears to have been doubtful whether it would be wise to take notice there- of, and his feelings on that matter, as contained in a letter to Mr. Forster, written half-an-hour after he had perused the hon. member for Cork's submission, clearly show that he was opposed to any course of action which might even be construed as savouring of a compact. It was, however, impossible not to take notice of Mr. Parnell, his letter was in reality an appeal for liberty, though addressed to a gentleman unconnected with the Government; and the Govern- ment being already pledged to the hon. member's pro- gramme before he had actually formulated it, it would have been an injustice to have kept him and his friends longer in durance. There is clearly no evidence of compact here. But it is said Mr. Parnell promised peace in Ireland! He did no such thing. Mr. Par- nell knew, no one knew better, that the Land Act was slowly working its way and making itself felt, he also knew that if the arrears difficulty were settled and a scheme of peasant proprietory established, or the Bright clauses of the Land Act expanded, that then there would be no grievances to redress, and as a mat- ter of course the Irish people would be more conten- ted and outrages would cease. The peace in Ireland, therefore, alleged to have been promised to the Government was to have been brought about, if brought about at all, not by anything Mr. Parnell or his friens were to do, but it was to be accomplished rather by the efficacious measures of legisleion which the Goverment were to carry through Parliament. With respect to the alleged promise to the Govern- ment of the Parliamentary support of the Irish party, it would be well if our Conservative friends would re- member that as a general rule Irishmen have in the past, as they will doubtless in the future, allied them- selves with the Liberal party, to whom they are more indebted than to the Conservatives for the political privileges which they now enjoy, and of which they were so long deptived. From the Conservatives they I have nothing whatever to expect but coercion ; on the other hand, the Liberals can claim the credit of having. at least tried to rule Ireland by the ordinary law, and even if they have failed once in this respect their failure will not prevent them trying it again when the 1 condition of the country permits of it. It need, conse- quently, cause no surprise if the Irish members should be found again co-operating with the Liberal party for the passing of Liberal measures. To return, however, to the question of the compact, it is ovbious from all that has yet transpired that the first step in the Kilmainham transactions was taken by Captain O'Shea, and not by either the Government or Mr. Parnell; that supposing the Government were aware that the member for Clare was communicating with the member for Cork there is nothing to show that the latter knew anything of the negotiations of the former with the Government; and that even although Mr. Parnell's letter did fall into the hands of members of the Government and gave 'rise to his release, there was no arrangement expressed or implied in connection therewith. The result is creditable alike to the head and heart of. the member for Clare; and we are at a loss to under- stana why, now that all is known, these negotiations should have lost te the Cabinet the services of Mr. Forster. He was a party to the exchange of views with the member for Clare up to a certain point—until Mr. Parnell's letter was written. Mr. Forster on his own showing would have released the hon. member on his promising not to offend against the law. The letter practically contained that promise, but whilst every other member of the Cabinet was agreed that it was sufficient, Mr. Forster held a different opinion, and would have exacted from the member for Cork a humiliation, so to speak. It was too much to expect that. The episode and the discussions which have arisen out of it have not inaptly been described as a "storm in a tea cup ; " but be this as it may, it has given an opportunity for a display of party feeling within the walls of St. Stephen's such as has seldom been witnessed before. Such a display is not calcu- lated to promote the tranquility of Ireland in any degree, but then it affords the Tories an opportunity of making what capital they can out of a grave crisis in the history of the Executive—when on the contrary they ought to loyally give the Government their sup - port—and that is something. Whether the discussions will bring the desired capital is another question.

RUNCORN WESLEYANS AND THE EDUCATIONAL FUND. —On Sunday evening, the Rev. George Hack preached at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, and a collection was made on behalf of the Wesleyan Education Fund. THE WIDNES NEW WESLEYAN METHODIST CHAPEL. —The plans for the erection of this building have been pre- pared by Mr. Issitt. architect, of Bradford, and the contract has also been advertised.

WIDNES VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN SUNDAY Soma,. —The Rev. W. Parsonson preached twice at Victogia-road Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday, on behalf of this school; and in the afternoon an address to parents, scholars, and friends was given in the Lacey-street schoolroom by Mr. Thomas Brown, of St. Helens.

A. DANGEROUS PRACTICE.—AIfred Lines,a respectably dressed young man, residing at 89, Cholmondley-street, Widnes, was charged at the Warrington Police-court, yes- terday, with having, on the 29th April, when a passenger by the Cheshire Lines Committee, entered a carriage of a train while it was in motion, contrary to the 12th bye-law of the committee.—A detective in the employ of the commit- tee said as the 8.58 p.m. train was leaving Warrington Cen- tral station on the day in question, the defendant came up the steps, rushed at the train as it was passing him, and after several attempts succeeded in getting into a carriage. Defendant left the door open and the train went a consider- able distance with it open. The defendant had a very nar- row escape of being injured, and the committee thought it their duty to bring the case before their worships to put a stop to this dangerous practice. Defendant had no ticket, and be was warned several times to keep back, but he took no heed. The penalty was not exceeding 40., but the de- fendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined ss. and costs—total 20s.

TRIAL OF RUNCORN PRISONERS AT K NUTSFORD SESSIONS —At these sessions which have been held during the week, the following prisoners from Runcorn district have been tried : —Emma Carter, found guilty of stealing a brush, a jua.,and other articles, the property of James Eddie, and sentenced to 12 months' hard labour.—Joseph Taylor, flatman' was indicted for having assaulted Mary Ann Brookes, with in- tent to ravish her. He was found guilty of an indecent assault, and sentenced to three months' hard labour.— Walter Barker, William Hogan, and Thomas Blakernore, were indicted for breaking into a flat at Bancorp, and steal- ing wearing apparel belonging to Thomas Weedall and Peter Pool, tnaster and mate. Barker was sentenced to five years' penaheervitude, several prior convictions having been proved against him ; and the other two prisoners were dis- charged. Barker was next charged with Thomas Lane, with having broken into a flat at Runcorn, and stolen a pair of boots and some wearing apparel, the property of William Waring. Lane pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, with hard labour. The charge against Barker was withdrawn.—Alice Higlifield was in- dicted for stealing a dress, and necktie, and a necklace, the property of Mary Barnett, at Runcorn, and was sent to jaol one month with hard labour.—Alfred Moores, a deaf and dumb man, was convicted of having attempted to commit a criminal assault on a girl named Emily Shaw, aged 12. He was found fuilty of an indecent assault, and was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment, with hard labour. TIM BLUE RIBBON ARMY AT WARRINGTON.—TL weekly meeting, held in the Co-operative Hall, on Saturday evening,last, was largely attended, and was very successful The Rev. T. Rippon, who presided, announced amid cheers that Mr. Murphy had promised to be with them next Satur- day afternoon. During the evening addresses were delivered by the Rev. John Yonge, the Rev. J. B. Anderson, of Liver- pool; Mr. Henry Varley, of London; and Mr. R. Garnett. On Monday evening a tea was given in the Co-operative Hall, to the workers and all who had taken an active part in the recent mission. About 230 personsesat down to the tea, and afterwards the Rear. T. Rippon requested all who were willing to take part in visiting and looking after those who had taken pledges to come forward and give their names to the secretaries. A large number did so, and it is under- stood lists will shortly be handed to them of those who signed the pledge in order that they may look them up and see after them. Votes of thanks were given to the secre- taries and those who had charge of the arrangements, and Mr. Jon W. Hall requested the visitors to inferin any who had taken the pledge, and who need a little moral support, that if they would join the Good Templar Order they would there find an opportunity of spending a night a week corn_ fortably and pleasantly, and receive all the aid and assistance the Good Templar Order could afford. The remainder of the evening was given up to the young folks, who spent a very pleasant and enjoyable evening in indulging in a variety of games. BLUE RIBBON ARMY MEETING AT RUNCORN. —On Thursday evening, a public meeting, which had not been advertised, and was poorly attended, was held in Bethesda school-room, Runcorn, under the auspices of the local branch of the Blue Ribbon Army. The Rev. f. Williams presided; and, after devotional exercises, called upon the Rev. Edward Moore, of Warrington, who delivered an exhaustive speech on the liquor traffic. He said the gathering was a little dif- ferent from what he had expected, as be had supposed it was one for the purpose of considering the best methods of carry- ing on the work of the branch which had been formed. The meetings lately held in Warrington had been of a most suc- cessful character. The Public Hall had been crammed night after night for a fortnight. There had been a choir consist- ing of 120, and 8,723 new pledges had been taken, "besides I 300 or 900 ribbons." He could tell them of many most in- teresting cases of social reformation. It was really amazing j what a hold the drink traffic had on this country. The ' speaker then alluded to the great support rendered to the revenue by the liquor trade, and alluded in grateful terms to the fact revealed in the last budget that there had been a decrease in the receipts from this particular item of £3,00,000. There could be no question that the liquor traffic was a frightful cause of crime, wretchedness, pauperism, disease and death; and the amount of social and temporal good which they would get from the abolition of it would wore than compensate for any additional taxation that might be required. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Moore next referred to the great change which had come over the customs of society on this question, and to the fact that many gentle- men of the highest standing were associated with the tem- perance cause. He next dwelt upon the evil influence which he considered was exercised by moderate drinkers, who caused many who bad not become fond of the intoxicating cup to imagine they could partake of it with impunity. 'He con- tended that the wearing of the blue ribbon had a tendency to encourage those who were struggling with the temptation to drink, who, when they saw the ribbon felt that he who wore it was a foe to the drink trade. The friends of this movement were determined to goon; to fight on; to pray on, and victory would yet be theirs.—The Chairman said that if he thought the wearing of a blue ribbon on his part would help any one else, he should be glad to wear it. He urged all teetotallers to go in for the entire extinction of the traffic, and especially to speak in favour of the Sunday Closing Bill.—Mr. Joseph Wilson Boyle delivered a brief humorous address.—Mr. Shaw, seamen's. missionary, said the object of that meeting was, amongst other things, to re- organise the committee. Many, in the first flash of this movement in the town, had given their names upon the corn- ' mittee who no said that the claims of their business would not permit them to come to the meetings. He said that the expenses incident to the visit of Mr. Murphy and his party had been £lO 95.; and after Mr. Wilson had nobly.effered to pay that sum, the committee said "No; you are quite wel- come to what has been taken for the tickets and at the doors. You are thoroughly welcome to your expenses."—The meeting terminated with the pronouncing of the Benediction by the Chairman. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— At the weekly meeting of this class, on Wednesday evening Mr. H. Fitton, Wesleyan schoolmaster, Weston, read a paper on' Oliver Cromwell." Mr. Fitton first reviewed the lead- " ing-events of the great rebellion. Oliver's father, be said, I wag a gentleman of undoubtedly good family, and moderate means, living at Huntingdon, and, as some said, a brewer. Thia statement was, however, by no means certain, as it rested entirely on vague tradition. Cromwell's mother's name was Elizabeth Steward—said to have been a deseen- dant from the Royal Stuart stock of Scotland. Oliver was born,on the 25th April, 1599; received a fair education at the public school of Huntingdon, and entered Cambridge on the very day that Shakespeare died. The marriage of Crom- well, and his conversion to the tenets of the Puritans; the struggles of the Long Parliament with . the sovereign were next s-poken of; and the war in which the forces of the future'Protectoa proved so victorious, was briefly alluded to. Speaking of the execution of Charles, Mr. Fitton said his in- dividual opinion was that Cromwell did not desire that the I King should be put to death. Cromwell did all in his power I ' to mediate between the king and the army, even at the risk! of his own life ; and it was not until Charles's baseness,' treachery, and incurable falsity rendered him unworthy of , further consideration, that Cromwell allowed himself to be I influenced by the clamourous demands of the army. Allud- ing to the manner in which the Protector governed the I I country, Mr. Fitton said he made it the first power in I I Europe. Cromwell's foreign policy rested simply on the I declaration, "I will make the name of Englishman to be ' respeCted, and to be more terrible in Europe than the name of the ancient Roman was ; " and he did very much to fulfil I that vow. The Dutch were ruinously beaten in a series ot brilliant victories, which were only eclipsed by those of I Nelson. Jamaica was captured by Blake, and at the battle of Santa Cruz, Spain was humbled in the dust. Dunkirk was acquired by the mighty Oliver; and the pirates of Bar- bary, long the terror of English traders, disappeared before our fleet. A letter from Cromwell to the Duke of Savoy, secured freedom and protection to the persecuted Vandois. lEngland at that time, in the words of the glorious John Milton, was rousing herself like a strong mareafter sleep, and , shaking her invincible locks; or as an eagle renewing her mighty youth, and kindling her undazzled eyes at the fall midday beam." Attempts were made to assassinate him, but it was only when death struck his favourite daughter, that his' lioß heart gave way. "I would be willing to live," said the dying man, "to be further serviceable to God and His people, but my work is done; God will be with His people." On the night of Cromwell's death, a terrific storm, which tore up the trees, took place, and seemed a fitting ac- companiment to the departure of his mighty spirit. When the sun rose on the morning of the anniversary of his battles of Dunbar and Worcester, it was found that, quietly and peacefully, he had entered" that undiscovered country from whose bourne no traveller ere returns." For him life's tempest was over, and heaven's eternal calm had begun!
On Sunday afternoon and evening Mr. Henry Varley, evangelist, London, preached in the Warrington Public Hall to good audiences, and delivered two able discourses.

The artistic county bazaar in St. James's Hall, Manchester, in aid of the Lancashire Independent College, was brought to a close on Tuesday evening. The total re- ceipts have been £15,200, and the expenses are estimated at £2,600, leaving a balance of £12,600 in favour of the college. The receipts of the Liverpool bazaar, held a few weeks ago for the same object, amounted to £3,000.

THE LANCASHIRE HUSSA.RS.—This fine regiment of yeomanry arrived in Southport on Saturday for their annual eight days' training. The regiment consists of four troops, the A troop being from Asbton-in-Makerfield, the B troop from St. Helens and district, the C troop from from the dis- trict of Newton-le-Willows, and the D troop from Ormskirk and neighbourhood. The regiment numbers close upon 300, including officers, non-commissioned officers, and privates. The second part of the" Glossary of the Lancashire Dialect" has been issued. It is published jointly for the Manchester Literary Club and the English Dialect Society. The first part appeared as long ago as 1875, and the editors, Messrs. J. H. Nodal and George Milner, express their regret for the unavoidable delay that has occurred. The part now issued completes the vocabulary, and is a mine of amusement from the quaint phrases and the quaint customs which it records. In congratulating the editors upon the conclusion of this part of their tail we may state that the the third and concluding part will contain introductory chapters on the literature, grammar, and pronunciation of the dialect. There will also be an appendix of omitted words towards which contributions are invited. It is hoped that the third part will be ready early in 1883.—Athenaamt. RUNCORN AMATEUR BICYCLE CLUB.—The annual race for the championship came off on Saturday, on the Aston course, which is about seven miles in length. The competitors assembled at a point near Sutton Weaver station, and amongst the spectators were a considerable number of ladies. Six wheelmen started at half-past four, viz., Messrs. F. Bate, W. White, J. Timmins, W. Jones, A. Crosby, and A. R. Norman. When nearly a quarter of the distance had been run, Bate went to the front, and at the end of the first lap they crossed the tape iu the following order :—Jenes, Crosby, and White. Norman, Jones. and White now gave up the contest, but Crosby continued to run. In the second lap Bate fell, and had to steer into a hedge, with a disabled machine, owing to a horse being in the path. Shortly after Crosby came up, and lent Bate his machine, with which he went forward quietly until the end of the race, as it was quite evident that any attempt to overhaul Timmins would have proved a failure. The time was—Timmins 30 min. 20 sees.; and Bate 36 min. 25 secs. Mr. W. Kay acted as starter, Mr, W. Pate as.; indp;e, and Mr, Arthur Timmins as referee and timekeeper. The annual dinner afterwards took place at Wilson's Hotel, kept by Mr. Jackson. Mr. Edward Marwood, one of the vice-presidents, occupied the chair, and Mr. J. H. Salkeld, the vice-chair. Messrs. J. D. Jones, Thos. Bate, and John A. Rushton were present as visitors from the R.W.B.C. ; and also Mr. John Marwood, of Liverpool. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts had been pro- posed, the Chairman gave "The champion of the Runcorn Amateur Bicycle Club.' He spoke in very complimentary terms of Mr. Timtnins, and banded him the first prize—a silver medal with gold centre. He also presented Mr. Bate with the second prize—a silver medal. The winners having responded, the Vice-Chairman proposed "Success to the Runcorn Amateur Bicycle Club," which Mr. F. A. Smith acknowledged. The toast of "The unsuccessful competi- tors" was responded to by Mr. Arthur Crosby. The toast of "The visitors" was acknowledged by Mr. J. D. Jones, who spoke of the kindly feelings existing between the Amateurs and the R.W.B.C. M. Frith responded to 'The president an officers of the club." " The town and trade of Runcorn" was given by the Vice-Chairman, and repliA to by Mr. A. Timmins. Other minor toasts followed.

A SALVATIONIST CHARGED WITH BIGAMY. Eliza Hathaway, a captain of the Salvation Army, who has been carrying on successful missions in Yorkshire, was committed for trial yesterday by the Kidderminster magis- trates for bigamy. The second husband—Thomas Bradley —did not appear to advantage in his cross-examination, and admitted that he offered to drop the proceedings if the pri- soner would live with him again. He asserted that this was a trap to get the prisoner into custody. She was bailed , out.

At the Liverpool Wesleyan District meeting, this week, Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, of Runcorn, was appointed one of the gentlemen to attend the enzuing conference during it finan cial session.

Many of the Widnes ratapayers are enquiring whether there is any truth in the report that at the last meeting of the joint Highway and Health Committee, the fact was elicited that the Hutchinson trustees, in the early part of 1880, forwarded a communication in which they asked the enormous sum of £5,500 for the wayleave over half a mile length of road in respect to the sewerage scheme. I understand that a question is to be asked on this subject, which is of vital importance to the Widnes ratepayer, at the next meeting of the Board. Certain gentlemen main- tain that the contract for the sewerage scheme has not vet been let; and some of the advocates of economy say that if this be the cue, C.te Board ought to pause before they adorit a scheme which may land the township in a very heavy expense.

At the meeting of the branch of the Blue Ribbon Army in Runcorn, on Thursday evening, the Rev. E. Williams, who presided, told a story which caused much laughter. It was to the efect that a fortnight ago, he was at a certain rail- way station, about 60 miles from Runcorn, and he saw a young man who was wearing a piece of blue ribbon in his coat. Another passenger walked up to the young man, and said,' What does it require to be a member of your army ?" The reply was—" Simply a strong will, and a determination that you will neither taste, touch, nor handle:" The couple were then joined by another person upon the platform, who said, "I don't believe in your army, for if total abstinence be right, 'why did Peter say to Abraham Take a little wine for thy stomach's sake." Said the young man of the blue ribbon, ." I don't know that 'Peter ever said any such thing to Abraham." The reply of the lover of stimulants was— " Don't you? Then I know what you are! You have never read your Bible !"

It is stated that Mr. Oopenheim, who for some time has acted as legal adviser to the Widnes Local Board, has sent in a bill of £6OO for legal charges. lam also informed that the account stands at that amount after having passed through the hands of the taxing master. __

DRAVII OF bin. Jorm Ruin; OF RUNCORN.—We regret to announce the- death of Mr. John Rigby, of Run- corn, at the advanced ago of 89 years. Mr. Rigby was at one time a very prominent character in the local historY of Runcorn. His funeral, which took place at the Parish Church on Thursday afternosn, was of a very simple char- acter. Besides several late tenants and friends of deceased, Only the nearest relatives were present. The mourning coaches were occupied by Mrs. Leicester, only surviving sister of deceased; Mrs. Hughes, daughter of deceased; Miss Hughes, granddaughter • Mr. Frederick Rigby; son of deceased ; Mr. John Rigby, Q.C., of London; and Mr. Car- ruthers. The service was read by the Rev. J. J. Bryant. RUNCORN FE POLIO LIBRARY COXIIITTER.—On Thursday the monthly meeting of this committee was held in the Commissioners' Board-room. There were present Messrs. Handley (chairman pro. tens.), Simpson, Briscoe, Riley, and Brookes (secretary). A resolution was passed that the Commissioners be asked to pay into the fund of the committee the sum of £5O. The committee continued the consideration of the draft rules, and it was resolved on the motion of Mr. Briscoe, seconded by Mr. Riley, that the draft be printed, and a copy sent to each member, and that the committee stand adjourned to June Bth, for the purpose of finally revising the rules anti to make arrangements for opening the Library.

div.p: ST. HELENS CORPORATION WATER BILL.

The St. Helens (Corporation) Water Bill came before the Committee on private bills yesterday, Mr. Playfair presid- ing. The bill, which was unopposed, was passed and ordered to be reported to the House.
DRUNKENNESS AT WORKING MEN'S CLUBS.

An inquest was held yesterdiy, at Burnley, on the body of James Miller, French polisher, aged 20 years. .The de- ceased was a pianist at the Cattle Market Hotel, and on Sat- urday night left the place at 12 o'clock. He went to the Albion Working Men's Club and remained there till six o'clock on Sunday morning. He had drink at the hotel and also at the club. On leaving the latter it is supposed that he fell down the stairs. He was immediately after- wards carried home and attended by a doctor, but died on Wednesday. The coroner passed a very severe stricture upon the clubs of Burnley generally and this one in particular, which he described as an accursed institution which ruined thousands of young men. The jury concurred in the obser- vations of the coroner, and returned a verdict of accidental death through falling whilst drunk. The coroner disallowed the expenses of the witnesses connected with the club.
THE CRISIS IN EGYPT. THE ENGLISH AND FRENCH FLEETS.

A Candia telegram of Thursday says :—Vice-Admiral Sir F. Beauchamp-Seymour, on board Her Majesty's ironclad Invincible, adcompanied by the gun vessels Bittern and Falcon, together with the French squadron, under Vice- Admiral Conrad, consisting of the Gallissoniere, Forbin, and Aspic, left Sucla Bay yesterday evening for Alexandria.

div.head: CORONATION OF THE CZAR.
div.p: THE CORONATION OF THE CZAR.

A St. Petersburg telegram of yesterday's date says:—The Minister of the Imperial Household is stated to have issued a circular to the Court dignitaries, informing them that the coronation of the Czar will be celebrated at Moscow, on September oth, and that the festivities on the occasion will last a fortnight. The Moscow Exhibition will be opened on the 29th inst. Prince Alexander, of Bulgaria, left here yesterday, for Moscow.

div.head: SHIP BURNT AT SEA.
div.p: A SHIP BURNT AT SEA.

A special cable message to Lloyds', date Caps Verde Isles, on Thursday, states that the barque Celaeno, of London, 6SI tons register, bound from Liverpool t,3 Rio de Janeiro with a full cargo of general goods, has b2en totally destroyed by fire in the North Atlantic. The crew took to the boats, were picked up by a passing vessel, and landed at St. Vincent on Thursday. The ship anti cargo were valued at £20,000. \
SERIOUS POST-OFFICE ROBBERY IN MANCHESTER.

At Bootle, yesterday, Jane Lewis and Janet Brookcs, servants, were charged with stealing a cash box, £4O in gold, and a great quantity of , postal orders, the property of the Postmaster-General. Brookes's sister was employed as a domestic by the postmaster of St. Luke's, Manchester. She stole the property on the 13th instant. and handed it to her sister to keep at her lodgings in Liverpool. She being afraid, handed the property to Lewis, who was in respectable service in Bootle. The police apprehended Lewis and traced the theft. The prisoners were handed over to the Manchester police.
NORTH-WEST RIDING ELECTION. The counting of the votes was proceeded with yesterday moruing and the result was announced as follows : ISAAC HOLDEN' (L) A. E. GATHORNE HARDY (C)
Majority

The returning officer declared the result of the poll at one or two-minutes before noon, and in the presence of an im- mense and enthusiostic crowd. Mr. Holden, the successful candidate at once proceeded to the Liberal Club, from the window of which he addressed a very larg crowd, who re- ceived the intelligence with tremendous cheering. Mr. Gathorne Hardy, the Conservative candidate, also delivered a speech to his supporters from the Victoria Hotel, and ex- pressed himself not unsatisfied with the reduction of the Liberal majority obtained at the general election in 1880. The Conservative party generally, however, do not disguise the fact that they expected their c tndidate to approach Mr. Holden much nearer than the result has shown him to have done. The news was wired to all parts of the division, throughout which the greatest interest and enthusiasm was shown.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIARENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.
THE KILMAINHAM TREATY.—Lord CARLINGFORD, repiy. to Lord Oranmore, said he had had no communication with the suspects in Kihnainham.

THE- EDUCATION CODE.—Lord NORTON moved to refer the education code of 'B3 to a Stlect Committee to remedy its defects. He complained that public money went to the children of the middle class, of the system of grants by individual results, and levying a fixed standard all over the country. —Lord aiRLINGFORD said the most of what was complained of was not created by the new code, but had been adopted by Parliament 20 years ago. He hoped the House would not assent to the motion.—The Duke of Richmond, Bishop Carlisle, and Earl Fortescue also spoke. The motion was withdrawn.
Several bills were forwarded, after which the House adjourned.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

NOTICE OF MOTION.—Sir E. IN ILMOT gave notice that in cpmmittee on the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Bill he should move an amendment to limit the power of appeal from decisions of the judges to sentences of death and penal servitude for life.

TELEPHONE COMPANIES FAwcErr said some appli- cations for license for telephone companies to work London were under consideration. There was no intention on the part of the post office to purchase the business of any par- ticular company. RIVERS CONSERVANCY BILL—Mr. DODSON, replying to Mr. Duckham, said he hoped to pass the Rivers Conservancy Bill this seFsion.

ORDER OF BUSINE'S.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir S. Northcote, said that in the event of the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Bill icing read a second time that day, he should press the second reading of the Arrears Bill on Monday. It was yet doubtful whether there would be any Whitsuntide holidays. THE PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELAND) BILL.—The ad- journed debate on the motion for the second reading of the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Bill was resumed by Mr. SEXTON, who stated his objections to the bill. He condemned the measure as one of unheaed of severity, and one that would never have been required had it net been for the irritating, ceaseless, and causeless application a the provisions of the Protection of Life and Property Act by the late Chief Secretary for Ireland. He strongly objected to annulling trial by jury in Ireland, because the Irish judges were merely a body of promoted politicians, political land- lords, and past marshalls of Her Majesty's Government.— Mr. GLADSTONE said the utmost importance was attached to the rapid progress of the bill, and appealed to members to defer suggestions of amendment until committee. He justi- fied the Government proposing such measures, and, referring to the public feeling as regarded the atrocious assassina- tions in Phoenix Park, he said he had received over 600 addresses, almost all coming from public bodies and many from Ireland. There was not one of them that did not speak language of wrath and resentment, and expressed-the hope that the Government would adhere to their intentions of giving full strength and full, justice to the people of Ire- land with respect to the bill. It would be idle for him to say thst the Government did not regard it as one of the 'deepest importance ; further, they considered it was abso- lutely necessary that it should pass that House with its 1 main lines unaltered.—Mr. PARNELL said it was not intended to oppose the bill unfairly, and further, he believed the Government only intended to use it against crime ; but other Governments had said the SAITIe thing when they brought in Coercion Bills for Ireland. He believed the Bill would not meet the object required, acid he expressed deep regret at the great crime that had been committed, as it prevented the Government proceeding in the path of conciliation. He wished for longer time between the second reading and conamittee.—Mr. BROADHURST expressed great dislike to portions of the Bill.—Mr. HEALY said if the Government really intended to Use power with moderation, they should show their bona files in dismissing Mr. Clifford Lloyd.—Mr. A. GREY supported the Bill, believing the present state of things required stringent measures.—Mr. STOREY opposed the Bill, because it would fail to produce the results the Government desired, and because it would not secure capture of criminals or detect crime in Ireland.— Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the Government could not delay the committee over Tuesday; but any particular clause that was objected to on the ground of an amendment not pre- pared would readily be postponed.—Mr. Mitchell Henry and Mr. Callan also spoke.—On a division the voting was as follows :—For the second reading, 383; against, 45; majority against, 333. The sitting was afterwards suspended.

LYItENI PETTY SEssroxs.—These sessions were held on Friday, the Bench being occupied by Mr. Norris and Mr. Stanton. There was no business of public interest transacted. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT LY:llll\l.—The Rev. W. Inman, of Blackpool, preached the anniversary sermons at the Primitive Methodist Chapel. Lymm, on Sunday afternoon and evening last, when collections were made in aid of the trust fund. A tea meeting was held on Monday evening; and afterwards several addresses were delivered.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

DARNHALL Scrroors.—These schools having been repaired and rendered more comfortable, some time ago a bazaar was got up to meet the expenses, which were considerably over £lOO. The sum realized not being the amount wanted, and many of the articles not sold, another bazaar was held last week, which was followed by an entertainment of a mis- cellaneous character. A portion of " Midsummer's night dream "and " Cinderella " were selected for representation, and some songs and music were given. There was a very good audience, who seemed greatly to appreciate the efforts for their amusement.

OVER FAIR.—The annual May fair was held on Wednes- day last. There was a very good attendance of cattle and pigs, and sales were very brisk. The shows and booths Szc. as usual were very numerous, and the day being fine they were greatly patronize I by those who always make a holiday of the fair day.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

PRIMITIVZ METHODIST ANNIVERSART.—On Sunday last two sermons were preached in the Primitive Metho list Chapel, Lanehead, Lowton, afternoon and evening, by Mr. W. E. Parker, of Manchester. The choir, under the leader- ship of Mr. John Ashton, sang very well. Mr. Wm. Cooke presided at the harmonium. The collections during the day amounted to £26 4s. 4d. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSAIIY.—On Sunday last, two sermons were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Gollyorne— morning and evening—to good congregations, by the Rev. W. J. Powell, of Manchester. The sermons were very effec- tive. The choir sang with their usual goad taste the hymns and anthems selected for the occasion. The collections. during the day amounted to £2l is. Mr. G. Ball, of Golborne, addressed the scholars and teachers in tne after-. noon.

GOLBORNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—At a meeting of the members of the above association, on Thurs- day evening:, May 11th, the following resolutions were unanimously adopted :—" That this meeting of the members of the Golborne and D.strict Liberal Association desires to place on record its deep sense of horror and abhorrence at the fearful assassinations of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. T. H. Burke; and begs to tender to the relatives of the deceased gentlemen its profound sympathy, and trusts that they may have sufficient strength given them from above to enable them to bear this heavy and grievous affliction." Also, "That this meeting desires to assure the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone of its sympathy and support in these try- ing circumstances, and of its unabated confidence in the present Ministry." ' CHILD RUN OVER AT GOLBORNE.—On Tuesday morning last, a child about 18 months old, belonging to Wm. and Sarah Wilcock, residing at Bank Heath, was run over by a cart owned by Adamson and Co., contractors and builders, Askton, while playing on the road opposite Cobden Ter- race, near to the child's home. The man in charge was carting bricks from Messrs. Garton's brickyard. In coming up the brow opposite the place named he went behind the cart to assist the horse Pup the brow, and while thus engaged the child by some means came in contact with the cart, was knocked down, and the wheel passed over one of its arms from hand, to shoulder. Dr. Worsley was called in, carefully examined the child, and ordered it to be taken to the Wigan Infirmary at once. _

SUDDEN DEATH AT Got BORNE.—On Thursday morning a woman named Mary Biackmore, of .131:yuu, aged-about 64, years, arrived in Golborne by the train due at 6-40 a.m. She came to inform her SOP, who is employed by Messrs. Garton, bricktnakers, that his father was seriously ill. She saw her son in the brickyard, informed him of the sad news, and left him about a quarter to eight a.m. to return. A man named Benjamin Waterworth left the brickyard with a load of bricks immediately after her. When he got to the bridge which spans the brook near Coblen-tertace he saw her lying on the ground, he stopped his cart, and tried to lift her on her feet, but failed. He then called to her son, who came immediately, and before assistance could be renderei she was dead. She was carried to her son's residence near to where she was found. In one hour from her arrival in Golborne she was a corpse. Her son is not aware that any- thing was the matter with her health when she left him.
