Z A.;mitage. "INFESTED WITH BEGGARS."—A grey haired man named William Thomson was charged with begging in Bewsev- road.—r.c. Glasson, who apprehended the prisoner, said he had two-pence in his 'possession.—The Chief-Constable : That neighbourhood is infested with beggars.—Prisoner : I don't know what neighbourhood I was in. I never was about the town before in my life. I am sorry it has hap- pened, and I hope you will deal as leniently as possible.— The Chief-Constable: You beg like an old one. You must have been hero before.—Prisoner : No, sir ; I never was here before, or any place like it.—As prisoner was an old man he was discharged on promising to leave the town, which he readily agreed to do.--Jarnes McGuinness was charged with a similar offence by P.C. Glasson.—lt was. stated that this was a different case to the last, as the pri- soner belonged to the town, but "never would work."—He was committed for seven days hard labour. MiscELL.ixEous.--Edward Larkin, basket maker, was summoned by James Chantler for 10s. compensation, by reason of defendant haying broken his contract of service, and defendant, who did not appear, was ordered to pay the amount at the rate of is. a week.—Thomas Morris, 17, Tan- ner's-lane, was bound over to keep the peace 12 months for having assaulted his wife on the 18th May.—Winifred Rourke, a well known character, was summoned for having, on the 17th inst„ made use of malicious threats towards Mary Kerley. The language said to have been used was of a most disgraceful character. "Your worship, gent:emen," said the defendant, "it's all through a married man, and because I have a bad name, and have been up here so often, they put it all on me." Defendant was ordered to be bound over, or in default seven days' imprisonment. Defendant: I can't get any bail, sir.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

The first meeting of the newly-elected waywardens was held in the Surveyor's office, Masonic Chambers, on Wed- nesday. There were present Messrs. Robert Homghton, Joseph Hartley, Broadhurst, J. Fakelough, Jas. Wright, Geo. Lawton, John Stonier, Edward Marsh, Samuel Bent, Jas. Turner, Win. Royston, Henry Woolf, Reginald Owen, Joseph Pennington, Jas. Houghton, John Grounds, H. B. White (clerk), Longland (deputy clerk), and Thompson (surveyor).

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.
The CLERK said the first business would be the election of a chairman and vice-chairman.
Mr. HARTLEY moved, and Mr. ROYSTON seconded, thai Mr. Robert Houghton be again elected chairman. This was carried unanimously, as was also a motion thai Mr. Joseph Hartley be appointed vice-chairman.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Gmeral Purposes and Finance Committee was ap- pointed as follows :—Messrs. J. Fairclough, J. Hartley, Samuel Breadbmt, Jas. Turner, Wm. Royston, Jas. Wright, R. Owen, junr., Jas. Houghton, and Geo. Lawton.
THE SURiEYOR'S ESTIMATE.-DISCUSSION ON THE RATH.

The CLERK read the Surveyor's estimate for the year ending March 1883. It stated the gross estimate for district roads was £1,747 7s. 7d • main roads, £921 Os. 91; improve- ments, £1,095; salaries, £320; geoeral expenses, £5O; total, £4,133 13s. 44., which would require a rate of 91 in the pound. In reply to a member, the SURVEYOR said the Board had a balance in hand of about £6OO, and there were materials in stock to the amount of £4OO.
Mr. ROYSTON : What does a penny in the make throughout the district?
Thee SURVEYOR : £459 6s. 7d.

Mr. PENNINGTON said the rate of Pd. in the pound was laid last year that the Board might get a good balance in hand and having now got that balance he thought the rate ought to be lowered. The county rate was now, much larger than it previously was, and yet they were paying the same highway rate, thus getting no benefit from the larger balance, in hand. He knew the farmers found great difficulty in paying the rates, and as before many years past the repairing of roads would be put upon a broader basis than it was at present, the Board ought to hold their hand until this matter was settled. The subject was engaging the attention of Parliament every year, and he had no doubt that but for the troubles in Ireland, something would have been settled this year. The Board ought certainly to receive the benefit from the county contributions of about £4OO or £5OO. He moved that the rate be reduced from 9d. to Bd. Mr. ROYSTON seconded the motion, pointing out that a penny in the now produced a much larger sum than it did some years ago. Mr. HARTLEY proposed an amendment that the rate be Pd. in the £as last year. It was true the Board had a balance in hand, and it was also true that they had been striving for some years to get a balance in hand. (Hear, hear). They , had up to the present always been behind, and had in con- sequence to pay interest where they ought not to have paid, and in his opinion it would be much better to continue the rate as last year. A penny in the £ was a large sum in the aggregate, but separately it was only a small amount, and he thought there would be less difficulty in paying it now than there ever had been, considering the bright prospects for farmers.

Mr. OWEN seconded the amendment. • He considered it 'would be false economy to reduce the rate to Bd., and stated that in Croft they wanted all the rate they could get in Order to keep the roads in the condition they had been for , Some time past, which was very bad. A is. rate would be better for Croft.

Mr. PENNINGTON remarked that a penny in the £ made a great difference to himself individually and to scores of othtk. BROADHURST, in supporting the amendment, said they were forgetting that the canal and railway companies were „the greatest ratepayers and upon them would fall the great r, burden-of the rate. Me. HARTLEY observed that at the present time the Board t-hacl'enty about £7O really in hand. Mr. PENNINGTON replied that they would receive the • money from the county, and £6OO was the real balance. The amendment was then put, when n. voted for it, and four against. ' A Pd. Tate will therefore be levied, and the Finance Com- mittee was einpowered to sign the precepts.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 20, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 20, 1882.

States, where their friends expect they will escape detec- tion. There is still no news of any important arrest for the murders in Dublin. In every case so far as can be as- certained, either on this side of the Channel or in Ireland it- self, the arrests which have been made are of no importance.

The Rev. Canon Murphy, parish priest of St. Kevin, drop- ped dead in the pulpit on Sunday morning, after exhorting the congregation to assist in discovering the assassins. The Duke of Devonshire has requested the newspapers to state that Lady Frederick Cavendish and other members of his family have received so many communications expres- sing sympathy with them in their sufferings that it is im- possible to acknowledge them separately, and they there- fore desire through the press to return their most grateful thanks for the kind feeling which has been shown towards them.

It has been officially announced by the Lord-Lieutenant that, in addition to the reward of £lO,OOO for information that will lead to the conviction of the murderers, the Govern- ment are prepared to give a reward of £lOO for information that will lead to the arrest of any person who has harboured or in any way assisted the assassins. A rumour that gained some currency on Saturday evening, and was very widely spreid on Monday, to the effect that the four men who had Murdered Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke had been arrested by the Dublin police, was every- where received with feelings of deep satisfaction ; but, un- fortunately, the story was not confirmed. The Government have granted a pension of £4OO per annum to Miss Burke, the sister of the late Under-Secretary for Ireland.
Spccial prayers will be offered next Sunday in all the Congregational churches in the kingdom for Ireland and its rulers.

Unsuccessful as the police have so far been, they still believe that they will eventually capture the murderers. Their inquiries lead them to believe that there have been no fewer than twelve persons engaged in the tragedy, some of these—armed, it is believed—being in the cab that was seen near the spot when the assassinations were committed, while others were loitering about in the immediate neigh- bourhood, ready to give assistance if required. It is believed, too, that the diabolical plot was directed against the lives of eight persons, not only against those of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and that the assassins are still in Dublin and all together, being afraid to trust each other.

Cardinal McCabe arrived in Dublin on Thursday night, and was presented with an address of welcome. In reply, his Eminence expressed horror at the recent assassinations, and hoped the assassins would be captured. Earl Spencer on Tuesday received deputations from Dublin University and Queen's College of Surgeons, when addresses were presented. The address from the University expressed feelings of deep humiliation at the recent assassinations. His Excellency, in reply, expressed his determination to pursue a vigorous policy to root out crime.

div.head: 'IRISH ASSASSINATION
div.p: THE 'IRISH ASSASSINATION
LETTER FROM THE QUEEN.

Miss Burke, sister of the Under Secretary, has received the following autograph letter from her Majesty the Queen : " Buckingham Palace, May 10th, 1882. "Dear Miss Burke,—Though not personally acquainted with you, I am anxious to express to you again in writing how deep and sincere my sympathy is with you in this hour of affliction and bereavement, and how much I deplore the loss of one who had devoted his life to the service of his Sovereign and country SO loyally, faithfully, and ably. It is impossible to express the horror which I, in common with the world at large, have experienced at the dreadful event of last Saturday; and whilst nothing can make up to you and to poor Lady Cavendish for the loss of a beloved brother and husband, the universal sympathy which is felt for you may, I hope, be soothing to you. Trusting that your health may not suffer, and praying that God may support you, believe me, sincerely yours,
(Signed)
VICTORIA."
LETTER ERONI THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE.

The Chancellor of the University has sent the following reply to the address of condolence adoptad by the Senate at the Congregation held on Thursday last : "Chatsworth, Chesterfield, May 15, 1882. To the Vice Chancellor and Senate of the University of Cambridge. Gentlemen,—l thank you from my heart for your address of condolence. I have derived a melancholy satisfaction from its language expressive of your sympathy and of your feelings of horror and detestation at the foul crime of which my beloved and excellenr son has been the victim. It has afforded me no small consolation to remem- ber that he has perished, as you remind me, in the per- formance of his duty. He went to Ireland, as I know from his own lips in the conviction that he ought not to shrink from the acceptance of the post that was offered to him, and in the earnest hope that he might be of service to his country, and now that he has fallen I pray that it may please Almighty God to overrule this fearful calamity to the restoration of peace and goodwill in Ireland.—l am, gentle- men, your very faithful servant, DEVONSHIRE."

div.head: HOMAGE TO LADY F. CAVENDISH.
div.p: HOMAGE TO LADY F. CAVENDISH.

A deep impression has been produced in Ireland by the letter of Lady Frederick Cavendish. It has been suggested to have it placarded all over the country. The Irish are a people of deep feeling, who will appreciate her ladyship's noble sentiments. No patriotism in ancient or modern times ever reached a higher level of moral elevation. The remark has been heard, "When a woman writes such a letter, it re- minds you of Golgotha, and Father, forgive them.'"

AN ACKNOWLEDGMENT FROM THE PREMIER. The following has been published :-"Mr.Gladstone continues to receive many hundreds of letters and telegrams, mostly on behalf of public meetings of political assnciations, expressing indignation at the crime recently committed in Dublin, and sympathy with the friends and relatives of the deceased. A large portion of them further express con- fidence in her Majesty's Government and approve of their Irish policy. Mr. Gladstone can only repeat his regret that it is impossible to acknowledge these communications iddividually, and that he is obliged to content himself with this general expression of his gratitude and apprecia- tion of the tone and spirit in which they are conceived."

div.head: SUPPOSED DISCOVERY OF THE CAR.
div.p: SUPPOSED DISCOVERY OF THE CAR.

Telegraphing on Monday, a correspondent says :—The police have at last succeeded in tracing the car used by the assassins into the city, which turns out to be one let out for hire. •It was hired and paid for by some person unknown to the owner, anil who he could not identify, and was brought back shortly after eight o'clock in the evening with the horse covered with foam. There was no trace of blood on the car, which is accounted for by the fact that it had no cushions, and the assassins covered the seats with rugs which they afterwards carried away with them. It has also been ascertained that the assassins alighted from the car at the corner of a particular street in the city, which is now re- ceivirT all due attention at the hands of the police. From inquiries in another direction, the police have also discovered the man whom they believed to be, and have no doubt was, the driver of the car on the occasion of the assassina- tion, and the greatest efforts will be made to obtain informa- tion from him. The police are doubtful whether they can at present connect the chain of circumstantial evidence against this man should he decline to inform, but at 'pre- sent the prospects of the assassins being trought to justice arc more hopeful than ever since the murder. ALLEGED FIENDISH PLOTS: ASTOUNDING

div.head: STATEMENTS.
div.p: STATEMENTS.

The Paris Voltaire published on Sunday a communication relative to the Irish crisis which cannot fail to attract atten- tion. It proceeds from "a correspondent who, through his relations with the Russian Nihilists, has on several occasions supplied important information which has been justified by facts." The writer says :

The assassination of. Lord Frederick Cavendish and of Mr. Burke has given rise to the most improbable suppositions. People have been surprised that, on the very day on which the new Secretary of State for Ireland took official posses- sion of his post, he was murdered in company with the Under-Secretary, Mr. Burke. This is the explanation. Some months ago a secret society, essentially political in character' and having apparently at least nothing in com- mon with the Land League, Home Rule, or even with the Fenians, was formed in America. Its object is to render the English administration in Ireland well-nigh impossible through terrorism. The principal plan is the assassination of all the high officials who may be sent to Ireland by the Government. The organisation of this society is extremely powerful. Its chiefs have addressed themselves to the lead- ing revolutionists in other countries, asking them to recom- mend them energetic men qualified to facilitate the execu- tion of their sinister projects. Their means of action are very great, as they have enormous sums at their disposal. They have sub-committees in the principal Irish towns. The assassination of Mr. Forster, the late Secretary of State for Ireland, as well as that of Lord Cowper, the late Viceroy, had been ordered some months ago, and its execution has only been prevented by considerations of expediency. Lord Ir. Cavendish and Mr. Burke are the victims of this first sentence. All the representatives'of the Englis4 Government are doomed. Machines such as those employed for the " execution " of the Emperor Alexandra are introduced into Ireland. On the day of the assassination several aifilies ap- pointed by the foreign auxiliaries were in Dublin. Three of the murderers are already abroad. The £IO,COO sterling promised by the Government for the discovery of the assas- sins will not procure the arrest of one man. Events of the utmost gravity are coming on in Ireland, and all the efforts of the English Government to seize the organisers of this terrible society and to prevent the execution of their plans will prove ineffectual.

div.head: LATEST FROM DUBLIN.
div.p: THE LATEST FROM DUBLIN.

A Dublin correspondent telegraphs later, that there is absolutely nothing fresh to record relative to the murders. A number of reports are in circulation respecting the car, but the police have not discovered any additional clue to connect the vehicle which was hired from a local car pro- prietor on the evening of the murder with the assassins. The police, however, are more sanguine now of the discovery of the perpetrators of the crime than they were last week, but they do not disguise the fact that in the almost total absence of any evidence as to the identification, a conviction will be impossible even should they succeed in arresting the mur- derers, unless one of the party tarns informer. The carman is the only one of whom they have any hope in this direc- tion. The fear of being arrested has now become so general that the peasantry who have occasion to travel outside their own immediate districts apply to the constabulary for pass- ports. This course is invariably resorted to by the lar.ie number of emigrants leaving the south of Ireland for America.

div.head: NEW YORK STORY.
div.p: A NEW YORK STORY.

New York telegrams state that information has been tele- graphed to the United States Government that the four murderers of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke are believed to be on board the Cunard Steamer Scythia, which left Liverpool on Saturday, the 6th inst., the day on which the murders were committed, and which arrived at New York at eleven p.m. on Tuesday. The British Minister at Washington is said to have been instructed by the Foreign qffice to demand of the American Government the arrest nd ettradition of the fugitives as soon as they landed, and in accordance with this request a body of selected United States marshals, acting under a special mandate from the President, went out in a revenue cutter to meet the steamer .110 arrest the suspected persons. A Reuter's despatch states that no suspicious person was found on board the Scythia, '!and that no arrests were made.

div.head: POLICE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE ASSASSINS.
div.p: POLICE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE ASSASSINS.

The Police Gazette, or Hue .and Cry contains the follow- ing description of the four men wanted for the murder of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, the Chief and Under Secretaries for. div.head: PUBLIC MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: PUBLIC MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

A requisition having been presented to the Mayor request- ing him to call a public meeting to express horror and indig- nation at the murder of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and sympathy with their bereaved families, his Worsbip convened a meeting for this purpose at the Warrington Public Hall, on Saturday evening. The meeting was well attended, and amongst those present were a large number of Irishmen. The Mayor (Alderman Plckmere) presided, and he was supported by the Revs. E. C. E. Carlton, S. Wilkin- son, J. Yonge, J.- Eglinton, J.A. Beet, T. Rippon, Father Feeny, Father Pozzi, and E. Moore, Aldermen Davies, Holmes, and Chandley, Councillors Broadbent, Caldwell, Mackie, Messrs. G. T. Moore, I'. Flood, and others. The MAYOR, who was received with applause, said they were met that evening to express. their horror and indigna- tion at a most foul murder, but before going into the matter he would read a few letters which he had received from two or three gentlemen showing the reason why they were not present that evening. The first, his Worship said, was from Walton Hall, and stated that Lady Greenall's mother was very ill, and she had had to go to London to see her. Of course, Sir Gilbert was very much upset, and that was the reason why he could not be present. Sir Gilbert added that the murders in Ireland had been most cruel and terrible, and they had shocked the nerves of every right-minded person Councillor Monks wrote from Ambleside—" I should have attended had I been at home, to show my sympathy with the noble House of Cavendish, who for generations have given men to the service of their country. (Hear, hear). I hope the meeting will be a success, and that the resident Irishmen will denounce the crime as one of those blunders calculated to foster hatred and jealousy. What is wanted is the growth of feeling which shall make Irishmen feel that they are as much a part of the nation as any Scotchmen, or Englishmen. (Applause). I hope one result of this blow to Ireland will be to unite us together as Britishers, and that Irishmen will see,—whatever injustice may have been done them in the past,—there is every disposition to be generous. to them now." (Applause). His Worship then went on to say that be had called the meeting in accordance with the requisi- tion very numerously signed. He did not know whether they had all heard the news which had come to the telegraph office, and also to the newspaper offices, that the assassins had been caught in Dublin. (Cheers). Of course they would hear further, and they hoped it was true. (Hear, hear, and applause). They were assembled that evening with one feel- ing, and he hoped an unanimous feeling, to show by their presence their Lorror and indignation at the savage butchery which was executed upon two innocent, confiding men in Dublin about that time in the previous week. Lord F. Cavendish went over to Ire- land, as he might term it, with a white feather in his hand, almost to preach good will and bring the hearts of the dis- obedient to the wisdom of the just. (Applause.) He had not been in that country more than a few hours than he was struck down by the hand of the assassin together with Mr. Burke, who was with him, and who was merely a servant of , the Crown, and bad to carry out any of the measures which the Government thought proper to pass for that unhappy country. They must all deplore that, and if any gentleman wished to speak on the subject he should be glad to hear him. But he must say this, they must eschew all party polities—(applause)—and religious cre%ls. (Applause.) They must all unite for one purpose, and that was to show as loyal men their indignation at the dastardly outrage which had been committed. (Applause.) Ho would not trespass further, but he was sure of this, that all political parties and creeds in that hall, Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchmen, would join with one voice in supporting the resolution, which he would request one of his friends to read to them. Warrington had been a loyal town ever since he could remember; and was long before that; aud he could only conclude by saying what they would all say that he supported our Queen and country, and "God save the Queen." (Applause.)

Alderman DATIES moved the first resolution :—" That we, the loyal inhabitants of the borough of Warrington, desire to give expression to our horror and indignation at the foul murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and our heartfelt sympathy with their bereaved families and relatives, and unabated devotion and loyalty to our Queen and Constitution; and fervently hope Almighty God will vouchsafe to Her Ministers wisdom and power to overcome the enemies of this Realm." (Applause.) After remarking that he stood before them knowing no difference in politics or religion, he said it had been a mistaken policy through- out to treat Irishmen at all differently to Englishmen. (Applause.) The difference between us ought to have been done away with long since: and when we speak of the nation we ought to speak of Irishmen exactly in the same tone as we speak of Englishmen. We expect in the days of our trouble, when we are fighting our enemies, Irishmen, whenever that day comes, will be found shoulder to shoulder with Englishmen to maintain the Constitution and the kingdom. Speaking to the resolution, he said our great Bard said—
"Murder most foul as in the best it is, But this, most foul, strange and unnatural."

That two innocent men walking in broad daylight on a Saturday evening in the city of Dublin, one of the capitals of the Kingdom, should be struck down by assassins, was a thing they could scarcely comprehend. Words could hardly express their horror and indignation at a foul murder like that. He then showed what manner of men had been mur- dered in Dublin. He gave an instance where Lord Frederick Cavendish visited a tenant on the estate of the Duke of Devonshire in Ireland, and they told him, not knowing who he was, that they could not pay their rent and that they thought they would be ejected. Next morning they received a cheque from Lord F. Cavendish for the full amount of the arrears, and a few sovereigns more to speed the plough. (Applause.) That was the sort of man that *as struck down in Dublin last Saturday evening. ("Shame.") He should like Warrington to show that they had equal regard for a noble man who was also murdered— he meant Mr. Burke. Mr. Burke was an Irishman and a Roman Catholic, but it had been suggested that he was not a friend of the Irish. He, however, quoted from a paper to show that Mr. Burke provided more facts, more figures, and practical information generally, for the framing of the recent Irish Land Bill than any other person. They were called together to give expression to their horror and indignation at a naturaCcalamity. After speaking of the terrible blow it must have been to the relations of the deceased to receive the news of the murder, the alderman said he expected that every man in the room would vote and fhat the vote would be unanimous. (Applause.) The Rev. Father FEENY, who was cordially greeted, said in obedience to the request of the Mayor he rose to second, and that with all his heart, and with all sincerity, the resolu- tion which had been proposed by Alderman Davies. If left to himself he certainly would not have risen, but would have preferred to wait until older men had spoken, and people who were more officially thrnwu in their midst. But perhaps if they looked at the object of the meeting, there might be a -reason why be, not old in years, might be allowed to come before them at such an early stage to speak out to them his own candid opinion, and also his protest in the name of the Irish and English Catholics in Warrington. (Applause.) It was difficult for any man to speak with any- thing like the intensity of feeling he ought to express in words as regarded this double murder, committed the previous Saturday evening in Phoenix Park in Dublin. He was well aware that as this dual crime was committed in the capital of Ireland, the finger of reproach was first of all pointed at Irishmen, and secondly to Catholics ; and therefore it became his imperative duty as a clergyman of the Church of Rome—(applause)—to speak out his mind candid,v and fearlessly with reference to such a resolution as had been proposed that night, and come forward with 110 uncertain voice to tell them distinctly that. from the bottom of their hearts as clergymen of the Church of Rome, and as those thrown in the midst of the Irish and English Catholics of the town, they felt the utmost dismay, consternation, and '
(Dia i(;Ei
grwhi,bLd

intense disgust at the awful deed, which surely was a blot upon the three countries. (Applause). They were all aware a week had already passed, and men's minds as time went on seemed almost to be paralised with the feeling which was uttermost in their hearts—the feeling of indigna- tion and horror at the foul crime—and it was with Dome pleasure that evening, and they hoped it was true, that they heard the assassins had been captured. (Applause.) He might say if they had kept their ears and eyes open during the past week and scanned the columns of the different newspapers, in justice to Catholics this dual crime had been put at the doors of secret societies. Perhaps they would allow him, as a priest of the Catholic Church, to tell them what was the distinct teaching of the Catholic Church as regarded these secret societies. In the first place there had been some talk in the papers of the past week of passing a Coercion Act—and they all knew what that meant— specially directed against secret societies. Many of them, of course, would admit that this was almost the first time he thought in the history of England that they had found need or necessity for such an Act as was mooted at the present time in the House of Commons; but when they came to consider the heinousness of the crimes committed— he might say without parallel in the history of this country —they would not think as Irishmen, Englishmen, and Catholics that any Bill was too strong to try to grapple with these awful deeds. (Applause). He would ask them, all loyal men of Warrington, what was a secret society? He knew something, as did every Catholic priest of the Church of Rome, of the definition of a secret tociety. They knew that it was an organisation of men who knew each other in their secret chambers and their council rooms, and who kept up the acquaintance outside, whether in their business or in their homes, by secret signs and passes. These men, whatever secret society they might belong to, however , evil it might be in principle, were known to each other but they were not known to the outside world, and in that was a special evil against which they should guard themselves. (Hear, hear). He was not speaking that evening of secret societies in England. There might be secret societies—he believed there were—in England which in themselves as far as they could see were hononrable, and they did not know that ever they had contemplated any crime which could be translated into an act of disloyalty to their country; but he must say, as a priest, that the Church of Rome con- demned all secret societies. (Applause). Perhaps some gentlemen might think that was rather hard, but if they condemned secret societies at all, it was very hard to draw the line, and to be consistent, and to be logical, though they might feel it in some instances, they must condemn all ; and the Church of Renee, he was glad to say, would be the very first to back up anything in the, shape of a Coercion Act directed against secret societies. (Applause). It was no new thing for the Church of Rome to encourage an act against secret societies, and he was dwelling upon this topic for a purpose, because he told them there was an evident sign in the three kingdoms that such an Act el,ould come into force, and wisely so too. But though it might be new to Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchmen, it was no new thing in the Church of Rome, for Pope after Pope had issued their coercion.acts in order to uproot the evil which was now threatening our society. Pope Pius VI. forbade the priests to have contact or sym- pathy with secret societies, the same was again strengthened and confirmed by Pius VII., and Pius IX. who had had one of the longest reigns in the Church of Rome—and all of them must surely have heard of his wise and generous heart and especially his loyalty to England—time after time coun- selled his cardinals, bishops, and priests to do all in their power in order to level down the influence of secret scicieties. (Applause). As to the Catholics of Warrington there was not one of them who would stand up or in any way encourage and back up these foul assassins who belonged, he was sure, to some secret society. (Applause). More than that, he believed when these men were brought to justice they would find that they were not even Catholics or Irishmen. (Ap- plause). He believed sincerely that they were American desperadoes, men whose whole career mentally, and physi- cally, and in every other way they could work, was for the overthrow of their own empire, and of every church and every religion. (Applause). They had no sympathy with such men, and in the Church of Rome they would never have a home, they would never have a shelter, and they would never have any protection. In conclusion, he was glad to be able to meet them and to say with all sincerity, and with all the emphasis that he could command, that he protested in his own nettle, in the name of his fellow priests, and in the name of Irish and English Catholics of Warrington against this foul crime, and he wished every man would support and strengthen the resolution, which was not only for their own good and credit, but which was also for the good and credit of the whole United Kingdom. (Applause). The Rev. S. WILKINSON seconded the resolution, remark- ing that he was sure the relatives had their sympathy and their prayers. The resolution was unanimously carried. The Rev. J. YONGE moved the next resolution, as follows: —"That his Worship the Mayor be respectfully requested to forward on behalf of this meeting copies of the foregoing resolution to the families of the late Lord Frederick Caven- dish and Thomas Henry Burke, Esq , and also to the Home Secretary." The rev, gentleman could not forbear observing that he thought the character of the nation had been tested by this terrible and sudden trial, and had borne the test in an admit able and sublime manner. (Applause). Time nation had manifested a patience and self-control which had been truly admirable. The Rev. J. EGLINTON seconded the resolution, and trusted the news the Mayor had given them would prove to be correct—(hear, hear)—and that they might learn' the lesson to which reference had been made by this catastrophe. It had been his privilege to share the hospitality of Ireland. He had passed through its breadth and much of its length, and had had fellowship with its people. He loved them so much, and had talked about them so frequently in public and private, that the remark had been made, as people left the building in which he had spoken, "Surely he must be an Irishman." (Laughter.) He never took upon himself to deny it. He rejoiced very much in the spirit which had been manifested by the great bulk of the people of this country and in Ireland in reference to the event, and he thought they had therein some illustration of the fact that the highest kind of liberty was self-imposed restraint. He hoped the leaders of public thought and opinion, and to a very great extent leaders of the feelings of the great mass of the people, would be restrained from free—too free—ex- pressions which, being misinterpreted, sometimes led to sad results. (Applause.) He came to this town from Liver- pool, and had been brought into frequent intercourse with the inhabitants of that city, both Catholic and Protestant; and he had reason, therefore, for what he , now said. He had very great pleasure in seconding the resolution. (Ap- plause.) The MAYOR here read a telegram, which stated that con- flicting reports prevailed in Dublin, but the police were very reticent.

The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, in supporting the resolu- tion, said he would like to echo with all his heart the words of Father Feeny, that the men who had been guilty of this deed were not Irishmen. He also would like to remind those present—at least he could not forget—that about two years ago there was a meeting held in that hall of the pub- lic of Warrington—he supposed Englishmen and Irishmen of Warrington came—to support a measure which had for its object the relief of the suffering boor through the deficiency of the harvest; and he thought it was fad that all this should have been forgotten, and that such a state of things such as had lately existed in Ireland should con- tinue, to the discredit of everyone connected with that country. If this sort of thing was to go on he certainly, should forget he was an Irishman, and should cut his con- nection as soon as possible. He also would like to say in reference to the house of Cavendish, especially in regard to Lady Frederick Cavendish, what perhaps some of them did did not know—that that lady was no stranger to this town, for somewhere about three years ago she visited the very poor neighbourhood of Factory Yard, Bank Quay, and she spoke to a gathering of poor women, showing her kindness and interest in them in a manner which he was sure these women appreciated. (Applause.) He was exceedingly glad that the Government had now resolved to deal firmly with the sad state of things which existed in that country. (Applause.) Of course some of them did not think it required the death of these two noble men to prove the necessity of very stringent and extreme measures; but at any rate they were all united, and the Government, he was sure, might count upon the support of every loyal man and every Christian man in this country. In the reso- lution something was said about loyaltyn to the British Crown. He thought they ought not to forget that although it was proved to them beyond demonstration that many good men had gone in for the separation and dissolution of the British Crown, undoubtedly a certain number of men had used that cry for the purpose of carrying on a very evil and he might say infamous agitation; and he hoped every man in Warrington, whatever his political creed, would bear that in mind; and that there would be no paltering on one side or the other on this question whenever it was placed before them at any political crisis—when a general election took place. Whoever was guilty of paltering or tampering with the question, which meant disloyalty to the empire, would deserve the scorn and reprobation of every man of the community. (Applause.) - Mr. THOMAS FLOOD supported the resolution, and referred to the hospitality of the Irish people. He said Ireland had the misfortune to he overrun with professional agitators and "carpet baggers," who were not true Irishmen, but were of foreign extraction. In the whole of the speeches of the Irish patriots they would not find a sentence encouraging the people to shed the blood of their fellows. Go where they would, through the length and breadth of the land, and see anyone with a spark of Irish feeling within him, his heart would be found drooping with regret that such a calamity should have come over the country. He was proud to hear the sentiments of the English people, which were noble sentiments, and would encourage Irishmen to persevere in maintaining that position in society that they had a right to occupy. He maintained that Ireland occupied a better position in the world under England than she would dis- united. He hoped the announcement that had been made might be true, and he was confident all Irishmen would stand up and with one voice proclaim their joy and satis- faction that the villains had been brought to justice. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Councillor BROADBENT briefly addressed the meeting, remarking that they must not visit the crime wholesale upon the Irish people, but upon the dastardly villains who had committed it. The resolution was then carried; and a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, on the proposition of Alderman HoLmEs, seconded by Alderman CHANDLEY.

Lord Egerton of Tatton, who has been Euffering from a severe attack of bronchitis, is in a much better state of health, his lordship, although still conflned to his bed- room, being able to sit up for several hours each day.

div.head: FRODSHAM,
div.p: FRODSHAM,

CATTLE MART.-Mr. J. J. Steward held his usual fort- nightly sale of fat and store stock last week, at the Queen's Head Hotel. There was a fair attendance of buyers, and the stock realised good prices. Five fat beasts from Mr. Henry Lowe, of Alvanley Hall, made from £l6 ss. to £24 2s. 6d. Three fat cows from Mr. J. E. Bate average £l7 29. GI Fat sheep made from 40s. to die.; fat lambs, 40s. to 50s.

FRODSHAn VOLUNTEER CORRS.—On Saturday this corps had a march out in full dress, accompanied by the band, and were afterwards kindly entertained to supper by Mr. Ralph Bate, of Netherton, the officers present being Captain Robert Ashton and Lieutenant Harrison.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWI,T.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWI,T.

The annual Sunday school sermons were preached at Brunswick Wesleyan chapel, on Sunday last, by the Rev. Mayson Penn, morning and evening to immense audiences; no less than a thousand being present. In the afternoon, a service of song entitled " Gideon " was given by the choir and Sunday school children, which was very well rendered. Miss Greenall presided at the harmonium. Mr. Parr con- ducted, and the collection for the day amounted to £5O 12s. 9d., which was considered very good. The May fair took place in Newton on Wednesday. The weather was fine, and the show of cattle was very ',rood. In the evening there was a large concourse of people about the stalls in the street near the Town Hall. 1.0.G.T. HOPE OF EADLESTOWN LODGE. The usual weekly session of the above lodge was held on Monday evening last, a fair attendance of members being present. The digest of the business for the District Lodge was well discussed, and the lodge representatives were instructed bow to vote on the various items of business. Further arrange- ments were made for the District Lodge session to be held in the Wesleyan school-room, on Saturday, when it is in- tended to have an open-air as well as an indoor public meet- ing after tea. After business had been transacted various members contributed to the enjoyment of the evening with melodies, Sankey's solos, 41.7 c. A very pleasant and harmoni- ous session was closed in the usual form at 9.30 p.m.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.
In the House of Commons on Monday, Mr. Knowles pre- sented a petition from the medical practitioners of Wigan for exemption from increase of the taxes on the carriages used in their profession.

At Wigan, the other day, a dataller named John George Bibby, of Hallgate, Wigan, was charged with having matches in his possession in the Hindley. Deep Pit. The matches and a pipe were found in the defendant's possession, and it was sworn that he recently declared he would blow up the pit. He was sent to prison for a month. DEATH OF AN ER-111.P. Information was received in Wigan on Wednesday, of the death of Mr. Henry Woods, of Bishop Waltham, Hants, senior partner in the firm of Wil- liam Woods and Son, cotton spinners and colliery proprie- tors, Wigan and Blackrod. The deceased gentleman repre- sented Wigan in Parliament in the Liberal interest from 1857 to 1874, when he suffered his first defeat. Since then he has taken no part in local politics. ASSAULTING THE PoucE.—On Wednesday morning, at Wigan, James Blackledge, a collier, was committed to gaol for two months for comtnitting a serious assault on the police on Tuesday night in Wallgate, where petty riots have been rather frequent. The officer was knocked down and seriously kicked, and William Brackel, a civilian who went to his assistance, was also badly used, and during the scuffle lost nearly £7 which he had in his pocket. The ber.ch warmly commended Brackel for his courageous conduct.

div.head: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.
div.p: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.

The Rev. F. Minton has been appointed chairman of the Middlewich Burial Board for the ensuing year. Mr. Samuel Fitton has been re-elected Chairman of the Nantwich Highway Board; and Mr. Booth Vice-Chairman. A proposition for a shilling rate to meet the expenses of the Nantwich Local Board for the half-year ending Septem- ber 29th was unanimously approved by the Board at their last meeting. The annual supper of the Northwich Rugby Football Club took place on Saturday evening last, at the Blue Barrel Jnn, Castle-Northwich. Mr. J. T. Brunner, president of the club, occupied the chair. About 20 gentlemen sat down to dinner.

NEW MAGISTRATES FOR CHESHIRE.—At the adjourned seesions, held at Knutsford on the 16th lost, Mr. Clement William Swetenham, of Swetenham, and Mr. William Henry Verdin, of Wharton, qualified as magistrates for the county of Chester.

The Northwich Guardians at their last meeting resolved to petition against the Poor Removal (Ireland) Bill, the main provision of which is that from the passing of the Act it shall not be lawful for any pauper to be removed or con- eyed to Ireland from an parish or union in England to which the pauper may be chargeable. if he shall have resided ha England, Scotland or Wales for three years before becom- ing so chargeable. The Cheshire Yeomanry assembled for their eight days' training at Chester the other morning, under the command of Captain-Commandant, the Duke of Westminster. Tke Wirral troop, which joined the county yeomanry for His, first occasion, presented a smart appearance. The military drill and evolutions will be carried out daily on the Roodee. Is SIIE HIS WIFE ?—At the Altrincbam Police Court, on Wednesday, Peter Howarth was charged with disobeying an order of the magistrates to contribute 15s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife. The defence was that the woman was not prironer's wife, although she positively swore she was, and that the order was therefore illegal. The prisoner still refused to pay, and was committed to prison for a month in default. Mr. Evans gave notice to move the court above.

At the monthly meeting of the West Eddisbury Highway. Board held at Chester, on Saturday, Mr. H. Linaker, Frod- sham was re-elected chairman, and Mr. H. Beswick, vice- chairman. A question of a peculiar nature was raised by a letter addressed to the Board, in which the writer complained of the obstruction caused by hobby horses, swings, shooting galleries, in public thoroughfares at Frodsham. The 'grievance was one generally felt, and nearly all the leading inhabitants had made complaints on the subject. The clerk said the Board had power to stop shooting galleries, but he was not so certain as to the others, as he believed the lord of the manor bad a right to allow these people to go there. The matter was adjourned for investigation. AN APPEAL CASE.—lsaacs v. Goodall.—This case was heard on Saturday, in the Queen's Bench Division, before Mr. Justice Grove and Mr. Justice Watkin Williams, sitting in banco. Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C. (instructed by Messrs. Moore and Son, Warrington), stated that this was an action of detinue of three horses, the defendant on the record being a livery stable keeper at Altrincham, although the real de- fendant was Lord Stamford. The case was tried before Mr. Justice Cave and a common jury at the Manchester Assizes, and resulted in a verdict for the plaintiff for is. damages and the return of the horses. He (Mr. Russell) now moved for a rule to set aside the verdict, on the ground that it was against the weight of the evidence, and that the learned judge misdirected the jury ; in fact, he contended that there had been a• complete miscarriage of justice. In March, 1881, a man named Buckley, a tenant under Lord Stamford, gave the plaintiff a bill of sale for £9O in respect of a loan of £7O to a third party. That bill of sale was not registered, and in the following month Buckley gave another bill of sale to a person named Townend. The second instrument was registered, and the plaintiff became the holder of it from Townend. At the end of April, Buckley, owing Lord Stamford £370 for rent, a distress was put in, and the goods were sold by auc- tion, but at the sale Lord Stamford's agent caused the greater part ofithe goods to be bought in,out of consideration for Buckley. The agent then entered into an arrangement with Buckley, by which the latter was to surrender his ten- ancy, and in future to manage the farm as bailiff for Lord Stamford, the property which had been bought in, including the three horses in question, remaining on the farm. In August it came to the knowledge of the "agent that the plaintiff contemplated seizing the goods on the farm, treating them as belonging to Buckley, and he accordingly gave the plaintiff notice that the farm, stock, and crops had all been surrendered to Lord Stamford in consideration of the rent due and accruing. Notwithstanding that notice the plaintiff came with a number of roughs and endeavoured to effect a seizure of the property on the farm. That invading force was met by several persons in the interest of Lord Stamford, and the plaintiff was prevented from carrying off any of the property except the horses, the sub- ject of the present action. The horses were removed to the defendant's stables, and the defendant gave them up to the agent on getting Lord Stamford's in- demnity. The only fact that gave the plaintiff the fragment of a case was this—ln December Mr. Cocks suc- ceeded Mr. Greenwood as agent to Lord Stamford, and Mr. Cocks and the solicitor, apparently not knowing the details of the arrangement at the sale, and fhinking it requisite that Lord Stamford should have further security, took a bill of sale from Beckley for property, including the three horses. That came to the knowledge of the plaintiff, who, he imagined, concluded that as Buckley was purporting to assign the property of Lord Stamford in December, 1881, it was Buckley's to assign, and he accordingly resolved on the seizure. The bill of sale then executed was undoubtedly inconsistent with the transaction at the auction, but he (the learned counsel) pointed out at the trial that if the transac- tion at the auction was really genuine the property thereupon passed from Buckley to the purchaser, and that the fact of Buckley afterwards purporting to grant what he could not grant did not give him any title to the property. Notwith- standing the evidence, the jury in substance found that the transaction was a colourable sham all through, and he now submitted that their verdict could not be in any way sup- ported by the testimony.—Their lordships granted a rule nisi for a new trial.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting took place on Tuesday afternoon, at the Workhouse. There were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner. J. Lockwood, Messrs. R. Ashton, Andrews, G. Whitlow, W. Whitlow, Stokes, Wallington, Norman, Picker- ing. Highfield, Hazlehurst, Weir, Darbyshire, Canapkin, Midwood, Henry Linaker (clerk), and Mr. W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). Mr. R. ASHTON was voted to the chair, on the motion of Mr. ANDREWS.

THE AUDIT. A communication was read, from which it appeared that the Government auditor would attend the Poor Law Offices, Frodsbam, on the 6th proximo, at half-past two, for the par, posss of auditing the union accounts. THE NEW HOSPITAL : MR. NORMAN ON EASY GOING. GUARDIANS.

Mr. Twos. NORMAN submitted a report from the Hospital Committee, in reference to the completion of the building and connecting the sewer with the present system of sewer- lag, from which it appeared that a further sum of £6OO would be required. The master had suggested that the new hospital should be fenced, and that the male and female portions be divided by a wall six feet in height. Also that the dead-house be removed, and so altered as to prevent in- mates on the female side seeing what is going on in the dead-house. The committee inspected the premises, and it was resolved that the doors to the present dead-house be re- moved to the workhouse. The committee also agreed that the new entrance doors should ,be fixed in the outer wall, where the contractors had made a temporary entrance. The committee had asked the architects to give an estimate, and they left it with the Board to decide whether the fence was necessary and desirable. The question of the sewerage from the workhouse was considered, and it was resolved that it be recommended that the clerk write to the North Stafford- shire Railway Co., for the purpose of ascertaining if they would allow the drainage from the workhouse to be turned into the canal at the Bnncorn side of Preston Brook tunnel, the work to be done to the satisfaction of their engineer. The DEPUTY CLERE had a letter from the engineer's office of the railway and canal company, Stoke-upon-Trent, stat- ing that IN must decline to allow the sewage to be turned into the canal. The company found sewage a very great nuisance at the present. The Runcorn Union was sure not to be reduced in size, but rather increased, so that the nuisance would consequently become greater. This, of it- self, would be a sufficient reason to refuse the request, but there was another, viz, that it would be wrong in principle to permit the canal to be polluted, as one of the first things thatwould occur would be that soms officer of the Guardians, or other public body, would b_e instructed to take proceed- ings against them for causing a nuisance. If he could be of any assistance in giving facilities fur pipes to be laid across the cempany's property, in providing the sewage ivorks, he should be glad. Mr. RIGBY : That is what I expected. Mr. ANDREWS: Why was not all this considered when the contract was let? Mr. NORMAN: We did not go into all the details at the time. Why weren't you here to look after the matter? We have nothing more to do with attending to it than your- self. .

Mr. ANDREWS: The committee with which you are con- nected have had all to do with it. Mr. NORMAN: Well, I am only like you on the Visiting Committee; and Jam decidedly of opinion that those Guard- ians who will not attend the meetings of committees have no right to come here and pitch into those who have done so. (Hear, hear.) The speaker afterwards proceeded to say that 12 months ago, himself, the clerk, and other gentlemen were appointed to lock into the proposed sewerage for the building, which was estimated to cost about £6OO. They went to Preston and brought from that town a scheme which was not to cost more than between £2OO or £3OO. A reso- lution WaS passed that Mr. Bancroft's plans be thrown over, and a scheme by Mr. Charles Linaker, which was to cost a great deal less money, adopted. He had had some talk with Mr. C. Linaker, who said he would not have anything to do with the sewage scheme in any shape or form. Something must at once be done. They must not forget that the requirements in connection with the workhouse had largely increased. When the pace was built there were only about 50 inmates, and now there were something like 200. The sewage was really in a scandalous cc:adition. A committee had been appointed to look into the sewerage scheme some time ago; but, personally, he did not intend to have any- thing to do with it, for he was blamed by certain people for involving the Union in considerable expense. (A. laugh.) Notwithstanding all these sort of charges, he was prepared to maintain that he did his very best, according to his ability, to prevent the ratepayers being put to any unnecessary ex- pense. He moved that Messrs. Geo. Whitlow, Rigby, Mid- wood, Andrewe and Lowe be appointed a committee for the purpose of dealing with the sewerage question,—(laughter) —and then they would be able to see if they could come to any better decision in respect to it. Mr. W. WHITLOW: I do not see that the committee have done anything yet, and we cannot mend that which has never been started. (Laughter.) Mr. NORMAN: We have brought forward a scheme, sir. After some further discussien it was proposed by Mr. NORMAN that the report pass with the exception of that part relating to the separation walls. Mr. WALLINGTON asked if something simpler than a six feet wall would not answer the purpose mentioned in the re- port. _ _ _

Mr. ANDREWS; The place is more like a prison than any- thing else. Mr. Hazlehurst seconded the [nation, and said the question for consideration was whether they should have the new hospital in a hail finished state, or make it so that it would be a credit to them. There were always extras to a large work of such a description, and what was proposed to be done was not anything in the way of mere extravagance. Mr. ANDREWS enquired whether it was not very misleading, to the Board when items of such a character were not in- cluded in the estimates at first submitted for the work. Mr. NORMAN believed that the original estimates submitted by the architect, amounted to between £2,700, and £2,800; and in addition there was £l7O for the heating apparatus, and £llB for the removal af the engine house. Mr. ANDREWS remarked that there was no peace at the Board from one meeting to another, owing to some matter being brought forward, involving extra expense. Mr. NORMAN must say that he had never seen better work done by bricklayers. Mr. ANDREWS: We are not talking about the quality of the work. Mr. MID WOOD said the extras were a very serious thing indeed. They were at first told the work would cost £2,400; and now they had got to £3,000. He certainly could not concur in the tone of Mr. Hazlehurst's remarks. e Mr. NORMAN replied that he should be glad if Mr. Mid- wood would tell him how they were to make room for 50 extra beds and spend only between £4OO and £5OO. He believed that the accommodation they were now providing would prove sufficient for between 30 and 40 years. Mr. Dansey,rsCrovernment Inspector, had lately visited the house, and spoken strongly about the contractors not getting on with their work. Mr. CHALLoNErtelesired to know if it was not a fact that the Board had appointed the Building Committee specially for the purpose of dealing with this very matter. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that if Mr. Midwood had attended the meetings of the committee, he would have known what was being done, and any objections which he might have desired to make could have been considered. Perhaps if Mr. Midwood had not been absent at several meetings of the committee, he would have been able to save some of the money it was now proposed to spend! Mr. MIDWOOD said he made the necessary enquiries as to £4OO extra being required, and on that point he was satis- fied, but now it was proposed to spend another £2OO. In reply to Mr. W. Whitlow, who said he was always given to understand that it was not original estimates that paid the builder but extras, Mr. NORMAN said the work to be done would be charged for according to a schedule of prices in the original contract. The resolution in favour of the adoption of the report was i passed unanimously. Mr. DARBYSHIRE, whilst in favour of a partition wall being put up, said the Board ought not to sanction any such large item of expense for the work as was suggested. Mr. RIGBY also objected to the sum proposed to be spent. The consideration of the question was left over. MR. CHALLONER AND MR. NORMAN ON "THE GRUMBLERS." Mr. NORMAN again moved the appointment of a commit- tee to look after the sewerage, as given above. Mr. CHALLONER : I second that. (Laughter.) Mr. ANDREWS : I shall never act, even if you keep my name on the committee. Mr. RIGBY : Will a member, if he cannot agree with his colleagues, be allowed to retire and throw up the sponge ? (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: I should think so, at any time. Mr. MIDwOOD : I must beg to withdraw my name. . Mr. MIRY: Yes, and you may withdraw mine. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. CHALLONER : Yes, this is always the way. Here we have a lot of men, including some of the biggest grumblers upon the Board, who will not take hold of the work, but who will criticise to any extent. You ought certainly to take your fair share of the work by going upon the com- mittees of the Board. Mr. RIGBY : Well done; go into us. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Mnewome : I work as hard as any member of this Board, and I am put upon as many committees as it is thought desirable to place me upon. My reason for with- drawing my name in this particular case, is that I find a good deal of fault in respect to the action which has been taken about this matter. Mr. NORMAN said he was, perhaps, as large a ratepayer as most men in the Runcorn Union, and he had worked for it as bard as any member of the Board, but his reward ap- peared to that of being branded with foul names. It was only a month ago that Mr. Whitlow told him the Runcorn Guardians were always getting the Union into some scrape or another! Mr. ANDRF,WS (to Mr. Norman): Build a workhouse for yourself, and stop on the other side of the brook! Mr. NORMAN: I should be very glad if that were done. Mr. ANDREWS: Well you had something to do with it

when the point was decided. Mr. HAZLEHURST : I do not consider it fair that gentle- men should allow themselves to be nominated for the posi- tion of Guardians, and refuse to act on committees. When they permit themselves to be nominated, it is understood they are willing to do the work of the Board. Mr. DARDYSIIIRE : I must say that ".1 feel it "to be found ita dt with so often, after I have been doing my best to Norther the interests of the Union, according to my ability, and if I followed the bent of my own feelings, I should with- draw from every committee. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. W. WHITLOW moved an amendment in favour of a committee of the whole Board being appointed to consider the question: and Mr. MiDwooD seconded the motion. Ten members voted for the amendment, and seven for the original resolution, which was, therefore, declared lost. The proceedings then terminated.
THE BEGGING NIIISANCE.—DanieI Gill was &Int to gaol for seven days for beErging in Victoria-road, on Tuesday evt ning.—P.C. Thompson proved the case.

ALLEGED BREACH OF THE PEACE. INTERFERING WITH POLICE OFFICERS.—MichaeI Kelly, of 48, Elizabeth-street, was charged with a breach of the peace; and P.C. Pitt with an assault upon Kelly, who was defended by Mr. Thomas Beasley.—P.C.'s Pitt and Snowden gave evidence to the effect that late on Saturday night, they were in Elizabeth- street, Moss-bank, when a boy came to them, saying that a man named Mulvey was beating his wife. They went to the spot, and found that Mulvey was causing considerable dis- turbance, they requested him to leave the house, and, as he would not do so they put him out into the backyard. Kelly then came up and shouted that they were murdering Mulvey. He interfered with them very rnua in the discharge of their duties, and they had ultimately to take him towards the p')lice station, as he would not give his proper name. They let him go upon his telling them his right address. —Mr. Beasley contended that the action would not have been brought against his client if the officer Pitt had not received information that he was to be summoned. Even assuming that what the witnesses said was true, a more trumpery and unfounded charge was never taken into a

court: The defendant saw the officers at the top of Mulvey, and as he heard him call out, he thought he was being abused. All Kelly did was b say "Don't kill the man," which was certainly no offer_ce in the eye of the law. He was instructed that almost before Kelly had said a word he was struck upon the jaw by Pitt, who wanted to fight with him. Kelly refused, and then Pitt told Snowden to put the handcuffs upon him, and in this condition he was taken a considerable way to the police station. At Messrs. Pilking- ton's railway gates defendant was released, and the two officers there smoked a pipe together.—Defendant was called, and gave evidence in support of Mr. Beasley's statement.— The Bench said they did not consider Kelly was altogether free from blame in the matter, as what he did amounted very nearly to an interference with the police. The night was, however, dark, and under the circumstances they would not call upon him to fird sureties. They hoped he would be careful to avoid anything of the kind in the future. Both summonses would be dismissed. IMPORTANT DECISION AS TO LOCAL BOARD RATES. A summons was heard in which the London and North- Western Railway Company were charged with non-payment of the balance of a certain rate. Mr. Thomas Beasley, who represented the Local Board, said the railway company were assessed at a considerable sum in respect of property owned in Widnes. Amongst other subjects of assessment was formerly an engine shed, which some time ago the company "determined to disestablish" and build a new one. This was accordingly done, after which the overseers went to look at the erection, and amended the valuation list. An amendment of the dis- trict poor rate followed, and the shed was assessed in the in- creased sum of £2O. The objection raised by the company was that they were assessed in respect to both the old and the new shed. Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, produced the copy of the general district rate, laid on.the 9th August last year. The company were served with the rate in Septem- ber, and an amended demand note was afterwards handed them in December.
Mr. Spencely, magistrates' clerk, pointed out that more than six months had elapsed since the rate was first de- manded, and this, he believed, invalidated any claim to re- cover.

Mr. Beasley contended that the first demand was not a legal one, as it was incorrect. He quoted a case in which the West Derby Local Board had sought to recover certain private improvement expenses. The matter came before the County Court judge, and it was proved that two demands had been served upon the property owners. It was held that the second demand overrode the first. The jurisdiction and powers o; that police court were for all purposes like that, to all intents the same as a County Court. Mr. Spencely : The jurisdiction is given to this court by statute, which expressly limits the time within which the demand for the rate must be made. You have a special court erected for a special purpose, with a limited time in which to exercise that purpose, and the time having gone by, there is no cause of action. After a short legal argument of no public interest, Mr. Spencely said Mr. Beasley had already proved, by his own witness, that the first demanl for the rate was made in Sep- tember of last year, and if there was anything further of in- terest to place before the court on the matter, the Bench would like to be put in possession of it. In reply to certain questions, Mr. Allen said he sent the corrected demand because there were some errors in the first. Mr. Beasley said the amnunt in dispute was the balance of an account of £3OO odd, and it was included with some 15 or 16 other items. Mr. Spencely : I don't see that it is a balance at all, but a specific rate. Mr. Rigby, late rate collector, was then put into the box, but it was not thought necessary to examine him. The Bench dismissed the summons, and declined to grant an appealfor a case as to whether they had jurisdiction as to the demand made in December.

THE ALLEGED BRUTAL KICKING CASE.—COMMITTAL OF THE ACCUSED.—John Fitzharris was brought up on remand, charged with unlawfully wounding Wm. Myers. The only fresh evidence taken was that of the wife of Christopher Maddocks, who said that on the evening of the 15th April, at about six o'clock, she heard a noise near her front door. Some angry words passed between the complainant, the prisoner, and his brother. She saw Wm. Fitzharris knock the complainant down, and kick him in the chest. The prisoner John Fitz- bards was standing by. She told the men that it was enough to "leather " Myers without kicking him.—Sergt. McGregor proved apprehending the prisoner, who did not reply to the charge.—Mr. W. T. Husband, who appeared for the defence, contended that his client, who was not proved to have committed the offence, had been most unjustly kept in custodv.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, and admitted to bail.

STEALING BOOTS.—Mafgaret Kelly pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of boots, the property of John Mulroy, of Sutton's-lane, on Monday night, and she was ordered to pay a fine of 203., or, in default, be sent to gaol one month— Thomas Randles (11), Samuel Mercer (9), and Thomas McGreevy were charged with stealing two pairs of boots from the pawnshop of Mr. Horatio Syred, Waterloo-road, on Tuesday week. The goods were qbtained possession of by breaking through the warehouse wall. They were worth 12., and were pledged by one of the prisoners at the shop of Mr. J. B. Itnison, the one pair for 23. 6d. and the other for 33. 6d.--Each of the prisoners was sentenced to receive six strokes with the bitch rod.
