div.head: DUBLIN ASSASSINATIONS.
div.p: THE DUBLIN ASSASSINATIONS.

PULPIT REFERENCES. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. The Rev. T. Manton Armson preached at the Runcorn Parish Church on Sunday evening, and, after referring to the declaration of the Saviour, "The Prince of this world cornett, and bath nothing in me," proceeded to briefly speak of how contrary to such a state of mind was the disposition of the wicked men, who could plot and carry into execution the awful crime perpetrated in Dublin a few days ago, which had startled the entire civilized world, and convulsed England to its centre. Sympathy with the bereaved had been expressed from the palace to the cottage. ST. PAUL'S, RUNCORN. On Sunday evening, the Rev. George Hack preached at St. Paul's Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, to a large congregation. In concluding his discourse, he said it might truly be said that the whole country had received a terrible shock through the news of the cruel assassination which had occurred in Phcenix Park, Dublin. They could not find language strong enough to express their execration at the terrible murder. He was sure that he need not bespeak the prayers of that Christian congregation for the noble father, who, on the previous Thursday, followed to the grave a noble son, of whose abilities he was so justly proud. Neither need he bespeak their sympathies for the other relatives of Lord Cavendish, and of Mr. Burke, who had lost their lives by a most foul crime, which had caused so much sorrow and agony. Might he not also. say that night, that tide was a time when the Christian patriot should rise abovelhe political partisan, and when every Christian man and woman should, at the throne of grace, ask God to assist the Executive Government, who were now attempting, in the face of such terrible difficulties, to maintain law and order against the very demon spirit of lawlessness and crime? He knew of no politics in that pulpit ;—he had never adopted the course of bringing politics before a public congregation. Surely, however, he might say that the old man at the head of the Government, whatever might be their political feeling, had their sympathy and prayers that night. It was deeply to be regretted that upon the head ot Mr. Gladstone there should have come a sorrow so great, and upon his mind a difficulty se gigantic, now that he had passed the allotted span of human life. He was, therefore, sure they would be doing the right thing in saying, as a Christian congregation, " God bless the Prime Minister of England." But even amid the darkness there were some elements of encouragements. They could not but, be struck with the universality of the detestation which had been both felt and expressed with regard to this outrage. There had been manifested a great uprising of the British people, whose conscience had been outraged; and that people were saying to-day to all lawless men that the time had come when lawlessness must be a thing of the past, and assassina- tion must no longer befoul our fair fame. He had felt proud to witness the tender sympathy which the country had shown for the families which had been bereaved. He had also been delighted with the judicial attitude of the British people, who whilst they were in favour of the acoption of sharp measures for the punishment of the criminals, were never- theless, determined to continue in the work of trying to to remove every grievance of which Irish people might complain. We had no quarrel with the Irish nation, for we belonged to the same empire, and gripped hands as subjects of the same Queen. Their fervent prayer, therefore, was that out of this terrible evil there might come a great good, and out of this awful storm, a beautiful tranquility and calm. Surely all hearts would barn with love to Lady Frederick Cavendish, who, instead of breathing retaliation against the Irish people, was anxious that the policy which her husband went to Ireland to inaugurate, should be con- tinued, saying that she should find it her dearest consolation if out of her great affliction should come blessing and pros- perity for the Irish people. Might God bless our country, and bring to us peace and prosperity ! PARISH CHURCH, WIDNES. Preaching at this church, on Sunday morning, the Rev. W. H. Duggan, curate, briefly referred to the tragedy. He said that we should be lacking as a people did we not take the opportunity of expressing our detestation of the cowardly act perpetrated eight days ago. Time need not be taken up in speaking of the scene of the tragedy, for with that, un- fortunately, all. were familiar. They could only earnestly hope that the cowardly assassins would soon be tracked by human justice; and also that the bereaved might receive Ernfort from Him who alone could give it! At the evening service, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, 'leer of Widnes, ministered at the same edifice, and touched upon the; ,subject incidentally, whilst preaching upon the ascension. It I'CP, he said, a characteristic of our common humauity to dwell in lingering WY° 90 the last smile, the last epoch, or the closing words of lives now gone from It was in this spirit that we found ourselVes taking up our morning papers, and dwelling upon all that they told us of the closing actions of the late Chief Secretary for Ireland. How we looked for his words, evidently so few and so sparingly given.to us; and we could but be convinced that many hearts at Chatsworth were feeling the truth of this, and that the voice whose echo had not yet died in their memories was still before them in their deep and pitiable bereavement. The thought that the Chief Secretary went on that solemn Friday night, as a man determined to do his duty, only intensified the thrill which had passed from the the heart to the very extremities of the Empire. The fact that he had been stricken down as a servant and represen- tative.of our country only tended to add to the feeling of indignation for the whole act by which he had met his death ; whilst the assertion made that he was bearing the olive branch of peace, only deepened the emotion Still dear to us, was the remembrance that the deceased, like many another hero, died almost with the words on his lips, "I go at the call of duty." In conclusion, the speaker said he had read of one of world-wide fame who came and fell in the cause of duty, who, God and man, was smitten down not merely by the sudden stroke of the assassin, but who was even at the present time wounded by weapons which cut deeper than steel—even the cruel words of malicious men!

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, litUNCORN. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor of this place of wor- ship, made a special reference to the assassination in his evening sermon, which as preached from the appropriate text, " Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked ; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity." (Psalms lxiv, 2 v.) Having briefly described the principal incidents of the assassination, the preacher teid that Lord Frederick Cavendish was new to his official work in Ireland when the unhappy event occurred, having been, in harness little more than 24 hours. The mission of the deceased nobleman to Ireland was one of peace. It was well known that his appointment expressed the firm intention of the Government to pursue a policy of conciliation; and almost the last offi- cial act of his life was to complete, in conjunction with Earl Spencer, the necessary arrangements for the release of every suspect in Ireland, except eight, who were confined, on charges of committing crime, or treason-felony. He went to the Irish people seeking to geather all the distressed and oppressed under his protection, but "they would not," and no sooner did he make his appearance than they thrust through and took his inheritance. It had been the lot of England to lament the decease of many a young statesman, whose death had been hastened by overwork in the service of the State. He, however, 'thanked God that it was seldom the country was called upon to weep for one whose life had been cut short by the knife of the assassin. Although political ex- citement often ran higher, in our land, and the animosity of opposing parties was exceedingly bitter, yet it never ap- proached murder by a long way. The stoutest antagonists in the political arena could meet on the most friendly terms when the fight was over. He believed he was correct in saying that not since the murder of Perceval, then First Lord of the Treasury, seventy years ago, had the assassina- tion of a statesman disgraced the annals of English history. It was not surprising that when the report of the tragedy became whispered abroad, every Priton felt dumbfounded, and, as it were, seized with a feeling of stupefaction—some- thing akin to paralysis. When, however, the details of the event were published, with an account of the horribly mutilated appearance of the bodies, stupe- faction turned into intense indignation, and the most utter loathing of soul was felt for the miserable and cowardly ruffians who had committed the deed. This, then, was his justification for speaking on the subject that evening. Had the murder been one similar to those so frequently com- mitted in this country, he should not have thought it worth his while to dwell upon the subject for a moment, but the crime was altogether of so exceptional a character, and it had occasioned such genuine and widespread sorrow, that not to denounce such an atrocity, and endeavour to make it impossible in the future, seemed to invoice a degree of indifference which, in a minister of Christ, was most reprehensible. Where high-minded and honourable men were holding the offices of State, and some of their number were suddenly struck down by the band of villainy,it behoved a Christian minister to speak boldly in their defence, and denounce those who shed innocent blood. Let them remeniber that in a town like that, the pulpit was the only place from which he could speak with any chance of being heard. In dealing with this matter they must be care- ful not to overlook the fact that in England the Govern- ment were responsible to the people ;—the soverign could not retain the members of the Government in office in spite of the people. If there were grievances of which the Ministry refused to take cognizance, the people could then turn them out of cffice. Such being the case, it was the greatest blunder—nay more, it was an act of insanity to re- ort to anything but argument and persuasion in order to obtain a redress of their grievances. Once they had truth and righteousness on their si le, all they needed to obtain the goal of victory was patience. Even allowing that the cause of Ireland was fully as bad as .the most zealous of her sons had depicted it, still that was not a reason why they should resort to other than moral force. If in future the ways of that unhappy country were righted, which they all hoped and prayed they would be she would owe no thanks to those who for months past had kept up a reign of terror, dealing out misery and death to the law-abiding part of the community. The reverend gentleman next urged the desir- ability of continuing the policy lately inaugurated by the present Government, and referred in touching tones to the letter written by Lady Cavendish on the subject. The blood of the martyrs was said to be the seed of the Church, and let them hope that out of the blood so profusely shed of late, there would arise a harvest of lasting peace and joy to Ireland. There was "something rotten " in the state of the sister isle ; and it was this rotteness that fed the fiendish spirits of revenge and jealousy. But in what did this rot- tenness consist? Ist, in a lack of patience to await the arbitrament of God. When there was injustice God would, sooner or later, bring it to light. Secondly, it consisted in the sophistical and jesuitical doctrine that the end justified the means, The language of men who dia such deeds aa

those of which he had been speaking was, "Let us do evil that good may come." Thirdly, it consisted in an utter in- capacity to appreciate the value of a human life; and, fourthly, in a spirit of general lawlessness. The remedy for these things was the gospel of the grace of God. When Irishmen had learned to take their Bibles in their hands in- stead of revolvers, they would have their grievances re- dressed in half the time which they would in any other way.

div.head: RTJNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RTJNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Dutton Workhouse. Mr. Robert Ashton occupied the chair, and there were also present the Revs. J. Lock- wood, J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. W. Whitlow, G-. Whit- low, Stokes, Wallington, Andrews, Pickering, Highfield, Hazleburst, Weir, Darbyshire, Midwood, Campkin, Chatloner, Rigby, Henry Linaker (Clerk), and W. H. Linaker (Deputy Clerk).

THE ADVANCE TO APPLETON TOWNSHIP. A letter was read from. the Local Government Board, re- questing to be furnished with a statement as to the advance of £2,000 (patt of £2,921) for the purpose of works of sewerage and sewage disposal, for the contributory plac!, known as Appleton. The CLERK said the necessary Statutory declaration on the matter had been made by him. IMPORTANT MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.-EPIDEMIC OF

div.head: MEASLES.
div.p: MEASLES.

Mr. John Grant Bride, (medical officer) wrete on the 13th ,1 Inst. to the Chairman, stating that he bad to report anl epidemic of measles at Antrobus. Over 29 cases were known up to that date. Most of them had been visited by him, and full instructions as to cleanliness and isolation given to those in charge of the children suffering from the disease. It was very gratifying for him to pay a small tribute to the intelligence of the people of the village and neighbourhood. His suggestions and directions were equally well received. More readiness and anxiety to do all that was needful in such cases, he never before ex- perienced. After conferring with the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the vicar of Antrobus, and Mr. Coppock, the master of the schools, (whose child was also suffering from measles) he determined to write to the Clerk to the Authority requesting him to send a recommendation for the schools at Antrobus to be closed for a short term. This was done, and the re- commendation was at once complied with. He was happy to state that no further extension had occurred, and that all the cases were doing well. Measles had also broken out at Appleton and Helsby, but in each township the outbreak was limited to one case. He regretted to report another death from scarlatina at Newtown (Frodsham), in the case of the son of Roger Davies. The disease also existed at the house of David Hughes, in the same street, Newtown. Another case of scarlatina had come to his knowledge as existing at Halton. Whooping cough had also broken out in a cottage occupied by a man named Hignett, at Quarry Houses, Manley. He had done his utmost to repress these various outbreaks. Opinion in Frodsham seemed to indicate extreme measures on the part of the authority. He, how- ever, submitted that nothing harsh had been done; and moreover, individual interests should never be weighed in the same balance with remedial measures in sanitary matters.

div.head: CLAIM BY MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS.
div.p: THE CLAIM BY MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS.

Mr. CHALLONER reported that the deputation appointed in respect to this matter had an interviaw with the execu- tors at Mr. Linaker's office. The executors asked £BO, but ultimately agreed to accept £65. It wa4 also agreed that the Authority should pay the expenses, which it was said would not be £5. As to the expenses of the deputation, he should be satisfied if the meeting agreed to allow them two guineas each. Hehad pleasure in moving the adoption of the report. Mr. ANDREWS seconded the motion. Mr. MIDWOOD wished to know if the bill of costs was ready as to the claim now under consideration.
The DEPUTY CLERK: No. Mr. MIDWOOD asked if the £2,879 given last Board meet- ing as the cost of the contract included the expenses of the clerk of works.

The CLERK said he had often stated that it would be a great assistance to him if gentlemen wishing to have infor- mation, as to any special matter, would intimate the fact to him. He was not able to give the information asked for that day. The DEPUTY CLERK: ;f2,800 odd is the amount of the engineer's estimate for doing the work. The CLERK (to Mr. Midwood): Will you give notice to produce all the accounts? Mr. MIDWOOD : No, I will not. The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Midwood, will you give notice to produce them at the next Board meeting? Mr. MinwooD: No.
The CLERK : We have neither the accounts or the ledgers here.

Mr. RIGBY suggested that the books and other matters ought to be stored at the Workhouse. The CLERK: It appears that Mr. Midwood, who has had so much to do with contracts, and told the Board at their meeting a month ago, that he know more about them than any member present, does not appear to know that tenders do not include the charge for a clerk of works! Mr. CHALLONER : There are the contractor's money, the cost of a clerk of the works, the engineer's costs, and various other little costs besides.

Mr. M IDWOOD : I think you will remember, Mr. Chair- man, that I asked for details in reference to this matter, and I thought I had been furnished with them, but I find I have only got a portion of them. I, therefore, want to know what they are.
't he CLERK : I( Mr. Midwood wishes to pursue a straight- forward course

Mr. MIDWOOD (warmly) : I always do pursue a straight- forward course, and as long as I am a member of this Authority I shall continue to do so ; and I will not be ac- cused by Mr. Linaker, or by any member of the Board, of not taking such a course! The CHAIRMAN said that the clerk could not carry all the union books to the workhouse every Board meeting, and he considered it would be better if Mr. Midv.'ood gave notice of such a question. The DEPUTY CLERK remarked that all the accounts in connection with Mr. Wright's matter would be in by next Board day. There was the claim made by Mr. Robert Ashton.

Mr. RIGBY moved that all the accounts in connection with the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship sewerage scheme should be produced at the next Board meeting. Mr. ANDREWS: It Will fill some of the ratepayers' pockets before it is done. _ _

Mr. MIDWOOD : R will empty some of them, you mean. Mr. CIIALLONER asked the members who had referred particularly to this question how it was that they had not tried to keep down the expenses relating to it from its very inception. For two years he had been engaged "fighting this question tooth and nail," but he found noone who would stand by his side during that time. In fact, he believed he was shunned in Frodsham, and Frodsham Lord- ship because of his action in respect to it; and they had members on that Board to-day who were grumbling at the accounts, and yet did not once support him when he was fightimg this battle almost alone. The matter ought to have been stopped when it was first considered, but the practice of several of the members was to let a project go on until it could not be stopped, "and then the row began." ;He hoped they would adopt his advice, and in the future exercise their faculties of criticism when a proposal was first submitted. Mr. RIGBY: I hope you are not referring to me. Mr. CHALLONER : I am referring to no one member par- ticularly. Mr. RIGBY : Well, you know I am an old member,

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Henry Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. Thomas.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Henry Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. Thomas.

AN OLD OFFENDER.—George Brown, a man who has been previously eonvicted, was fined 20s. and costs, or in default of payment one month's imprisonment, for having been drunk and disorderly in Church-street ou the 13th inst. STEALING Two PIGEONS.—James Bushell was charged with stealing two pigeons, value 25., the property of Henry Corrin, on the 13th inst.—The prosecutor said he was a blacksmith, living at 31, Rutland-street, and kept a number of pigeons in a cote in the back yard. On the previous Wednesday evening the prisoner came to his house, and asked if he had a strange pigeon in his possession. He told him he had not, and allowed him to look in the cote, as he said he wanted to buy some pigeons. Bushell then left. About nine o'clock on Saturday night he (witness) locked up his pigeons safe, and counted them, finding there were 21. Amongst them was the one produced in court, which he missed at eight o'clock on Monday morning, and another now in the possession of Sergeant \Valley. The last-named was a dark blue one, and returned to the cote about a quarter to twelve on the day it was stolen. He gave information to the police, and afterwards went to the prisoner's with Sergt. Walley. Bushell asked hint "not to be hard with him, and he would pay for the pigeons." He found that the door of the cote had been pulled down.—P.C. Noden gave evidence to the effect that he went to the prisoner's house in Bridgewater-strset, with Sergeant Walley, and found the two stolen pigeons. Prisoner said he had bought them from a man named James Dunbobbin.—ln reply to the usual charge, prisoner denied having stolen the pigeons, and said they must have entered the cote without his knowledge. He had lost birds in a s:milar way himself.--He was fined 20s. and costs, or in default of payment one month's imprison- ment.
SETTING A HORSE ON FIRE. THE DANGERS OF AMATEUR HORSE DOCTORDM.

William Cunningham, a man about 40 years of age, employed as an ostler, was charged with having cruelly ill-treated a mare by setting fire to it on the 29th ult.—Mr. Osmond Harper, an officer of the R.S.P.C.A., living at Altrincham, appeared to prosecute, and btietly opened the case.

Alfred Elwell, a young man employed as a boatman by Messrs. Price and Son, of Round Oak, Staffordshire, who gave his evidence in what was, apparently, a very unwilling manner, said be was the owner of the mare which was used to tow his vessel. For some time the animal had been suffering from skin disease, and on the 29th ult. he came to Runcorn and took it to Mr. Heywood's stables, near Waterloo-road. On the Thursday after he arrived, defend- ant told him that if he would get some paraffin oil and rub the mare well with it, it would cure the skin disease. On the night of the 29th ult. he followed out this advice, and rubbed the animal with the oil in the presence of a man named Roberts, his (witness's) sister, and defendant. He commenced to do so about nine o'clock, and defendant re- mained in the stable all the time. The first remark which Cunningham made was to ask him what sort of oil he had got, and he told him paraffin, on which he inquired whether it would "blaze." Defendant was told it would, on which he observed that the statement was not true, and poured some upon the ground, and struck a match, with which he tried to ignite the liquid. The match died out, on which defendant lighted another, with which he set fire to the mare's tail. The flame passed along the entire of the back and sides, and he rushed to the top of the stall for the pur- pose of setting the animal at liberty. She was burned very badly, and the only observation defendant made on seeing how cruelly he bad punished her was to the effect that he wondered she had not been worse injured, as there. was a quantity oi straw at the top of the stable. .The mare had since been killed, The Chairman : How is it that she has been destroyed P Mr. Harper I saw it was impossible for her to recover and I suggested she should be killed, as she was in such a dreadful condition.

Mr. Johnson (deputy magistrates' clerk) to witness: Was the man sober at the time? I believe he was.—Did you give him any authority to do this? No, sir.—Did you ad- vise him at all? No, sir.—Did you consent to his setting fire to the horse? No, sir.—Did you hear him say any- thing when he set fire to the mare's tail? No, sir. In re-examination by Mr. Harper, witness said no objec- tion was made to the mare being put in the stable owing to her being affected with skin disease. It was quite true that something had bern said about the paraffin oil taking out the disease by burning the hair without injuring the mare. This was the only horse he owned, and he had not yet com- pleted paying the sum he agreed to give for it. Since the occurrence, he had been out of work owing to the mare having been destroyed. By defendant: It is true that when I said I had nothing to keep me on if I left the animal in the stable, you told me I could let it stay in the stable until it was better. Mary Ann Elwell, sister to the last witness, gave corro- borative evidence.

Mr. T. R. Hartley, officer of the R.S.P.C.A., said he saw the mare in Mr. Heywood's stables on the 2nd inst., and it was burned from the hock down to ties withers. The skin was off in the places where it had been burned, so that the muscles could be distinctly seen. The animal was a grey one, and somewhat aged, but appeared to have a very strong constitution. On seeing defendant, he asked him how he same to do such a stupid thing as to set fire to a dumb animal, on which he said "I don't know; but it is done now, and I must make the best of it." He next said to him "Wets not you aware that hair would blaze without any oil being put to it ?" and defendant replied "Well, no one told me it would blaze, and I didn't think it would." Mr. Harper next made a statement to the effect that he laid the information in the case, and saw the mare in Mr. Heywood's stable. He appeared' to be an animal which would be very useful for boat purposes. He described the state of the mare, which, he remarked, was in a dreadful state, and no veterinary surgeon had been called in to see it. The smell arising from the poor ccreature was very offensive, and as the defendant was not in a position to have it "slung up" and properly attended to, he suggested it should be destroyed, which was accordingly done. Defend- ant was present when he visited the place, s.nd saii the mare had been set on fire by gas, and not through his in- strumentality. Cunningham denied the truthfulness of the officer's state- ment about the gas. He went on to say that his attention was called to the animal by, a boatman, who said it had no right in the stable, as it was suffering badly from the itch. He merely told the witness Elwell that "he had beard if paraffin oil was rubbed on a horse it would not set fire to it, but draw the disease out." He was quite "as much put out" at what happened as the owner of the animal and his companions, who were perfectly willing the experiment should be tried.

Mr. Wm. Heywood, the defendant's employer, was called and said the man had worked for him about four months. He had always found him steady; and the statement which Inspector Harper had made as to his being in drink at the time the alleged offence was committed, was altogether false. Indeed, he had never seen defendant in drink. Mr. Harper: It was suggested to me by the witnesses; I was not there.

The witness wished to give an opinion upon what had taken place, on which Mr. Harper said: You are not here to offer an opinion, but to give evidence. It is for the Bench to form an opinion upon the case. Witness said the owner of the horse was very blameable for putting it in the stable, as "it was nearly eaten up with disease."

The CHAIRMAN said the magistrates considered the case fully proved against defendant, and it was the worst he had ever known itf his life. Defendant would be committed to Knutsford for two months with hard labour.
Mr: Heywood: Will your worships be kind enough to accept a tine, as defendant is a man with a large family.
The Chairman said the Bench could not do so.

Mr. Harper remarked that he might have asked the magistrates to grant compensation up to £lO, but as they had committed defendant to prison, the aspect of the matter was altered. The question would, however, probably come before a civil court for consideration.

Mr. Johnson: If that point were taken into consideration, the application would have to be separate from the present proceedings. Mr. Heywood (to the Bench) : Will you grant me a sum- mons against the boatman for bringing the horse into my stables?

Mr. Johnson: If you will apply at my office, and show me under what Act you require the summons, I will grant it you. This terminated the proceedings in the case. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit and C. W. Hazlehurst.

A CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY.—John Fishwick, about 22 years of age, was charged with stealing six pigeons, the property of Samuel Kennerly, of Weston, on the 16th inst. —Prosecutor said he saw the pigeons safe on Monday night, and those now produced in court were his.—Mr. Jackson, proprietor of Wilson's Hotel, deposed to the pigeons being brought to his house and sold there on Tuesday even- ing.—Prisoner was remanded Until yesterday, when he was brought up 192 fore Mr. S. B. Chadwick and discharged, as the witness was not able to SR ear he was the man seen at Wilson's Hotel.

PEESCOT WESLEYAN AxsrvuasAnY.—The seventy- second anniversary in connection with the above place of worship was held on Sunday last when the Rev. Wm. Humphries, of Manchester, preached morning and evening sermons in the Wesleyan Chapel, Eeeleston-street, Prescot. The congregations were good at both services and the ser- mons most impressive. In the afternoon a well rendered service of song entitled "Home, sweet home," was given by the Chapel choir, the connective passages being read by the Rev. W. Humphries. The choral portions of the morning and evening services were given by the Sunday school children in a very careful and pleasing manner. The col- lctiens which were in aid of the Sunday school funds amoumted to £l3 4s. Mr. R. Atherton, of Ecelestou-street, organist of the chapel, presided at the organ with his accus- tomed taste.

div.head: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
On Sunday, hymns and music suited to . the occasion, notably the hymn, .

_ God moves in a mysterious way His wonders to perform, were sung, and the special prayer for immunity from wars and tumults was used. The Vicar preached on the subject of the Phcenix Park tragedies both morning and evening. In the morning he took his text from Genesis iv, 8., "Where is Abel thy brother? The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground," upon which he remarked how the passions of men inclined them to deviate from the path of duty. At the close of his sermon the preachet said: And here I must conclude with a few remarks as to the cause of my having chosen the subject of the sixth com- mandment this morning. Saturday, the 6th of May, 1882, will ever be marked in the annals of the British Empire as the day which witnessed a crime absolutely unparalleled, even in the present blood-stained age. The news which the wire brought from Dublin last night week, and which had been authenticated beyond all question on Sunday morning last, when peaceful English folk were going to church, was so thoroughly startling that it was almost beyond belief, and yet in its issue it was found to be exact in all its ghastly details, and the lifeless bodies of Lord Frederick Cavendish, second son of the Duke of Devonshire, and Mr. Burke, who was a member of the Roman Catholic Church, of ancient family, and heir to a baronetcy, lying in the Chief Secretary's Lodge, were the sad vouchers of the truth of the story with which we are now only too sadly familiar. The character of the crime, its audacity, its hideous cruelty, and its far-reaching and unknown circum- stances; the noble sacrifice of the two victims, the one literally grey in the service of Ireland, and the other taking up a post of danger and difficulty at a critical moment, simply from a desire to save the ill-fated country from further exhibitions of a revolutionary spirit. I must not, however, said the Vicar, enter into particulars, for news- papers of the past week have already supplied you with them, but there is one aspect of the awful calamity which it seems to us ought not to be left out of sight, and it is, that although in this case public officials of high rank have been cruelly murdered yet the act is only a repetition of that which has been per- mitted to go unpunished month after month, week after week, with wearisome iteration, for now nearly two years. We must not—we cannot—be blind to the fact that such murders of those of Lord Montmorres and Mrs. Smythe were, in cold blooded cruelty, as foul as the crime on Sat- urday, and that the fate which has so unfortunately over- taken Lord Frederick and Mr. Burke is, in reality, only the natural sequence of the, let us say, apparent forgetfulness by the Government of a long chain of murderous deeds, to which this only adds another link. The blow has at last come home to the Government, and it has been felt again and again in many a desolated home, from which cries for retribution and justice have gone up; but only to be answered by official expressions of regret. The bring in a bill for the prevention of a repetition of such crimes is, of course, nothing more than the circumstances of the case require and demand; but the ruined homes and bereaved families of numberless persons, less exalted, perhaps, but not the less worthy of national sympathy and protection, have too long called, yet called in vain for some such legis- lation until now. The TicaT urged his hearers to unite in the national expression of sincere sympathy with the be- reaved ones, and again to pray, "That it may please Thee to succour, help, and comfort all that are in tribula- tion," and especially those who are so through this dire calamity.

div.head: RUNCORN IRISHMEN ON THE OUTRAGE.
div.p: RUNCORN IRISHMEN ON THE OUTRAGE.
On the evening of the 12th inst., a meeting of representa- tive Irishmen, which had been called very hastily, was held in St. Edward's Schools, Runcorn. Mr. John Kelly pre- sided.

The CHAIRMAN said they had met to denounce the crime which bad darkened Ireland, and to express their sympathy with the friends of the bereaved. He characterised the murder as one of the foulest deeds which had ever been committed.

Mr. J. P. COLEMAN proposed, and Mr. T. WILLIAMSON seconded, the following resolution :—" That this meeting cf Irishmen assembled in Runcorn desires to express the deepest abhorrence of the cowardly and atrocious murder of Lord Frederick Cavendis3ll and Thomas Henry Burke, and ex- presses tho earnest wish that the perpetrators may be speedily brought to justice." Mr. JOHN HARTY remarked that Lb supported the mottnn with reluctance, as, owing to his connection with the civil service, his motives might be misconstrued by some. He was sure that the black-hearted villains whose crime had aroused the world's honest indignation belonged to no section of Irishmen, but rather to a clique of imported cutthroats, whose occupation it was, and always had been, to live and fatten on the heart's blood of their country. The motion was put and carried unanimously, the audience rising to their feet and standing for a few moments.

Mr. GOODALL, in moving the .next resolution, strongly condemned the outrage, which he considered had done much to rob Ireland of the proud title of one of the most hospitable countries in the world. He moved, "That this meeting of Irishmen in Runcorn offers in heartfelt sincerity to the relatives of the deceased gentlemen an assurance of their profound sympathy in their sorrow, and assures them that all Irishmen throughout the country will do all in their power to render more certain the apprehension of the cowardly assassins who have done so much to bring disgrace on poor Ireland." Mr. HILL seconded the motion, and observed that the Marquis of Hartington had expressed his belief that the deed was not committed by Irishmen. The resolution was carried non dis; and after a compli- mentary vote had been passed to the chairman, the proceed- ings terminated.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day afternoon, Mr. Marsh ptesiding. There were also pre- sent Revs. T. Chambers, Barnacle, Finegan, Messrs. Hall, Fidler, Leigh, Gerrard, Fisher, Paris, Tyrer, Newsome, Leatherbarrow, Jackson, Buckley, Syder, Eatock, Meadows, P. Lorigton, Kenwright, Birchall, Birch, aud Tuson.

div.head: WIDNES ARREARS.
div.p: THE WIDNES ARREARS.

The CLERK stated that the balance in the hands of the treasurer was £3,063 4s. 11d. The Widnes overseers had paid in the exact amount of the county rate precept, £1,105 125., and he asked for a cheque for that amount to be for- warded to the county treasurer. The reason he asked the Guardians to draw a cheque for the amount was that last Saturday morning he received a telegram from county treasurer asking if the overseers had paid the money. He did not know that the money bad been paid, but he learnt that they had paid it, and Mr. Harrison, the union treasurer, wanted a cheque for the same to be forwarded to the county treasurer.

The CHAIRMAN : How was it paid in? The CLERK: To the credit of the township of Widnes. Mr. HALL said that the Guardians had-from time to time brought pressnre to bear upon the overseers of Widnes with but little effect, and now that pressure had been brought to bear from another quarter the money bad been paid into the union, and the clerk now asked for a cheque to be forwarded to the county treasurer. He should slid "no" to that; it must be paid to the union's account.
Mr. TYRER: it is to our own account. Mr. HALL: Then let it remain there.

The CLERK said the new auditor insisted upon the county rate precept being included in the general order, and the overseers had no right to be furnished with particulars of the caunty rate charges due from them. His impression was that the overseers could compel the Guardians to hand the money over to the county treasurer. Mr. LEIGH dissented from this, and mentioned an instance in which The overseers were ordered to pay the money. The CLERK said he had given his opinion of the law upon the subject. The Guardians having issued a separate pre- cept to the overseers that precept having been met by the overseers, the Guardians could not withhold that money from the county treasurer or apply it to the general purposes of the Union.

Mr. HALL said that they bad all along been putting pres- sure on the overseers of Widnes, who had, or whose assistant overseer had, made unfaithful promises that the money should be paid. In fact the rate should have been cleared off last March. Pressure was now brought to bear upon them for the county rate, and they as much as said " We will pay as we like." It was unfair to the other townships of the Union that the arrears of poor rate were not paid up, seeing that the money could be raised from the county. Rev. J. BARNACLE made use of similar expressions....

Mr. MEADOWS said that was quite right what was said by Mr. Hall and Mr. Barnacle, but they could not get over the fact that the money had been asked for a certain purpose, and they (the Guardians) were bound to pay it. Mr. BARNACLE: How is it money can be found for this,. and not for us.

The CLERK : I don't know ; I think the Guardians are suite as much to blame as the overseers. It the Guardians- had taken steps the same as the county authorities, Widnes would not have been in the position she now is. / The coanty requires the Guardians to pay this sum, the precept has been issued to the overseers, an the money has been paid into our hands. Although precepts for the county charge have been issued for a number of years separately to- the townships, the Guardians have no right to issue such separate precepts. If the money had not been paid by the overseers, the county authorities have an equal remedy against the Guardians, for they could go into the township if they liked, and charge 2s. in the, pound for collecting the money. If you don't pay that money Over to the overseers they can make you, Mr. LONGTON said now that matters were getting into shape in Widnes he thought they would have very little difficulty in future. They had already killed one or two assistant overseers in Widnes. They certaiuly killed one of the best assistant overseers, Mr. Fearn, and he was told that Mr. Rigby was heartbroken through fighting against the tide. He believed now they had got a man that would pull them up. There was no doubt the Guardians had not done their duty as they ought to have done. 1171 r. PARIS: Rigby had too many irons ih the fire. Mr. LONGTON: He had too much work, and he worked on Sundays as well to get things together. The Rey. T. CHAMBERS said that as they had entered into a promise, the Guardians were bound by honour to help the

ao t 01 overseers to collect the money, so as to Eget them trouble. IN THE HIGH COURT OF- JUSTlCE.—Chancery Division.—ln the matter of the Companies' Acts, 1862 and 1867, and in the matter of the Sankey Brook and Abhtons Green Collieries Company, Limited. The CREDITORS of the above-ramed company are required, on or before the sth day of June, 1887, to send their names and addresses, and the particu- lars of their DEBTS or CLAIMS, and the names and addresses of their solicitors (if any), to WILLIAM RICHARDSON, of Strand- road, Preston, in the county of Lancaster, Accountant, the official liquidator of the said company; and it is so required by notic3 in writing from the said official liquidator, are by their solicitors to come in and prove their said debts or claims at the Chambers of the Honourable Mr. Justkie Chitty, in the Royal Courts of Justice, Strand, in the county of Middlesex, at such time as shall be specified in such notice, or in default thereof they will be excluded from the benefit of any distribution made before such debts are proved. Monday, Ihe 19th day of June, 1882, at Eleven o'clock in the forenoon, at the said Chambers, is appointed for hearing and adjudicating upon the debts and claims.—Dated this 4th day of May, 1882.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.— NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that JOHN DOLBY, Esq., District Auditor, will attend at the Commissioners' Offices, Bridge-street, Runcorn, at half-past nine o'clock in the fore- noon, on Monday, the sth day of June, 1882, for the purpose of AUDITING the ACCOUNTS of the said Commissioners for the year ended the 25th day of March last; and notice is hereby further given, that the Accounts will be deposited in the office of the Commissioners, and be open to the inspection of all persons interested for seven clear days before the said Audit. May 11th, 1882. W. BROOKES, Eecretary.

RUN CORN AND DISTRICT STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY. Another APPROPRIATION will be made in BWIZESDA SCHOOL ROOM, RUNCORN, At Eight o'clock on WEDNESDAY EVENING NEXT, MAY 24, 1882. Members can participate by joining before that date, and paying four weeks' subscription. Entrance Fee, One Shilling per Share; Subscription, Sixpence per Week. Members enrolled and full information given every Monday Evening, from Seven o'clock 0 Half-past Eight at 10, Church Street, Runcorn. 'WM. HANDLEY, Secretary.

Tenders to be lodged at the offices not later than eleven o'clock on Friday, the 26th inst. The com- mittee do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gasworks, Warrington, 12th May. 1882.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—The Sanitary Com- mittee invite TENDERS for the purchase of all Horse Manure made at Corporation Stables, Town Hall, for twelve months, commencing Ist July next. The quantity averages about three tons fifteen cwt. weekly, and the purchaser will be required to remove the same regularly every week. Tenders to be sent to me, endorsed "Tenders for horse manure," not later than 21st June next. RALPEI NORMAN, Inspector. Nuisance Inspector's Office, T3wn Hall, Warrington.

COAL AND CANNEL.—The Lymm Local Board are prepared to receive TENDERS for the supply of such quantities of Coal and Cannel, to be delivered at their Gasworks in Lymm during the year ending 30th June, 1883, as may be required. The probable quantities required are about 500 tons of coal and 300 tons of cannel, but the Board reserve the right of increasing or decreasing the quantities mentioned. The p3rson whose tender is accepted will be required to enter into a contract, form of which can be seen at the Board Office any Tuesday or Friday afternoons. Tenders to be sent to the undersigned on or before the 30th instant, and endorsed Tender for coal and cannel." The Board do not bind them- selves to accept the lowest or any tender, T. J. RIDGWAY, Law Clerk to the Local Board, Lymm. Lymm, 12th May, 1882.
